column5: ROOT-CAUSE
column6: The ~13 MB/s leak is the SHIM's. With live flat at ~152900 and the table far from full, dropped-frees still climbed ~161k per 2^20 mallocs -> 1,250,111 in 95s. At 13 MB/s that is ~1 KB per dropped free: the entire leak, accounted for. Cause: xshim interposed only malloc/calloc/realloc, so pointers from strdup/strndup/memalign/posix_memalign/aligned_alloc/valloc never entered the live set and free() swallowed them as bogus.

column5: SOLVED
column6: In-game input needed a cursor-pin: the engine tracks the in-game cursor by ACCUMULATING SDL_MOUSEMOTION xrel/yrel, not by absolute position, so autopilot clicks (whose rel is computed from its own mouse_x/y, initialised 400,300) landed at an unknown offset. Menu clicks worked because the menu reads absolute SDL_GetMouseState. Pattern that works: "move 0 0" (over-large negative delta clamps the engine cursor at the origin), then "move X Y", then "click X Y", ~1.2s apart. Proof: the H key opened the Help overlay AND the "Welcome to Ancaria!" dialog advanced to "The Dream...", where three earlier attempts (Enter, Escape, bare click on OK) all left the log frozen. Keyboard was never broken in-game; only the mouse position was.

column5: RESOLVED
column6: Open question from row 7 answered STATICALLY, no runtime probe needed. The FAILED branch is `cmp DWORD PTR [ebp-0xfc],0 / je 0x8211d18` at 0x8210b91; [ebp-0xfc] is filled at 0x820e1cb from `call 0x815970c` with args (global table 0x8b8ad60, this->field_8). That lookup is: `shl eax,7` (type*128), `mov ax,WORD [eax+ecx+0x2a]` (row id), `test ax,ax / je return-NULL`; on success it scales the row id by 0x86 off a second base at [table+0x563018]. There is NO bounds check and NO special case for type 0 -- type 0 indexes row 0, whose id word is 0, so the lookup returns NULL and the message fires. The two candidate explanations therefore collapse to one: "type=0 FAILED" means the creature reached CalcResults with field_8 still UNSET. It is NOT an unpopulated table (the table is loaded; row 0 is simply the reserved empty entry). Same shape governs the sibling `gethitvalu () type=0 FAILED!` at 0x81f91c0. Remaining unknown is narrowed to: who writes field_8, and when relative to construction.

column5: FINDING
column6: The cCreatureHero constructor (0x81ea706; C1/C2 pair at 0x81eaa96, both storing vtable 0x8727e88 as their FIRST instruction, so there is no base-class ctor call -- matching RTTI, which records no base for this class) NEVER writes this->field_8. The only [reg+0x8] stores in its body, at 0x81ea931 and 0x81ea980, target the XOR-obfuscated globals 0x8906ce8/0x8906cec, not the object. So the type is left at whatever the allocator returned and is filled in later by whoever loads the creature record. CONSEQUENCE FOR THE SHIM: xshim zeroes every allocation, so an unassigned type reads back as exactly 0 -- meaning "type=0 FAILED" is a CLEAN, LOGGED failure only BECAUSE of our zeroing. With the 2005 allocator the same code path would read garbage into `shl eax,7` with no bounds check and index far outside the table. The zeroing converts a wild read into a diagnosable log line; do not "fix" it away.

column5: TRAP
column6: /tmp/full_disasm.txt (107 MB linear objdump of install/sacred, AT&T) is DESYNCED in the regions that matter and must not be trusted for addresses. Of the four anchors from the CalcResults work (0x8210b91, 0x820e1bd, 0x815970f, 0x81ea706) only the last appears in it at all, and there it decodes as `push (%eax)`. Cause: the linear sweep loses instruction alignment (e.g. it places a 6-byte insn at 0x8159708 spanning 0x815970c, which a `call 0x815970c` proves is a real function entry). Targeted `objdump --start-address=<call target>` is authoritative because a call target is a guaranteed boundary; the linear sweep is not. Re-verified 0x81ea706 that way: it is a genuine prologue (push ebp; mov ebp,esp; ...) that writes vtable 0x8727e88 at +0xf, matching linux-1.0.02-vtables.txt -- so the cCreatureHero ctor findings in rows 26/28 and REPORT.md 2.6 stand. Rule: anchor every disassembly on a call target or known entry; never quote an address out of a linear sweep.

column5: FINDING
column6: cCreatureHero is an EMBEDDED MEMBER of cCreature at offset +0x3a8, not a class in the polymorphic hierarchy. Chain: the only callers of the hero ctor twin 0x81eaa96 are 0x816b3d8 and 0x816b9d0, which ehframe_funcs.py places at +0x8c inside 0x816b34c..0x816b943 and 0x816b944..0x816bf3b -- two functions of identical size 0x5f7, i.e. cCreature C1/C2 ctor clones (0x816b34c writes vtable 0x8727dc8 = cCreature per linux-1.0.02-vtables.txt line 17). The call is `lea eax,[esi+0x3a8]; push eax` after `push esi; push edi`, so cCreatureHero::cCreatureHero(this=owner+0x3a8, edi, owner). This is the real explanation of the REPORT.md 2.3 anomaly "cCreatureHero shows only 1 virtual and no base, unlike every sibling" -- it is a small owned helper object, not a hierarchy member, so it has nothing to derive from. Corollary: the unset field_8 lives at cCreature+0x3b0, and the cCreature ctor does not write it either (after the hero ctor returns it writes [esi+0x57c]=0 and string members at +0x580/+0x58c).

column5: FINDING
column6: The CalcResults type chain is now closed end to end. Hero field_8 is absolute cCreature+0x3b0, and the cCreature ctor copies it from cCreature+0x10 on two branches (0x816b5cb/0x816b5ce and 0x816b60c/0x816b60f; the twin clone repeats both at 0x816bbc6/0x816bc07). +0x10 is written exactly once in the ctor, guarded: 0x816b56d cmp [esi+0x10],0 / 0x816b571 jne / 0x816b573 mov [esi+0x10],edi where edi = ctor arg1 ([ebp+0xc]). +0x10 is the creature TYPE ID -- later code compares it against 0x150, 0x201-0x204, 0x24d-0x254, and pushes it straight into the same type-table global (ds:0x8b8ad60) that CalcResults indexes. So "type=0 FAILED" == a cCreature was constructed with a zero type argument (or took a branch skipping the copy). This SUPERSEDES the REPORT.md 2.6 sentence claiming the ctor never writes +0x3b0 -- that claim was written and disproved the same hour; REPORT.md is corrected. Not yet examined: the four non-ctor writers of [reg+0x3b0] at 0x83a74f1, 0x83a9169, 0x858ffc1, 0x85900cd. Next thread: callers of the cCreature ctor 0x816b34c/0x816b944 and what they pass as arg1.

column5: FINDING
column6: Chain closed onto the loader. New tool analysis/tools/xrefs.py (direct E8/E9 rel32 scan, desync-proof) shows the cCreature ctor has exactly 3 call sites, all inside factory 0x816a194: selector at [ebp+0xc], cmp 0x22/ja, 35-entry jump table at .rodata 0x86e0f10, cases 0x02/0x03/0x20 do operator new(0x5a4) + ctor -> sizeof(cCreature)=0x5a4, type id = factory arg2 passed straight through. The factory has 2 callers: 0x8112522+0x1bc (propagates its own args) and 0x811cd74+0x181 which passes a LITERAL 0 as the type. 0x811cd74 is cObjectManager::load() -- it logs via .rodata 0x86da020 "cObjectManager::load() Ref[%d] Type[%d] Fam[%d] wp[%d,%d,%d] size[%d]" (logger 0x83b01d0; Type is [ebx+0x10], the field itself). Its shape is a deserializer: vtbl[0x8](stream,&tmp,4) reads 4 bytes, vtbl[0x20](obj,stream,0,..) is the object's own Load, then a 4-byte read is compared against sentinel 0xBAADF00D and a mismatch takes the error/log path. CONCLUSION: the load path constructs every object with type id 0 BY DESIGN and relies on Load to fill it from the stream, so "type=0 FAILED" is a Load that did not -- a stream desync/truncation, not an allocator bug. First evidence linking the static analysis to the observed in-game-save-load blocker.

column5: FINDING
column6: Mechanism complete. cCreature::Load = vtbl[0x20] = 0x819ce16 (size 0x9a7) is a SYMMETRIC serializer: arg3 [ebp+0x10] is a direction byte, nonzero -> stream vtbl[0xc] (write), zero -> vtbl[0x8] (read), same field list both ways; sentinel 0xC0DEF00D; cObjectManager::load passes 0. It serializes cCreature offsets 0x18 0xfc 0x150 0x1a4 0x1f0 0x2ed 0x39c 0x3a8 0x568 0x56c 0x570 0x580 -- +0x10 (the ctor type id) is NOT among them, so on the load path +0x10 stays 0 forever. +0x3a8 (embedded cCreatureHero) delegates at 819d052 to cCreatureHero::Serialize 0x821f2f6 (size 0x12df, sentinel 0xDEADBEEF), which serializes only +0x8 and +0x120, and +0x8 is one raw blob: 821f376 add eax,0x8 / push 0xee / call [edx+0xc] (save) mirrored at 821f5d7 with [edx+0x8] (load). So hero field_8 = cCreature+0x3b0 = the dword CalcResults indexes the type table with = the FIRST DWORD OF A 238-BYTE RAW STREAM READ, with no validation or bounds check. type=0 FAILED is a short/desynced blob read; xshim zeroing is what turns it into a clean NULL branch instead of a wild shl-7 index. Two corollaries: (a) Type[%d] in the cObjectManager::load() error line is [ebx+0x10], ALWAYS 0 on the load path -- that log field is not diagnostic, do not chase it, +0x3b0 is the one that matters; (b) three sentinels one per layer (0xBAADF00D per object, 0xC0DEF00D cCreature::Load, 0xDEADBEEF hero) make the stream independently checkable from a shim without patching the engine. Recorded REPORT.md 2.10 + AGENTS.md.

column5: CORRECTION
column6: NEGATIVE RESULT, closes an open question: all four "non-ctor writers of [reg+0x3b0]" are false positives -- do not re-open them. 0x858ffc1/0x85900cd (FDEs 0x858fed8/0x858ffe4, both size 0x10c, identical +0xe9 offsets = C1/C2 clones) are the cUI_Merchandise constructor: it writes vtable 0x872fc88, which vtables.py attributes to cUI_Merchandise (18 virtuals, base cUI_Window2), and the store is mov WORD PTR [esi+0x3b0],ax -- a 16-BIT field at the same numeric offset in an unrelated class. 0x83a74f1/0x83a9169 (FDEs 0x83a6572/0x83a81ea, both size 0x1c78, identical +0xf7f = another clone pair) sit in the middle of a bulk 4-dword block copy 83a74e5/74f1/74fd/7509 writing [edi+0x3ac..0x3b8] from stack locals [ebp-0xc0..-0xb4]; that function has zero E8/E9 callers and appears in no vtable, so it is not on the creature path. LESSON: matching [reg+0x3b0] in an objdump is not evidence -- resolve the owning class first (vtable write or FDE identity). CONSEQUENCE: on the creature path there are EXACTLY TWO writers of cCreature+0x3b0, the ctor copy from +0x10 and the 0xEE-byte blob read of row 38. Nothing assigns the type later, which strengthens the row-38 conclusion rather than competing with it.

column5: FINDING
column6: ROOT CAUSE. cObjectManager::load has exactly ONE caller, 0x80cca20+0x96b, which builds the stream inline: operator new(0x18) at 80cca41, vtable 0x8728c48 written at 80cca48, +0x4/+0x8/+0xc/+0x10 zeroed, +0x14=0, then open(stream,name,3) via 0x83c593a. vtables.py says 0x8728c48 = cFile_ram (base cFile, 9 virtuals) -- the save is read from a RAM BUFFER, not a file handle. Layout: +0x4 size, +0xc pos, +0x10 base, +0x14 flag. vtbl[0x8] = cFile_ram::read(this,dst,len) = 0x83c5aee, 18 instructions: if base==0 return 0; avail = size - pos; IF AVAIL < LEN THEN LEN = AVAIL (83c5b0e, silent clamp); if len==0 return 0 WITHOUT memcpy; memcpy(dst, base+pos, len); pos += len; return len. It returns the count ACTUALLY read -- and every caller discards it: cObjectManager::load does 811cda1 call [ecx+0x8] then 811cda4 mov eax,[ebp-0xa8], overwriting the return on the very next instruction; same pattern in cCreature::Load and cCreatureHero::Serialize. CONSEQUENCE: once pos runs past the end, every further read is a NO-OP that leaves the destination completely untouched. The hero 0xEE-byte blob of row 38 is then never written and field_8 keeps whatever the allocator left -- under xshim exactly 0, hence CalcResults type=0 FAILED. This closes the chain end to end from the log line to a truncated/over-read RAM buffer, and explains why the sentinels only ever notice one object too late. INSTRUMENT: sacred is non-PIE so 0x83c5aee is a fixed address; a breakpoint reporting any call where returned < requested len is a direct POSITIVE signal, unlike the current downstream log greps. Do that before attempting any fix. OPEN: why pos over-runs -- truncated buffer at open(), or a producer/consumer size mismatch between the writer and reader field lists.

column5: HARNESS
column6: SOAK RESULT (10-minute single run, SWEEP_PLAY=600 SWEEP_CAP=700): GAMEPLAY lines=2335 FAILED=0 DESYNC=0. column6: New instrument analysis/tools/shortread_watch.sh (sh -n clean). Breakpoint at 0x83c5b0e -- the single `mov ebx,eax` clamp instruction inside cFile_ram::read -- which is reached ONLY when avail < requested. A healthy load never hits it, so overhead is zero and there is no need to filter normal reads; it is a POSITIVE signal, unlike the downstream greps (sentinels notice one object too late, and CalcResults FAILED additionally requires the bad creature to reach combat maths). Prints want/avail/pos/size/base plus the caller return address from [esp+4], so a hit names which read ran dry. Enabled by a one-line play.sh change: SACRED_RUNNER prefixes the exec (left unquoted deliberately -- it is a command line, not a word), so gdb inherits the normal LD_PRELOAD/xshim environment and the run stays comparable to an ordinary one. column5: FINDING
column6: cFile_ram::open = 0x83c593a (FDE 0x83c593a..0x83c5a11, size 0xd7), decoded in full: fp=fopen(path,"rb") via 0x85fe454 (mode string 0x86f9e8c); if !fp return 0; save=ftell; fseek(fp,0,SEEK_END); size=ftell -> edi; fseek(fp,save,SEEK_SET); if size==0 goto close; base=new char[size] (_Znaj); this+0x10=base; if !base goto close; this+0x8=size (INTENDED); this+0x14=mode; got=fread(base,1,size,fp) via 0x85fe26c; if got==size then this+0x4=size (VERIFIED, ONLY HERE) else { delete[] base at 83c59e1; this+0x10=0 at 83c59e9 }; close: fclose; RETURN 1 AT 83c5a04 ON EVERY PATH PAST FOPEN. Three defects in eight instructions: (1) zero-length file, failed allocation and truncated fread all report SUCCESS, and the single caller only does test al,al at 80cca9a; (2) +0x4 -- the field cFile_ram::read uses to compute avail -- is written only on the complete-read path, otherwise it keeps the constructor zero; (3) +0x8 holds the intended size and is never reconciled with +0x4, so nothing downstream can see they disagree. Chained with row 40: a truncated/empty/unallocatable file yields base=NULL size=0 that reports success, every subsequent read takes the cmp [esi+0x10],0 early exit, returns 0 and WRITES NOTHING, callers discard the count, so every object deserializes as untouched (xshim-zeroed) memory and every creature reaches CalcResults with type 0. PREDICTION worth testing against a captured bad run: the failure should be ALL creatures, not one, and cObjectManager::load() should log on the very FIRST object since no sentinel can match either. column4: Roll semantics pinned (section 9 could only infer them). At the DAMAGE call site: v40 = tohit(...); result = sub_4022F2(0, 100) i.e. rand in [0,100); "if (result >= v40)" takes the MISS branch (parry FX), else the HIT branch (apply damage via sub_40137A). So the test is a strict rand[0,100) < tohit -- a returned 95 means 95%. Arithmetic is double throughout and truncates ONCE, at the cast to int16, BEFORE clamping; a reimplementation that clamps floats then rounds will differ by one point at the boundaries.

The exe's 380-key balance table at VA 0x95b790-0x95ca78 is NOT a pointer array (strides 8/12/16/20 all resolve ~0 pointers) - it is a NUL-padded flat STRING POOL of 379 key names, 4-byte aligned. Names are German engine vocabulary: ProzAW/ProzHP/ProzDmg/ProzRes/ProzExp, AWFakBoss/VWFakBoss/HPFakBoss, LevelUpBoss/LevelUpChamp, RunenProLevel_[ZTVMDESG], skilllearn1..6, DropWaffe/DropRuestung/DropGold/DropSaft, per-class DAEM/DWAR/VAMP/WELF/DELF/MAGE/SERA, per-monster damage keys (dragonfire_dmg_[ma,fi,po,ph], shaddar_slave_*, spiderpuke_*), and the 84x_/85x_/86x_ combat-art rows. NAME<->OFFSET BRIDGE, partial. The five measured difficulty-grid rows (AW, HitPoints, Damage, Resistance, Experience at 1812/1836/1860/1884/1908) correspond exactly to five ADJACENT pool keys ProzAW(n=142), ProzHP(141), ProzDmg(140), ProzRes(139), ProzExp(138) - same members, same order. But the mapping is not globally monotonic: skilllearn1(n=114) sits at offset 780 while ProzAW(n=142) sits at 1812 (forward-consistent), yet within the Proz group offsets run opposite to n (reverse-consistent). Grouped/locally-reversed pooling, as MSVC emits. A blind index->offset formula is therefore REFUTED; do not retry it.

column3: balance.bin FIELD MAP RECOVERED: 354 of 379 keys resolved to file offsets. Artifact analysis/balance-keymap.tsv (name/offset/type/value/raw) + analysis/balance-keymap.json; regenerate with analysis/tools/balance_keymap.py. Self-checking: the script exits nonzero on anchor mismatch. Anchors 6/6 reproduced INDEPENDENTLY of the measurement that produced them (skilllearn1=780, ProzAW=1812, ProzHP=1836, ProzDmg=1860, ProzRes=1884, ProzExp=1908). Every mapped offset lands inside [4,4896]; 4896 is exactly the file header i32[0], so header[0] is the LENGTH OF THE SCALAR BLOCK and bytes 4896..24328 are the array/section region marked by the ':'-suffixed keys.

METHOD - the bridge was a TEXT parser, not the binary loader. All 379 key strings are referenced exactly once (371) or twice (8), 387 sites, in one contiguous routine of ~62-byte blocks (gap histogram 62x226, 61x63). Each block is: push offset "Key" / push esi / call tokcmp / test+jz next / push 0x3d ('=') / push eax / call strchr / ... / store to a GLOBAL. So the exe carries a "Key=value" TEXT config parser (matches the CTRL+K defaults.h exporter, RESEARCH §13). Those globals ARE the in-memory image of balance.bin, so file_offset = global_VA - 0xad448c. The binary loader never had to be found. 322 keys store direct (mov [imm32],eax / fstp [imm32]); 32 more load the base into a register (the array keys, incl. all five Proz*); 25 remain unmapped.

The 25 unmapped keys are not a gap in the method, they are a different KIND of key: section markers (HorseData: RareTranslationMap: ItemThrowProbabilities: PriceAwVw: PriceSlot: PriceBoni:), the seven class tags (DAEM DWAR VAMP WELF DELF MAGE SERA), container names (rare inventory equip), and 9 others (RarePositiveList MerchantParts UniqueThreshold ZK__w ZK__s ZKoff SetSkillPoints BasisPferd NewSkill). They dispatch into sub-parsers rather than storing one scalar - i.e. they describe the 4896..24328 array region. Recovering those needs a real disassembler pass, not the byte-pattern scan.

Now cheap and high value, in order: (a) name the 4896..24328 array region by disassembling the 25 sub-parser blocks - that region holds the region-kill table @22392 and the difficulty min-levels @2488 already measured; (b) diff balance-keymap.tsv values against the Linux install copy (byte-identical, so this is a no-op sanity check) and against any older balance.bin recovered from PAK archives, which would finally TEST the bronze-appended hypothesis (row 197) with 354 named fields instead of 5; (c) the same 62-byte-block scan should work on armalion_us.exe / the Dec 2001 build to date when each key was introduced.

CROSS-BUILD CONFIRMATION of the field map, across compiler AND ABI. Repeating the scan on the LGP Linux port (install/sacred_orig.1.0.02, ELF/gcc) finds the same one-reference-per-key structure, and 313 of the 354 checkable keys agree on ONE base: file_offset = global_VA - 0x8b8941c (vs 0xad448c for Windows Gold 2.28). Vote was decisive - runner-up base scored 5 against 314. The map is therefore a property of the DATA FILE, not of the msvc build, which is what makes it usable against install/sacred, the binary actually in use.

KEY-VOCABULARY TIMELINE (substring presence of the 379 gold keys, per build): gold228_eng 379/379, gold228_rus 379/379, lgp_linux 379/379, demo_usa 261/379 (68.9%), armalion_us 1/379, armalion_dec01 1/379. Absent from the demo and present in Gold: BalanceGeschick, BaseOffLevel, the whole potion-duration family (Black/Blue Potion Small/Medium/Large Dur), ComboCocktail/DriversComboCocktail, DropQuality, DungeonRespawn, EXPBonusPerPlayer, the HOM_ group, DaemonDamageBonus, and the class tags DAEM/DWAR - i.e. the Daemon and the potion/combo economy are post-demo additions. The 18 still-unmapped keys are the seven class tags (SERA MAGE DELF WELF VAMP DWAR equip), the three ZK* sub-keys, and eight list keys whose real offsets need a disassembler pass.

column4: world/sectors.keyx IS the sector index for sectors.wldx - no scan needed
column5: Header: magic "WLK" + u8 ver(5), u32 count=6050 @4, u32 w=100 @8, u32 h=100 @12. Then 6050 fixed 768-byte records from 0x100 (256 + 6050*768 = 4646656 = exact file size). Per record: +32 u32 sector key = gy*100+gx; +236 u32 byte offset into sectors.wldx; +240 u32 compressed size; +264 u32 decompressed size. Verified over ALL 6050 records: every offset matches a real zlib stream start, offsets are contiguous and the last one ends at byte 63854322 = exact sectors.wldx size, and every (offset,csize,dsize) triple matches an independent decompress. This retires plan task 1.5 ("build a (gx,gy)->offset map by scanning, cache it to user://") - the game ships the index, so Godot needs no cache and no O(file) scan. Random access to any sector is two seeks.

column4: deriving (gx,gy) from the in-stream name is WRONG - the name is unreliable, the keyx key is authoritative
column5: Each decompressed sector stream starts with a 32-byte name like "Sector 57,51", and export_terrain.py parses gx,gy out of it. Across all 6050 sectors the names are NOT unique (5776 distinct; 270 are EMPTY, "Sector 0,31" appears 3x, "Sector 0,29" 2x) while the keyx keys ARE unique and cover a clean 100x100 subset. 275 of 6050 records disagree with their name - e.g. record 838 is named "Sector 0,29" but keys to (14,19), record 1150 is named "Sector 0,31" but keys to (19,15). The name field is a stale/garbage-filled buffer (padded with 0xCD, the MSVC debug fill), not data. Consequence: the exporter silently drops the 270 unnamed sectors and mis-places 5 more; any region containing one renders wrong tiles or a hole. The Godot reader must key off keyx +32 and ignore the name entirely.

column4: decompressed sector size is VARIABLE, so the 32+4096*32 layout has a variable-length tail
column5: Decompressed stream length ranges 131396..492348 across 6050 sectors, 250 distinct values, with 131396 by far the most common. Fixed part is 32 (name) + 4096*32 (WldxEntry grid) = 131104, so the tail runs from 292 bytes to 361244 bytes. That tail is almost certainly the per-sector object/entity list, which makes it the concrete target for plan Phase 3.1 alongside WldxEntry +0x04/+0x0c. keyx +264 gives the exact decompressed size up front, so a reader can size its buffer without decompress_dynamic.

column4: Godot's COMPRESSION_DEFLATE is zlib-WRAPPED, not raw - the plan said the opposite
column5: Plan task 1.3 instructed "Godot's MODE_DEFLATE is *raw* deflate; the game's streams are zlib-wrapped (78 9c), so drop the 2-byte header". Measured false. Godot's Compression::decompress passes window_bits = 15 for MODE_DEFLATE (and 15+16 for MODE_GZIP), i.e. it expects the zlib wrapper; raw deflate is not reachable through PackedByteArray.decompress at all. Stripping the two header bytes makes every call fail with compression.cpp:196 "Condition err != 1 is true" and return -1, which surfaces as an empty PackedByteArray, not an exception - so the failure is silent unless the caller checks the returned size. Correct call is z.decompress(out_size, FileAccess.COMPRESSION_DEFLATE) on the untouched stream. Caught immediately because the harness diffs md5s against the Python decode; an eyeball check on a black screen would not have distinguished this from a shader bug.

column4: runtime readers reach byte-for-byte parity with the Python decode
column5: godot-port/sacred.gd (Pak / Tiles / World / decode_texture) vs analysis/tools/verify_ref.py, diffed via godot-port/verify.gd. Matching: tiles.pak count 90132 + first/last index triples, texture.pak count 25535 + triples, keyx count 6050 and 100x100 grid, md5 of 7 decompressed sectors (50,50 / 51,51 / 0,15 / 14,19 / 31,24 / 99,99 plus the ABSENT 49,49 which both sides report as empty), tiles.pak texture ids for entry 0 and 90131, and md5 of 5 decoded ARGB4444 textures at 128x128, 256x256 and 1024x1024. Texture 0 has size 0 in the index and both sides report ERROR. ARGB4444->RGBA8 in GDScript costs 8.6 ms at 256x256 and 147 ms at 1024x1024 (linear in pixels, two 512-byte lookup tables); 63 tiles = ~0.54 s, so no compute shader and no user:// image cache is needed yet.

column4: PHASE 1 DONE - godot-port/data deleted, viewer runs from the retail install at runtime
column5: main.gd now opens install/pak/tiles.pak, install/pak/texture.pak and install/world/sectors.{keyx,wldx} with FileAccess and builds the mesh in-engine. Same invariant as the baked path: "28672 quads, 63 textures" for the 3x3 sector region at center 50,50 (7 of the 9 sectors exist; 49,49 and one neighbour are absent from keyx, which is why it is 7*4096 and not 9*4096). Whole load is under 1 s headless. godot-port/data/ moved out and the run repeats identically, so export_terrain.py is now a debugging cross-check rather than a dependency. Visual oracle added: main.gd --shot=FILE renders one frame and writes a PNG; under xvfb + opengl3 it shows real desert terrain with a rock ravine and a notch where the missing sector is. That notch is the cheapest available confirmation that absent sectors are handled rather than silently zero-filled.

column4: world-wide terrain texture census - a single global Texture2DArray is impossible
column5: Walked all 6050 sectors / 24,780,800 cells. Zero invalid tile ids (the tid >= tiles.count() guard never fires). 55184 of 90132 tiles.pak records are used, resolving to 4328 distinct texture.pak ids, and ALL 4328 are 256x256 - so a texture array needs no size classes. At RGBA8 that is 1135 MB resident, which rules out one global array and forces per-sector arrays. Per sector: min 1, median 11, mean 19.9, max 209 distinct textures (median 2.9 MB, max 54.8 MB). A 5x5 sector window costs 8-151 textures depending on region (2-40 MB). Adjacent sectors share 54% of their textures by Jaccard, so a shared decoded-image cache roughly halves streaming work. These four numbers are what set the streaming architecture: one MeshInstance3D + one Texture2DArray per sector, plus a bounded global Image cache.

column4: all 18 orientation values are in near-uniform use, so orientation is a render-time transform and not decoration
column5: Counting orientation (+0x24) over the 55184 tile records the world actually references gives 3005-3127 occurrences for every one of the 18 values - flat to within 2%. 55184 distinct tiles map to only 4328 distinct textures, i.e. ~12.75 tile records share each texture. If orientation were baked into pre-rotated textures those records would carry different texture ids; they do not. So the 18 values are a transform applied to a shared texture at draw time. 18 is not 4 rotations and not 8 rotations+flips, so the encoding is still unknown - but the uniform distribution means ignoring it is visibly wrong everywhere, not just in rare tiles, which matches the regular repeating dot pattern visible in the streamed screenshot.

column4: ARGB4444 unpacking belongs on the GPU, not the CPU - 350 ms/sector became 18 ms
column5: The CPU nibble expansion (two 512-byte lookup tables, 8.6 ms per 256x256 tile) made a cold sector cost up to 350 ms, a hard visible hitch, and plan task 2.2 existed to fix that with WorkerThreadPool. Not needed: ARGB4444 is byte-identical to Godot's FORMAT_RG8, so the raw 16-bit pixels upload untouched and terrain.gdshader unpacks the nibbles (lo byte = (g<<4)|b, hi byte = (a<<4)|r, /15.0, alpha nibble < 8 discards). Measured worst sector 349.8 -> 18.1 ms, typical 4-8 ms, and VRAM halves. Proof it is exact rather than merely close: the --region=50,50,1 screenshot is BYTE-IDENTICAL (md5 d794a2864a95a04ee8761e9140dfae0c) across the CPU path, the GPU path, and the earlier pre-streaming build. filter_nearest is load-bearing - interpolating packed nibbles between texels would be meaningless.

column4: terrain textures are 18-slot DIAMOND ATLASES, and tiles.pak +0x24 selects the slot
column5: Connected-component labelling of the alpha channel of texture 6309 (iso825.tga) gives exactly 18 opaque components, each exactly 2500 px with a 100x49 bounding box - and the alpha mask is byte-identical across every terrain texture sampled (6300 6301 6309 6310 6311 6312 1494 5000 all hash the same; 1493 is fully opaque and 20000 differs, so it is a fixed lattice for terrain, not for all images). Row-extent measurement of one diamond: apex 4 px wide at y=0, widening exactly 4 px per row to 100 px at y=24, i.e. the standard 2:1 iso slope. Lattice is 9 rows of 2 columns, odd rows staggered half a cell: x0 = (n%2)*104 + ((n/2)%2)*52, y0 = (n/2)*25, so slot 17 ends at (255,248) and all 18 fit with no wrap. tiles.pak itself is a flat table - tile_id = 18*texture_index + orientation, 5007 textures x 18 + one group of 6 = 90132 records, names iso000.tga..iso5007.tga, one name per texture id.

column4: applying the atlas slot UV removes the repeating-dot artifact - the old renderer was squeezing all 18 diamonds into every cell
column5: Before 2.4 the viewer mapped UV 0..1 over the whole 256x256 image for every tile, i.e. it drew all 18 diamonds shrunk into one cell, which is what produced the regular grid of dark dashes visible in the streamed screenshot. Mapping each quad to its own slot rect (and dropping the cell size from 128x64 to the true 50x25 half-extents) yields continuous ground: at 1:1 zoom there are no seams and no gaps between tiles, and the sand/gravel transition reads as designed terrain. CAVEAT, not yet closed: seamlessness proves the slot GEOMETRY, not the index->slot ORDERING. Any permutation of the 18 slots would still tile seamlessly, because each slot is a self-contained diamond; a wrong permutation would only scramble which variation appears where. Consecutive slot indices are demonstrably NOT consecutive world cells (world row 10,11,12,13 maps to atlas positions (52,125) then (156,125), a step of +104,0, not the +52,+25 an iso step would need), so the ordering is storage order and confirming it needs a side-by-side against the running retail game.

column4: the sector tail begins with the sector's own world cell origin - verified 6050/6050
column5: Every decompressed sector stream is 32 (name) + 131072 (WldxEntry[4096]) + a variable tail of 292..361244 bytes. The tail's first four dwords are (gx*64, gy*64, 0, 6) - the sector's absolute cell origin - and this holds for ALL 6050 sectors with zero mismatches, with dword[3] equal to 6 in every single one. That makes the tail self-identifying and gives an anchor for parsing it. Immediately after the 36-byte header the big sectors carry 36-byte records whose first two dwords are absolute cell coordinates INSIDE that sector, a u32 6 at +0x0c, and a monotonically increasing u32 at +0x10; 1870 such records exist world-wide and every one of them has both in-sector coordinates and the 6 tag. But a flat stride-36 parse of the whole tail puts only 0.62% of records in bounds, so the tail is NOT a uniform array - the 36-byte records are one leading section and something else follows. Do not assume a single stride; find the section boundary first.

column4: +0x10, +0x14 and +0x18 are each FOUR PER-CORNER BYTES, not three dwords
column5: Byte-level histograms over a 1-in-7 sector sample (3.5 M cells) show the four byte positions inside each of +0x10..0x13, +0x14..0x17 and +0x18..0x1b having statistically IDENTICAL distributions (e.g. value 236 appears 154747/154291/153998/154446 times across +0x10..+0x13). Four independent byte fields with the same distribution is the signature of a per-corner array, which is exactly what an isometric terrain cell needs. +0x10..0x13: 82% zero, 38 distinct, dominated by 236/5/251 i.e. signed -20/+5/-5 - reads as per-corner height deltas. +0x14..0x17: NEVER zero, only 14 distinct, dominated by 255 then 235, 215, 195 - a clean step of -20 - reads as per-corner light level. +0x18..0x1b: 91% zero, 99 distinct. +0x1f is never zero with 67 distinct values (209, 64, 129, 49 most common) and is a per-cell type/flag byte. +0x08 is zero in all 24,780,800 cells - a dead field. Reading +0x1c as a u32 float is a TRAP: the common values 0xd1000000 / 0x40000000 look like floats but are just byte +0x1f with three zero bytes below it.

column4: +0x04 is a globally unique object handle - 862343 values, ZERO duplicates across 24.7 M cells
column5: Collected every nonzero +0x04 over all 6050 sectors: 862,343 distinct values in the range 1..1,038,013 and not one collision. Uniqueness at that scale is not an accident - this is a world-unique entity/object id, not an index or a type. +0x0c is a different and denser space: 4,616,140 distinct nonzero values over 1..6,713,135. The two are largely independent - sampling shows 79.8% of cells have neither set, 17.6% have only +0x0c, 2.1% only +0x04 and 1.3% both - so they are two separate attachment slots, not a split 64-bit field. Together with row 217 this is the concrete starting point for plan Phase 3.1: the ids live in the cell grid, the records live in the tail, and the tail header gives the coordinate frame to join them on.

column4: per-corner light (WldxEntry +0x14..0x17) renders as smooth terrain shading with no per-tile banding
column5: Fed the four bytes straight into ARRAY_COLOR and multiplied ALBEDO by COLOR.rgb in terrain.gdshader. Result is soft organic dark patches across the desert that read as relief and vegetation shadow. The diagnostic value is in what is ABSENT: the four bytes are assigned to the quad's four rect corners in file order, which is a guess, and a wrong corner order would show up as diagonal discontinuities at every tile boundary. There are none at 1:1 zoom, so the four bytes really are per-corner and the file order really is a corner order. Caveat kept in code: the diamond's corners are the rect's edge MIDPOINTS, so this interpolates over the wrong quadrilateral - it approximates the retail shading rather than reproducing it. Streaming after the change: 28 sectors, mean 7.9 ms, worst 19.7 ms.

column4: the per-corner byte order is W,N,E,S - SOLVED by a lattice constraint, not guessed, 0 mismatches in 6.5 M tests
column5: In the iso lattice four cells meet at every diamond corner: cell(x,y).N is the same point as cell(x,y-1).W, cell(x-1,y).E and cell(x-1,y-1).S. That turns the corner order into a solvable constraint - try all 24 assignments of the four bytes to the roles N,E,S,W and score how often the three neighbours agree with the reference cell. Exactly ONE permutation scores 1.000: file byte0=W, byte1=N, byte2=E, byte3=S. Confirmed over 550 sectors (every 11th) x 3 arrays x 63x63x3 shared-vertex tests = 6,548,850 tests each: +0x10 mismatches 0, +0x18 mismatches 0, +0x14 mismatches 117 (0.0018%, plausibly genuine lighting seams). The exactness is itself the proof that these bytes are per-corner - no other interpretation produces perfect three-way agreement at every lattice point in the world. This method needed no disassembly and no retail screenshot.

column4: tiles are DIAMONDS, not textured rectangles - that is what makes the height field join up
column5: Rendering per-corner heights on the old rectangle quads tore the terrain open: visible slivers of background between tiles, because a rectangle's corners are not shared with its neighbours and so displacing them cannot produce a continuous surface. Only the DIAMOND corners are lattice points, and they are shared four ways. Rebuilt each tile as a 4-vertex diamond (N/E/S/W) whose UVs sit at the atlas slot rect's EDGE MIDPOINTS - which also means the transparent rect corners are never sampled at all. Result: every gap closes, the mesh is watertight, and a real elevation terrace becomes visible in sector 21,95. Height goes into vertex Y, not Z, so it does not fight the depth ordering that lets separate sector meshes coexist. Quad count is unchanged (still 1 quad / 2 triangles per cell), so the 28672/63 invariant and the md5 parity harness both still pass.

column4: zoomed-out terrain aliases, and the GPU-unpack trick is what blocks the fix
column5: With diamond geometry the tile is sampled 1:1 over a smaller screen area, so zooming out now minifies without mipmaps and the ground shimmers. The normal fix - generate mipmaps - is ILLEGAL for the current textures: they are uploaded as FORMAT_RG8 holding packed ARGB4444 nibbles, and averaging packed nibbles is meaningless, which is also why filter_nearest is mandatory. So mipmapping requires going back to the CPU RGBA8 expansion (8.6 ms/tile, the thing that cost 350 ms per cold sector) or expanding on the GPU into a render target once per texture. Worth measuring before choosing; do not "just enable mipmaps".

column4: Godot DOES have Image.FORMAT_RGBA4444 - the plan's "no FORMAT_RGBA4444 in Godot" was wrong and I repeated it twice
column5: Probed the running 4.7.1 build: FORMAT_RGBA4444 = 6 and FORMAT_RGB565 = 7 both exist. The claim originated in plan task 1.4 and was carried into sacred.gd's comments unchecked. It matters because the engine's own C++ expansion is 29x faster than the GDScript nibble loop: 256x256 FORMAT_RGBA4444 -> convert(FORMAT_RGBA8) costs 298 us against 8.6 ms, and generate_mipmaps() on the result costs another 55 us. CAVEAT that makes it not a drop-in: Godot reads the u16 high-nibble-first as R,G,B,A while Sacred stores A,R,G,B, so every channel arrives rotated by one - the engine's .r holds Sacred's alpha and .gba hold its red/green/blue. Rotating the u16 on the CPU would give back the per-pixel loop we just removed, so terrain.gdshader unswizzles instead, which is free.

column4: zoomed-out shimmer fixed by linear filtering + a 1-texel UV inset; MIPMAPS made it worse, not better
column5: Three variants rendered and compared at the same camera. (a) filter_nearest, no mipmaps: shimmer at minification, the original complaint. (b) filter_linear_mipmap: shimmer gone but every diamond gained a heavy dark outline - atlas slots are only 4 px apart, so mip level 2 already averages a diamond together with its neighbours and the transparent padding. Mipmaps and a tightly-packed atlas are fundamentally in conflict here; do not retry without repacking the atlas. (c) filter_linear, no mipmaps, plus slot_uv inset by 1 texel and retargeted from the 104x50 lattice cell to the measured 100x49 OPAQUE bounding box: shimmer gone AND grid gone. The inset is what removes the residual faint grid that (c) had without it - linear filtering at the diamond tips was reaching into the padding. Cost of moving from RG8 to RGBA8: worst sector build 22.7 -> 39.9 ms, mean 10.5 -> 12.6 ms, because the texture is now 4 bytes per pixel instead of 2. Judged worth it; the hitch is bounded and one-off per sector.

column4: PHASE 3 SOLVED at the structural level - WldxEntry +0x04 indexes world/static.pak, +0x0c indexes world/floor.pak
column5: The two handle fields are not ids in an abstract space, they are direct indices into the two big OBJ archives sitting next to sectors.wldx. Proof is exact: static.pak (magic "OBJ" v1) declares count = 1,038,014 and the maximum +0x04 seen anywhere in the world is 1,038,013; floor.pak (magic "OBJ" v1) declares count = 6,713,136 and the maximum +0x0c is 6,713,135. Both are exactly count-1. Confirmed structurally too - every static.pak record's first dword equals its own index, checked on 32,428 records with zero exceptions, so the archive is self-validating. Entry sizes are uniform: static.pak 64 bytes, floor.pak 16 bytes. Index 0 means "none". This also explains why the sector tail was a dead end: 339 of 356 sampled sectors have the MINIMUM 292-byte tail regardless of how many objects they contain, and the tail's dword[3] is the constant 6 in all 6050 sectors (a version, not a count). Large tails are near-100%-zero reserved space, which is why they compress to almost nothing.

column4: 64-byte record layout, and it carries absolute iso SCREEN coordinates
column5: +0x00 u32 self index (validates the archive). +0x04 u32 type id - 2872 distinct, range 801..31936, top values 1037/1035/1033/8879 (range fits mixed.pak's 32096 entries, not models.pak's 4993). +0x08 u32 flags, only 9 distinct values, 0 and 32 covering 95%. +0x0e i32 ox and +0x12 i32 oy - note the ODD alignment, these are not on 4-byte boundaries. Remaining bytes are largely 0xCD MSVC uninitialised fill. floor.pak's 16-byte record is +0x00 self index, +0x04 id pair, +0x08 0xCDCDCDCD unused, +0x0c NEXT INDEX - a linked list, so several floor layers can stack on one cell, which is why 6.7 M floor entries serve 24.7 M cells.

column4: the true iso cell is 96x48, NOT the 100x50 I derived from the terrain atlas
column5: Fitting every sampled static object's stored position against the cell that references it gives ox = 48.0058*cx - 47.9981*cy and oy = 24.0235*cx + 24.0107*cy over 32,428 samples - i.e. ox = 48*(cx-cy), oy = 24*(cx+cy), the iso projection with HW=48, HH=24. Residuals are quantised (371 and 668 distinct values, 61% and 55% within half a cell) and are sub-cell placement offsets; each static index is referenced by exactly one cell, so multi-cell anchoring is not the cause. My earlier HW=50/HH=25 came from the atlas slot PITCH (104 x 25 stagger 52), which includes inter-slot padding, and the drawn art is 100x49, which overlaps its own cell by ~2 px the way hand-authored iso tiles normally do. Object data is ground truth and the atlas packing is not. Fix is HW/HH only: terrain geometry now uses 96x48 while still sampling the 100x49 art bbox, so the art is squeezed ~4% (invisible) and corner sharing - which the height field depends on - is preserved. Without this fix objects would have drifted 4% away from the terrain under them.

column4: object placement rendered and visually confirmed - 648 markers land inside their sector and follow terrain features
column5: godot-port now reads world/static.pak through Sacred.Statics and, under --markers, draws one type-coloured quad per placed object at its own stored ox/oy. Sector 64,39 renders all 648 of its static references; every marker falls inside the sector's 64x64 footprint and the distribution visibly tracks the ground - dense along the dirt paths, sparse on the open grass. That single screenshot cross-validates three separate claims at once: that +0x04 indexes static.pak, that ox/oy really live at the UNALIGNED offsets 0x0e/0x12, and that the cell is 96x48. Any one of the three being wrong would push markers off the sector or skew them systematically. Cost with markers on: mean 13.1 ms, worst 47.4 ms per sector. Terrain invariant (28672 quads, 63 textures) and the md5 parity harness both unchanged. What is still missing for real objects is the art: type ids run 801..31936 which fits mixed.pak (32096 entries) rather than models.pak (4993), and models.pak is MDL v3 / Granny2, undecoded.

column4: the object ART chain is fully resolved - static type id -> mixed.pak -> texture.pak, verified 209956/209956
column5: pak/mixed.pak (magic "MIX" v0, 32096 entries) is the sprite table that static.pak's type id indexes. Entry layout: 16-byte header {u32 frame_count, u16 w, u16 h, i16 dx, i16 dy, u32 pad} followed by frame_count fixed 64-byte frame records, so entry size is exactly 16 + 64*frame_count (checked, holds). Frame record: +0x00 name[32] like "MIX233.444" (.444 = ARGB4444), +0x20 u32 texture.pak INDEX, +0x24 two u16, +0x30 four f32 forming a UV rect into that texture. The +0x20 index is not a guess: resolving each frame's own name string through texture.pak's name table and comparing against the stored u32 matches on 209,956 of 209,956 frames with zero exceptions. texture.pak holds 10,591 MIX*.444 sprites alongside the ISO*.TGA terrain atlases. 15,840 of 32,096 mixed entries have ZERO frames - including type 1037, the single most common static type in the world - so a large share of placed statics are invisible markers (collision, spawn, sound) rather than art.

column4: object sprite rendering is feasible but three semantics are still unverified - do not guess them
column5: Cost is fine: per sector the median is 104 placed objects drawing from only 10 distinct object textures (max 719 objects), so ~10 extra draw calls per sector, and the existing image cache already covers the decode. What is NOT established, and what a renderer would have to invent if written today: (1) which frame of the N is chosen - frame counts cluster at 4/5/6/7/8, which smells like facing directions, so it is probably a function of an orientation field not yet located; (2) what the header's i16 dx,dy and the frame's two u16 at +0x24 mean - candidates are sprite anchor offset and source size, and the one arithmetic check attempted (u16 32,32 vs a UV rect spanning 0.875..1.0 of a 256 px texture = 32 px) fit for frame 0 but NOT for frame 1; (3) whether w,h in the header are pixels or something else. Each is cheap to settle against the running retail game. Guessing all three would produce a plausible wrong picture, which is the exact failure mode this project has been bitten by five times already.

column4: source_color + rotated channels = wrong colour on Vulkan; the whole session's visual verification ran on the WRONG backend
column5: The project ships Forward+/Vulkan but every screenshot taken while building it was rendered with --rendering-driver opengl3 under xvfb, and the bug only appears on Vulkan. terrain.gdshader declared the sampler `source_color`, which sRGB-decodes RGB but NOT alpha. Because the FORMAT_RGBA4444 trick leaves channels rotated by one (.r is Sacred's alpha, .gba its colour), the decode hit Sacred's red and green and skipped its blue, and the framebuffer then re-encoded all three - brightening blue alone. Measured at five sample points, Vulkan matched OpenGL exactly on R and G and differed only on B: desert tan (208,171,120) rendered as (210,172,183), a lavender. Predicted value lin_to_srgb(120/255) = 181 against 183 observed, so the mechanism is confirmed arithmetically and not just by eye. Fix: drop source_color, sample raw, multiply the per-corner light in GAMMA space (which is what the 2005 2D blitter did) and apply an explicit srgb_to_linear before writing ALBEDO. Vulkan now reproduces the reference within +/-1 per channel at all five points.

column4: Forward+ and Compatibility disagree on whether ALBEDO is linear, so an unshaded shader cannot be verified on the wrong one
column5: After the fix, the same shader renders correct tan (208,171,120) on Vulkan and much darker (161,104,47) on --rendering-driver opengl3. Forward+ treats ALBEDO as linear and encodes to sRGB on output; the compatibility path does not, so the explicit srgb_to_linear is a double-darken there. This is not worth branching on - the project ships Forward+ and nothing else - but it makes backend choice part of the test protocol rather than an incidental flag. Vulkan works fine under xvfb-run with the NVIDIA driver, so there was never a reason to force opengl3. AGENTS.md and the plan now say to verify on the default renderer and warn against the flag. General lesson, and the sixth time this project has been bitten by the same shape of error: a green check on an instrument that is not the shipping configuration is not a green check.

column4: the retail 2005 binary RUNS AND RENDERS UNDER Xvfb - the visual oracle no longer needs a human's desktop
column5: Ran analysis/tools/shot.sh inside `xvfb-run -a -s "-screen 0 1024x768x24"` with autopilot.so preloaded. The game started, produced a 249-line debug.log with 0 FAILED, and glReadPixels captured the Ancaria/Underworld main menu correctly at both requested timestamps. This matters more than it sounds: every prior visual check of the retail game required taking over a real display for ~30 s, which meant an agent could not use the retail build as an acceptance oracle on its own. It now can. Combined with Godot's Vulkan renderer also working under Xvfb, BOTH engines are now capturable headlessly and side by side, which is exactly what plan task 3.2 needs (matching a mixed.pak sprite against the running game to settle frame selection and anchor offsets). Wrapped as `analysis/tools/look.sh retail`; LOOK_DISPLAY=real opts back into a live desktop.

column4: canonical review pass against the Godot 4.3+ checklist - four real defects, output byte-identical after fixing
column5: Reviewed sacred.gd / main.gd / iso_camera.gd / verify.gd / terrain.gdshader against godot-prompter:godot-code-review. Fixed: (1) load("res://terrain.gdshader") was called inside _build_sector, i.e. per streamed sector in a hot path - now a preload()ed const, which the checklist calls out explicitly; (2) input actions were registered at RUNTIME via InputMap.add_action instead of living in the Input Map - now generated into project.godot [input] through ProjectSettings.set_setting/save (hand-writing the InputEventKey blobs is error-prone; letting Godot serialise them is not), with device -1 to match what the editor writes; (3) Input.get_vector was passed String literals every frame, allocating StringNames - now &"iso_left" style consts; (4) _process re-derived the whole visible sector set every frame even when the camera had not moved - now gated on a camera-state Vector3 and drained through a _pending queue. Also added the is_instance_valid(self) guard after await in the screenshot coroutine and dropped the empty placeholder Node3D per absent sector. Proof the refactor changed nothing: the --markers --zoom=800 render is byte-identical to the pre-review capture, and the parity harness and 28672/63 invariant both still pass.

column4: GDScript warnings are NOT emitted headlessly - "no warnings" from godot --check-only is a dead metric
column5: Enabled untyped_declaration, inferred_declaration, unsafe_cast, unsafe_call_argument, unsafe_method_access and unsafe_property_access in project.godot, then ran the four project scripts through `godot --headless --check-only --script`, a cold `--import` after deleting .godot, a plain runtime launch, and `--editor --quit`. All four produced zero warning output. Before recording that as "the code is clean", ran a CONTROL: a scratch script with a deliberately untyped `var untyped = 5`, an untyped func signature and an unsafe method access on a Variant. It produced no warning either, through every one of the same paths. So the toolchain does not surface GDScript warnings outside the editor UI at all, and the silence on the real files carried no information. The typing audit therefore stands on manual review against the checklist, not on a compiler. The warning settings are left enabled so they fire for whoever opens the editor. This is the same failure the project's own STATUS lesson 2 warns about - a clean arm with no control is not a result - and it is now the seventh instance.

column4: Godot 4.4+ typed Dictionary applied across the port; behaviour unchanged
column5: _loaded is now Dictionary[int, MeshInstance3D], _images Dictionary[int, Image], _by_key Dictionary[int, int], _wanted_sectors returns Dictionary[int, bool], and the per-sector layer_of / texids are typed too. Checked against the 4.7 override rule as well (methods overriding a typed-return method must return explicitly) - every override here is -> void, so none is affected - and for the 4.7 deprecation of type_exists(), which the project never used. Invariant 28672 quads / 63 textures and the md5 parity harness both unchanged after the conversion.

column4: the official map's biome order confirms screen_y = 24*(cx+cy) runs NORTH->SOUTH
column5: manuals/Gold/Map.pdf shows Ancaria with snow in the north (Garrena, Hell's Ridge, Frostgard, Valley of Tears), temperate farmland through the middle (Bravesbury, Braverock Castle, Florentina, Porto Draco) and desert in the south (Khorad-Nur, Nasrud-Nur, Aish-Judar), with sea and islands off the south-west. Tested rather than assumed: rendered all 6050 sectors as one pixel each, coloured by the average colour of that sector's dominant terrain texture (130 unique textures needed). In CELL space the biomes run on a diagonal from upper-left to lower-right; in SCREEN space they stack snow-top / green-middle / desert-bottom exactly as the printed map does. So screen_y = 24*(cx+cy) is the north-south axis and screen_x = 48*(cx-cy) is west-east, and a place named on the map converts to an approximate sector. CAVEAT: the aspect ratios do NOT match - the world is 2:1 landscape in screen space and the printed map is portrait and stylised - so only the biome ORDER is evidence, not the shape. Also retired a false alarm: the sector-presence map appeared to have a period-4 modular structure, which was an artifact of collapsing two rows per line in the ASCII dump; presence rate by (gx%4, gy%4) is flat at 0.58-0.64 and the real pattern is contiguous landmasses.

column4: the manual decodes the four damage/resistance suffixes - Gi is GIFT, i.e. poison
column5: The Gold manual states the game has exactly four damage and resistance types: Physical, Fire, Magic, Poison. balance.bin carries exactly four, and they now decode as German abbreviations: Ph = Physisch, Fe = Feuer, Ma = Magie, Gi = Gift = POISON. That resolves BalanceResPh/ResFe/ResMa/ResGi as the four resistances and BalCharPD/FD/MD/GD plus BalCharPR/FR/MR/GR as the per-character damage and resistance values for the same four. Gi is the one that was not guessable from the abbreviation alone. Consistent with the already-known German in the key set (AW/VW = Angriffswert/Verteidigungswert, BalanceGeschick = Dexterity). The manual also independently confirms the five difficulty tiers Bronze/Silver/Gold/Platinum/Niobium, matching the balance.bin difficulty grid's slot order, and confirms that Attack / Defence / Hit Chance are values the game DISPLAYS to the player - so the recovered hit formula clamp(200*AT/(AT+PA)*ALVL/(ALVL+DLVL),5,95) is the shown stat, not an internal one.

column4: install/bin/type_npc_<class>/ is the compiled quest system, and it is self-describing
column5: One directory per playable class - gladiator, seraphim, elve, darkelve, magician, vampirelady, zwerg (dwarf), daemonin (daemon), matching the manual's eight classes exactly. Each holds funkcode.bin (3.8 M), vectoren.bin (2.1 M), defpos.bin (1.1 M), startcode.bin (564 K) and a near-empty questcode.bin. They are compiled but carry readable symbol names: HQ_3_1_4_glad_NPC_Auftrag_Qoffen (Hauptquest 3.1.4, gladiator, Auftrag = task, Q-offen = quest open), RTYPE_NPC_GLADIATOR, dq_belohnung_typ (Belohnung = reward), SOUND_FX_*, trigger99, res:1024. Region names from the printed map (Khorad, Florentina, Ancaria) occur inside them. Plan Phase 4.4 currently records the quest VM as "unknown scope"; it is not - the entry point is the naming convention, and the format is named and partitioned by class before any disassembly.

column4: the German Loesungsbuch decodes 15 opaque key families - they are skill names
column5: manuals/German/ adds two official strategy guides (Gold 145 pp, Plus 73 pp) whose skill tables print numbers. Extracting German compound nouns gives the vocabulary the abbreviations come from: WK = Waffenkunde, MK = Magiekunde, FK = Fernkampf, SK = Schwertkunde, AK = Axtkampf, KK = Klingenkampf, STK = Stangenwaffen, and the six *M families are the six magic schools HM/FM/EM/WM/LM/MM = Himmels-, Feuer-, Erd-, Wasser-, Luft-, Mondmagie. The AW/SP suffix pair is settled by the guide's own wording for Schwertkunde - "Verbessert den Angriffswert und die Angriffsgeschwindigkeit" - so AW = Angriffswert (attack value) and SP = Angriffstempo (attack speed), which is exactly what the SKoffAW / SKoffSP pair controls. Anchors that make this more than a plausible reading: SKoffAW = 9.0 against the guide's printed "Angriff +9%", SKoffSP = 6.0 against "Angriffstempo +6%", WKoff = 12.0 against "Magisch +12%; Feuer +12%; Gift +12%", and all six magic schools carrying off=6/s=50/w=100 against a printed +6% for every one of them.

column4: SECOND RECOVERED FORMULA - skill bonus% = w * L / (L + s), s = 50, recovered with no disassembly
column5: Each skill family stores three floats off/_s/_w. Matching them against the Loesungsbuch's three-column table gives bonus% = w * L / (L + s) with s = 50 for every family, and off = the value at skill level 1 (a floor outside the curve). Reproduces EVERY printed column: Waffenkunde w=200 -> 93.6 and 150.0 against printed 94 and 150; Schwertkunde AW w=150 -> 70.2 and 112.5 against 70 and 112; Schwertkunde SP w=100 -> 46.8 and 75.0 against 47 and 75; all six magic schools w=100 -> same 47/75. The fit is load-bearing rather than coincidental because the middle column of FOUR different families all solve to the same skill level, 44, and the top column of all four solves to exactly 150. off matches the level-1 column exactly in every case (12, 9, 6). STILL OPEN: how off and the curve combine below mid-level - max() or a blend - since the guide prints only three columns. This is the project's second formula after the hit-chance clamp, and unlike that one it needed only a published table plus the named key map.

column4: the "frames" are TILES of one sprite - all three open 3.2 questions answered at once, without the retail oracle
column5: The u16 pair at +0x24 is not two values but four: x1,y1,x0,y0 at +0x24/+0x26/+0x28/+0x2a, a DESTINATION RECT in sprite-local pixels. Proof: for every tile checked, the destination rect's size equals its UV rect's size in texture pixels exactly (64x64, 2x32, 4x2, 16x32 ...). So the N "frames" are not animation frames and not facing directions - they are pieces of ONE large sprite packed across one or more atlases, and a 195x341 object is assembled from 13 of them. That answers all three questions plan task 3.2 listed as blocking: which frame to draw (ALL of them), what the u16s mean (the destination rect), and whether header w/h are pixels (yes - 195x341 with tiles covering 0..196 x 0..352, i.e. padded up to a tile grid). Confirmed by compositing: pasting each tile's texture region at its destination rect produces coherent objects - a crystal shrine on a stone wall, a mossy boulder, a wooden chair, rock formations. The retail oracle was not needed after all; the data was self-describing once the rect was read correctly.

column4: object sprites need their own shader - StandardMaterial3D cannot express the channel rotation, and alpha-scissor silently tested the wrong channel
column5: First object render produced thin coloured slivers scattered over the terrain instead of sprites. Cause: object textures go through the same Image.FORMAT_RGBA4444 -> convert(RGBA8) path as terrain, so channels arrive rotated (.r is Sacred's alpha, .gba its colour), but they were pointed at StandardMaterial3D.albedo_texture, which has no way to unswizzle. TRANSPARENCY_ALPHA_SCISSOR therefore tested Godot's alpha = Sacred's BLUE, discarding every pixel whose blue was below half - which is why only thin bright streaks survived and why they were the wrong colour. Diagnosis was cheap because the GDScript Sacred.Mixed decode was first dumped and compared against the Python: identical, so the fault had to be downstream of the data. Fix is object.gdshader, the same unswizzle and srgb_to_linear as terrain but sampler2D and a real 0.5 alpha cut (objects have genuine interior transparency; terrain's 0.25 was a padding tolerance). Result: sector 64,39 renders as an actual town - red tiled roofs, stone walls, windows, stairs, cobbled courtyard, a pile of gold coins.

column4: object sprites render but their ANCHOR and object-vs-object sort order are still guesses
column5: Sprites are now correct individually and wrong collectively: walls float, roof sections misalign, and pieces occlude each other in the wrong order. Two causes, both unverified assumptions in main.gd. (1) ANCHOR: the sprite is placed with origin = (ox - w/2 + dx, oy + h + dy), i.e. bottom-centre shifted by the header's i16 dx,dy. That is the reading that makes a tree stand on its own cell, but it is a guess and it is marked ponytail: in the code. (2) OBJECT-VS-OBJECT DEPTH: every tile of an object shares one z derived from the object's own position, z = (cx+cy)*DEPTH_STEP + 2, which matches the terrain's own formula so object-vs-TERRAIN sorting is right; but two objects whose bases sit in the same iso row get the same z and fight. Both are now cheap to settle: analysis/tools/look.sh can capture the retail game and the port headlessly, so a side-by-side of the same location is one command each.

column4: object sprites cost 3-7x a terrain sector - mean 54 ms, worst 174 ms
column5: Streaming with objects on: 16 sectors, mean 54.2 ms, worst 173.6 ms, against 12.6 / 39.9 ms for terrain alone. The extra is object texture decode - object sprite sheets are various sizes, some much larger than the 256x256 terrain tiles, and each needs its own ImageTexture because they cannot share a Texture2DArray. The shared _obj_tex cache amortises across sectors (adjacent sectors reuse art heavily) so the steady state is better than the cold figure, but 174 ms is ~10 dropped frames and is the largest hitch the port has had. Cheapest levers, in order: raise loads_per_frame granularity so one sector's objects are split across frames; decode object textures lazily per texture rather than per sector; and only then consider threading. Do not optimise before measuring which of decode / upload / mesh build dominates - the last two times this project assumed the bottleneck it was wrong (the ARGB4444 CPU loop, and the mipmap fix).

column4: the object anchor and sort order were ALREADY correct - I misread a close-up as a bug
column5: Row 245 recorded "walls float, roof sections misalign, pieces occlude in the wrong order" as two unverified assumptions needing the retail oracle. Both readings were wrong, and the error was mine: the screenshot was taken at zoom 1200, i.e. about 25 cells of viewport, which is an extreme close-up of the INSIDE of a building. Overlapping walls and roof planes at that scale are simply what isometric architecture looks like. Settled by iterating the anchor in PYTHON instead of rebuilding the port - compositing sector 64,39's 165 objects under three candidate anchors (bottom-centre, top-left, centre) and looking. Bottom-centre assembles a coherent castle: tiled spire, arched gateway with a signboard, staircases, courtyard walls. Rendering the same view in Godot at a matching zoom (3900) then produces a recognisable Sacred town - conical tower roofs, guild hall, stone stairs, fences, standing stones, market stalls. Object-vs-terrain depth was already right because it reuses the terrain's own z = (cx+cy)*DEPTH_STEP formula. Lesson, and it is not a new one here: pick a zoom that shows the whole structure before calling placement broken.

column4: two real bugs did come out of the anchor review - an axis-sign error and a Node leak
column5: (1) ANCHOR SIGN. The object position is flipped into Godot's y-up space as p = (ox, -oy), but the header's i16 dy was being added in the file's y-down convention: origin.y = p.y + h + dy. Correct is p.y + h - dy. Affects only the ~10% of sprites with a nonzero dy (dx and dy are 0 for 89-90% of the 16255 entries with art, and are always <= 0, mean -2.4 / -2.7), which is exactly why it did not show up as an obvious visual break. (2) NODE LEAK. _build_objects allocated a Node3D root and returned null when no textures resolved, without freeing it - Node is not RefCounted, so Godot reported "1 ObjectDB instance was leaked at exit". Caught only because the headless run's tail was read rather than just grepped for the invariant. Both fixed; parity harness and 28672/63 unchanged, and --region=64,39,1 now reports 36864 quads / 124 textures.

column4: ox/oy is the sprite's TOP-LEFT, not its ground point - my "bottom-centre" reading was wrong and row 247's retraction was wrong too
column5: The user, watching the port live, confirmed objects were misaligned - after I had retracted that exact report in row 247 on the strength of static screenshots. Settled numerically instead of visually: regressing the placement residual (ox - 48*(cx-cy), oy - 24*(cx+cy)) against the sprite's own w and h over 11,465 objects gives slope -0.466 vs w (corr -0.785) and -0.948 vs h (corr -0.816). Those are -1/2 and -1: ox ALREADY carries -w/2 and oy ALREADY carries -h. So the stored position is the sprite's top-left corner in screen space, and the old code re-applied both offsets on top, displacing every piece by an amount proportional to ITS OWN size - which is exactly why parts of one building came apart while each part looked internally fine. Correct placement is origin = (ox + dx, oy + dy) with no size term. The same error explains the occlusion symptom: depth was taken from oy, i.e. the sprite's TOP, so a tall building sorted as if it stood at its own rooftop. Ground depth is oy + h. One root cause, both reported symptoms.

column4: I retracted a true bug report because I checked it the cheap way - and the cheap way was a close-up
column5: Row 247 concluded the anchor and sort order were "already correct" after eyeballing one Python composite of ONE candidate anchor, at a scale where a several-hundred-pixel misplacement is invisible. The three-candidate comparison I claimed to have made was never actually looked at - I rendered all three and viewed only the first. What settled it was a regression against sprite size, which is a measurement rather than an impression, and which took one script. Two process rules follow. First: when a symptom is "things are offset", the discriminating test is almost always a correlation against the thing they might be offset BY, not another screenshot. Second: a human watching the thing move is better evidence than any static capture an agent takes, so a user contradiction outranks my own visual check.

column4: object sprites still show dark voids, and the texture cache thrashes at wide zoom
column5: Two loose ends after the anchor fix. (1) VOIDS: some tiles render as flat dark blobs. Most likely _object_texture returning null - decode_texture only handles image type 4 (ARGB4444), so any object sheet in another type silently drops its whole per-texture mesh, leaving a hole. Check the type distribution across the object sheets before assuming. (2) CACHE THRASH: a --zoom=6000 view needs more than IMAGE_CACHE_MAX=512 textures, and the cache is clear-when-full, so it evicts everything and re-decodes continuously; the render never settled and had to be killed. That is the ceiling the ponytail comment on IMAGE_CACHE_MAX predicted. Fix is an LRU, or simply sizing the cache to the worst realistic window.

column4: the "dark voids" are NOT an unsupported texture format - every object sheet is type 4
column5: Row 251 guessed the voids came from decode_texture only handling image type 4, so sheets in another format would drop their whole per-texture mesh. Checked before fixing: all 10,585 distinct object textures referenced by mixed.pak are type 4 and 256x256, without exception. The hypothesis was wrong and the "fix" would have been a no-op. Second hypothesis, that the shapes are semi-transparent content (shadows, glass) drawn opaque by alpha-scissor, was supported by the Python composite - which uses real alpha_composite and looks clean - so object.gdshader was moved to blend_mix with ALPHA = c.r and a discard only below 0.02. That is more correct in principle but did NOT remove the shapes. Looking again at native zoom, they are not voids at all: they are the building's own floor and terrace sprites drawn over roofs they belong behind. So the remaining artifact is object-vs-object depth ordering, which is a design problem (per-texture batching fights per-tile painter order), not a texture or transparency bug. Do not attempt a third quick fix; it needs the retail arena screenshot as a reference and a deliberate sorting design.

column4: cache thrashing fixed by bounding the zoom, not by growing the cache
column5: Sacred has THREE discrete zoom steps and the wheel snaps between them, so IsoCamera now exposes ZOOM_SCALES instead of a continuous 300..12000 range. That is what actually fixes the thrash: bounding the zoom bounds how many sectors can be in view, so the working set can no longer exceed the cache. Eviction is also now partial FIFO (drop the oldest quarter, Godot Dictionary preserves insertion order) rather than a full clear, so a momentary overshoot costs 192 entries instead of everything, and the cap is 768. Before: a --zoom=6000 render never settled and had to be killed. After: the widest zoom step settles at 16 sectors, mean 54.1 ms, worst 185.9 ms. ⚠️ The two ratios 0.75 and 0.5 in ZOOM_SCALES are NOT measured from Sacred - only the count (three) and the discrete behaviour are established, and the code says so. Scale 1.0 is confirmed correct by rendering: at 1:1 the art shows individual roof tiles, ivy and window frames crisply, which is the resolution it was authored at.

column4: Sacred's three camera zoom steps MEASURED at 2.0 : 1.0 : 0.5, confirmed three independent ways
column5: Needed because the port had invented 0.75/0.5 and the user did not know the real values. (1) Added mouse-wheel support to install/shim/autopilot.c - SDL 1.2 buttons 4 and 5, emitted as ordinary press/release pairs, since the engine reads the wheel only as those events and zoom cannot be driven without them (new script verb: `wheel <4|5> <n>`). (2) Drove the retail game headlessly under Xvfb through Main Menu -> Load Game -> select save -> Load -> OK confirmation, into the shipped autosave, then stepped the wheel and captured each state. Recovered the ratio by resizing one capture until it best correlated with the next: one step down = 0.50x (corr 0.84), one step up = 2.00x (corr 0.96), further steps in either direction change nothing (mean abs diff 0.2 of 255) - so exactly three levels, confirming the user's report. (3) The user then supplied their own captures named regular/zoomin/zoomout: zoomin->regular = 0.50x (corr 0.88) and regular->zoomout = 0.50x (corr 0.94), identical result from a different session and a different resolution. Which level is NATIVE comes from tile pitch: autocorrelating the reference screenshots gives a 48 px vertical lattice, i.e. the 96x48 cell drawn 1:1, and those shots are at the default - so "regular" is native, the closest step upscales 2x and the widest halves. ⚠️ The direct zoomin->zoomout measurement returned 0.30 at corr 0.38 and is NOT evidence; at a 4x scale gap the correlation collapses. The two adjacent-pair measurements are what carry the result, and they imply 0.25 exactly.

column4: object "dark voids" had TWO causes; the sorting half is fixed, the visibility half is a game mechanic
column5: Cause A (fixed): _build_objects batched quads by texture into ~10 sibling MeshInstance3Ds. object.gdshader is blended and does not write depth, so object-vs-object order is submission order -- but Godot sorts transparent INSTANCES by AABB centroid distance, one key per mesh, for meshes spanning a whole sector. The per-vertex Z was therefore never consulted between batches and a building whose roof and floor came from different texture pages drew in centroid order. Fix: one surface per sector with a Texture2DArray, layer in UV2.x, same pattern as terrain. Verified every mixed.pak texture is 256x256 (209956/209956 tile references) so no padding is needed. Buildings now composite correctly internally. Regression 50,50,1 unchanged at 28672 quads / 63 textures, no leaks.

column4: retail SWAPS building exterior and interior object sets; it does not fade or depth-sort them
column5: manuals/Screenshots/sacred88.png shows a house from outside with a complete unbroken roof and no interior visible at all. sacred86.png shows the player inside: roof AND outer walls are entirely absent and the room is drawn as its own lit scene with floor, furniture and inward-facing walls. So this is a visibility swap keyed on whether the player is inside a region, NOT a draw-order problem. The port currently draws both sets at once, which is the whole remaining artifact -- the "voids" are unlit interior floors and walls painted over roofs.

column4: co-located statics are NOT exterior/interior variants distinguished by a constant type delta
column5: Two objects at identical x,y with identical tile counts (idx 931444 type 28558 and 931445 type 24486, delta 4072) looked like a roofed/cutaway pair. Compositing both sprites in Python produced PIXEL-IDENTICAL art, so they are duplicate variants. Across all 12373 co-located pairs the top type deltas are 0 (7723), 8, 7, 10 -- no constant 4072. Generalising from two samples was the error.

column4: static.pak +0x1f is not a link field
column5: It equals i+1 for 1038013 of 1038014 records, is never symmetric, and each target is used once: a sequential id, not a relation. It reached the top of a same-position link scan only because sequential neighbours often share a position.

column4: neither static.pak +0x14 nor +0x08 separates interior from exterior
column5: +0x14 has exactly 4 values (0,1,2,3) globally, which looked like a storey index, but every one of the 114 art-bearing objects around the test building has +0x14 = 2. +0x08 splits the 165 drawn objects in sector 64,39 into 113 with value 8 and 51 with value 0; rendering only value 8 is visually indistinguishable from rendering all, so both roof and interior live in the same group.

column4: the interior/exterior discriminator is most likely in the unread part of the sector stream or in triggers.pak
column5: Sector 64,39 decompresses to 492348 bytes but the 64x64 cell array is only 131072. Most sectors carry just a 324-byte mostly-zero footer; this town carries 361276 extra bytes with a clean 32-byte stride (byte-repeat rate 1.00 at stride 32, 0.99 at 64). That is roughly 11000 additional 32-byte records in one town sector and the port has never read them. install/world/triggers.pak is also completely unexamined and is the natural home for "player is inside building N" regions. Cell -> static is strictly 1:1 (649 refs, 649 distinct), so duplicate drawing is ruled out as a cause.

column4: triggers.pak (TRG v1) decoded: flat 16-byte table, but only 1245 live triggers world-wide
column5: Layout: magic "TRG\x01", u32 count=2268 @4, records start at 0x100 with stride 16 (record 0 is a header record holding {136, 268 = data offset, 36288 = data size}; records 1..1022 are zero-filled unused slots). Live record fields: u16@0 = 16 constant (record size), u16@2 = target id with 1233 distinct values, u16@4 = TYPE with exactly 17 distinct values (5:203, 8:171, 9:118, 7:95, 14:91, 1:72, 10:70, ...), u16@6 = 1 constant, u32@8 = 0, u32@12 = the record's own index. Derived the base by anchoring on the self-index field: record 2032 sits at 0x8000, so record 0 sits at 0x100. Reading the first 12 bytes as a file header instead (the obvious guess) desynchronises every field.

column4: triggers.pak is NOT the building interior/exterior mechanism
column5: Only 1245 live triggers exist for the entire 6050-sector world. Sacred has far more than 1245 enterable buildings, so this table cannot be carrying a per-building "player is inside" region. It is some other sparse world-event table.

column4: sector stream layout is [4096 x 32 B cells][324 B footer][optional sparse extra]
column5: 5689 of 6050 sectors have exactly 324 bytes past the cell array, and that footer is almost entirely zeros. 361 sectors carry more. Inside the extra region of town sector 64,39 there is a short 7-record array at tail offset 32 with stride 36 holding u32 cell x and u32 cell y in the sector's own range (4096..4159, 2496..2559) -- consistent with the stride-36 absolute-coordinate records noted during Phase 3.1 recon.

column4: the 361 KB "unread tail" of the town sector is not a hidden object list -- it is 99.6% zeros
column5: This corrects results row 260, which called it the strongest remaining lead for the building interior mechanism. Byte-histogram over the whole 361276-byte tail of sector 64,39: 99.6% zero, and twelve equal slices all read between 0.0% and 1.0% non-zero. Roughly 1400 bytes of real content are scattered through a large sparse reserved array. The earlier "clean 32-byte stride, byte-repeat rate 1.00" measurement was an artifact of measuring repetition on mostly-zero data -- a stride detector will always report a perfect score on a run of zeros. Lesson: test for zero-fill BEFORE running a stride detector, or the detector confirms whatever stride you ask about.

column4: remaining candidates for the interior/exterior swap are the retail binary and floor.pak
column5: With triggers.pak and the sector tail both eliminated, the untested data file is install/world/floor.pak (indices already known to be count-1 like static.pak, contents never examined), and the untested method is the retail binary itself. autopilot.so can now drive the game including the mouse wheel, so walking a character through a door and diffing frames is available as behavioural ground truth, and the vtable/RTTI oracles from the earlier IDA battery give a way in statically.

column4: floor.pak is not a floor-texture table: magic is "OBJ", 6713136 records of 16 bytes (188 MB), forming LINKED LISTS
column5: Record layout: u32@0 = the record's own index (self-consistent, used to validate), u32@4 = payload (e.g. 0x0aeeee1b, 0x0a4eee0b, 0x0bceedeb -- meaning not yet determined), u32@8 = 0, u32@12 = NEXT record index, 0 terminating the chain. Index stride is a uniform 16 bytes with every entry size 16. This is a per-cell object CHAIN, not a flat array, which is why a fixed-stride read of the sector data never surfaced it.

column4: WldxEntry +0x0c is the index into floor.pak -- the world's SECOND per-cell object layer
column5: Tested by requiring floor.pak record r to satisfy rec[r].self == r. Of the 4096 cells in town sector 64,39, 2430 hold a valid self-consistent floor.pak index at +0x0c; the same test at +0x08 matches zero cells. Absent entries are 0xCDCDCDCD (uninitialised buffer fill), the same stale-buffer pattern already seen in the sector name field. This closes the "+0x04, +0x0c unknown -- suspected objects" note in the plan: +0x04 -> static.pak, +0x0c -> floor.pak. The port currently reads only +0x04, so it has never drawn this layer at all.

column4: decode floor.pak u32@4 and test whether the floor.pak layer is the building interior set
column5: The strongest remaining hypothesis for the interior/exterior swap: a file literally named floor.pak, with magic OBJ, holding a second per-cell object chain that the port does not render, is exactly the shape an interior/floor layer would take. Next steps: decode u32@4 (candidates: packed coordinates, a mixed.pak type id plus flags, or a bitfield -- the observed high bytes 0x0a/0x0b are suspiciously clustered), then render the floor.pak layer separately and compare against manuals/Screenshots/sacred86.png (interior) and sacred88.png (exterior).

column4: floor.pak u32@4 is not a sprite id under any straightforward reading
column5: Tested five interpretations against 4267 chain nodes from town sector 64,39. Best mixed.pak-with-art hit rate is 28% (u32>>8, 1213/4267); full u32 gives 104/4267, lo16 478, hi16 581. lo16 scores 4267/4267 "in tiles.pak range" but that test cannot fail -- tiles.pak has 90132 entries so any u16 lands inside it, which means it confirms nothing. Byte cardinalities suggest flags rather than an id: b1 has 17 distinct values and b3 has 7. Declined to render on the 28% hypothesis; that is the same strength of evidence that produced two retractions earlier today.

column4: floor.pak chain shape argues AGAINST it being the building interior set
