column5: Chains are short and near-ubiquitous: 1280 cells of length 1, 687 of 2, 305 of 3, 107 of 4, 37 of 5, 13 of 6 -- 4267 nodes over 2430 of 4096 cells, about 1.8 objects per cell spread across almost the whole sector including open ground. A building interior would cluster into large per-building groups, not spread thinly everywhere. This is the shape of ground clutter or decals. Structural argument, independent of the undecoded payload.

column4: interior geometry is tagged BY ASSET NAME in German, with a per-storey suffix
column5: Found by string-searching the Armalion 11-12-2001 prerelease disc image for German building vocabulary (dach/innen/haus/indoor/interior/roof). Hits: "DCTower innenmitte 1A_1", "DCTower innenoben 1A_1", "DCTower innenunten 1A_1", "TH01 Innenwand oben 1_01", "TH01 Innenwand oben 1_02", "Schneiderin innen". innen = inside, Innenwand = inner wall, oben/mitte/unten = upper/middle/lower. So the authoring pipeline distinguished interior pieces by name and carried a storey level. The retail Linux binary is stripped and yields only sound symbols (SOUND_FX_ATMOSPOT_ARENA_INDOOR, SOUND_FX_INDOORFIRE_LOOP), so the prerelease disc is the naming oracle.

column4: find the retail name table that survives for static objects, and classify interiors by name
column5: Both tiles.pak and mixed.pak records carry a name[32] field, but mixed.pak tile names observed so far are generic ("MIX233.444"). Next: dump name[32] across mixed.pak entries and check whether any carry authoring names containing "innen"/"Innenwand"; if not, look for a separate object-name table in install/pak or install/bin. If retail kept the names, interior classification is a substring test and the renderer fix is immediate. If retail stripped them, the Armalion disc can still supply a type-id -> name mapping to port across, since many assets are shared.

column4: mixed.pak does NOT carry authoring names -- all 16255 art sprites are generic
column5: Dumped name[32] at +16 across every mixed.pak entry with tiles. Every one is of the form "MIX<n>.444" (MIX0.444, MIX1.444, ...). Zero matches for innen/aussen/dach/haus. So interior classification cannot be done from mixed.pak alone.

column4: install/pak/items.pak IS the retail object-name table and it KEEPS the German authoring names
column5: Found by grepping the whole retail install for innenwand/innenoben/innenunten: exactly one file matches, install/pak/items.pak. It contains the same names as the Armalion prerelease disc, including the per-storey tower set ("DCTower innenunten 1A_1", "DCTower innenmitte 1A_1", "DCTower innenoben 1A_1", plus 1B variants) and a large FINALE_INNENMAUER_0_* series. So retail did not strip the names -- it simply does not store them in mixed.pak. items.pak is misnamed the same way floor.pak is (magic OBJ, not floors).

column4: map items.pak entries to mixed.pak type ids, then classify interiors by name substring
column5: This is the last link needed for the building interior/exterior mechanism. Steps: (1) parse items.pak (expect the standard 256-byte pak header + index at 0x100, but verify -- floor.pak and triggers.pak both deviated); (2) establish the correspondence between an items.pak entry and the static.pak "type" field that indexes mixed.pak, most likely a direct index equality, testable by checking that entries whose name says innen/Innenwand are exactly the sprites that look like interiors when composited; (3) once classified, hide the interior set by default in main.gd and show the exterior, which is what manuals/Screenshots/sacred88.png demands. The storey suffix (unten/mitte/oben) is a bonus: it gives the per-floor grouping that a full enter-building implementation will need later.

column4: items.pak parsed: "ITM" v5, 32768 uniform 128-byte records, name at +0x37, mixed.pak sprite id at +0x10
column5: Standard pak header this time (256-byte header, u32 count=32768 @4, index at 0x100 of {flags,off,size}, every size 128). Name field located by scanning every record offset for printable runs: +0x37 wins decisively (samples SERAPHIM.GRN, GLADIATOR.GRN, MAGICIAN.GRN, DARKELVE.GRN at ids 1-4, i.e. the hero classes). 17408 of 32768 entries are named.

column4: items.pak +0x10 is the mixed.pak sprite id -- this closes the name -> art link
column5: Identity mapping is WRONG: using the items.pak index itself as a mixed.pak index gives 70.2% art for innen entries against a 77.6% baseline, i.e. no signal, and the DCTower innen* entries all resolve to zero-tile sprites. Scanning all record offsets for a field that lands on a mixed.pak entry WITH art, +0x10 wins at 100.0% for innen entries versus 82.0% for named entries generally (+0x00 also hits 100% on innen but only 68.2% overall). The mapping is sequential and coherent: items 12172..12177 -> mixed 1404..1409, with 86-100 tiles each, which is the right magnitude for building interiors.

column4: build the reverse map mixed_id -> name and hide interiors in the renderer
column5: The chain is now complete and every link is verified: static.pak type indexes mixed.pak directly (already proven, 209956/209956 tile references), and items.pak gives name -> mixed id via +0x37 and +0x10. So invert it: for each of the 32768 items.pak entries, record map[u32@+0x10] = name@+0x37. Then a static object of type T is interior iff map[T] matches /innen/i. Wire into godot-port/sacred.gd as a lazily-built Dictionary[int, String] (32768 records x 128 B = 4.2 MB, cheap to scan once at startup) and skip those objects in main.gd _build_objects. Verify against manuals/Screenshots/sacred88.png -- the roof over the test building in sector 64,39 should close up completely. Then check the storey suffix unten/mitte/oben, which is the grouping a real enter-building implementation will need.

column4: items.pak name lookup wired into the port and working, but the "innen" rule is FAR too narrow to be the mechanism
column5: Sacred.Items added to sacred.gd (builds mixed sprite id -> is-interior from items.pak +0x10 and +0x37); main.gd opens pak/items.pak, prints the count, and _build_objects now skips interior sprites, with --interiors to draw the inside set instead. Startup reports "items 272 interior sprites". Regression 50,50,1 unchanged at 28672 quads / 63 textures, no parse errors, no leaks. BUT the town render at sector 64,39 is pixel-unchanged: this building's interior pieces are not named innen. Only 272 of 17408 named items.pak entries match, so the name rule covers under 2% and cannot be the general mechanism. The plumbing is correct and reusable; the classifier is wrong.

column4: the interior set is not marked by the word innen -- look for structure in items.pak's other fields
column5: Name-token survey over the 17408 named entries shows building vocabulary but no general inside/outside marker: dchouse 622, dungeona 422, dareethianer 322, pirates 319, thronsaal 317, stronghold 315, dwarf 277, dungeon 275, bridge 270, hbridge 251, jail 239, orkhaus 238, stallung 226, arena 217. So innen is one authoring convention among many, not the rule. Next: the items.pak record is 128 bytes and only two fields are decoded (+0x10 sprite id, +0x37 name). Survey the remaining fields for one that separates the DCTower innen* group (items 12172-12177, known-good interiors) from their exterior siblings, which should sit at adjacent ids. That is a small labelled training set and the right way in -- much better than another substring guess.

column4: items.pak carries NO structural interior/exterior field -- the records are byte-identical apart from the sprite id
column5: Surveyed against a clean labelled set found by listing the DCTower neighbourhood: items 12172-12177 are "DCTower innen*" (interior) and 12178-12183 are "DCTower Wand(aussen)*" (exterior wall), adjacent ids from the same authoring session. Across all 0x37 bytes before the name, zero offsets are internally constant within each group AND differ between groups. The full records differ only at +0x10 (the sequential mixed.pak sprite id). So the classifier cannot come from items.pak field data; the name is the only signal it carries.

column4: my earlier "aussen" search missed every exterior entry -- the file uses the sharp-s
column5: The name survey in row 280 grepped /innen|aussen|dach|haus/ and reported no general inside/outside marker. That was partly my own encoding bug: the data spells it "aussen" with U+00DF (latin-1 0xDF), e.g. "DCTower Wand(aussen) u_1A_01", so the ASCII spelling matched nothing. The conclusion in row 280 still stands on the innen count alone (272 of 17408), but the vocabulary survey underlying it was measuring less than it appeared to. Any future name search over this data must handle latin-1 umlauts and the sharp-s.

column4: the interior/exterior swap is probably a per-BUILDING grouping, not a per-object property
column5: Three independent negatives now point the same way: items.pak has no structural flag (row 281), static.pak +0x08/+0x14 do not separate the sets (row 259), and the name convention covers under 2% of entries and is inconsistent between authoring sessions (rows 279-280). What has never been examined is how objects are GROUPED into a building. Candidates, cheapest first: (a) the 32-byte WldxEntry has +0x08 still undecoded and +0x04 is documented as a globally unique object HANDLE with 862343 values -- handles imply a referencing structure somewhere; (b) sectors.wldx per-sector extra region held a stride-36 array with in-sector cell coordinates (row 263) which could be building footprints; (c) behavioural ground truth by driving the retail game through a door with autopilot.so, which remains untried and is the only method that cannot be fooled by a plausible-looking data reading.

column4: static.pak carries no building-group id either -- objects are not grouped by any per-record field
column5: Tested by taking the 165 art objects of sector 64,39 and splitting them into a spatial cluster around the test building (34 objects within 400 units of the centre) and a distant group (16 objects beyond 1200 units), then looking for a u32 field constant within each and different between them. Zero candidates. The only low-cardinality offsets (+0x14, +0x18, +0x34, +0x38, +0x3c) hold the SAME value in both groups, and several are 0xCDCDCDCD / 0xCD-patterned uninitialised buffer fill -- the same stale-buffer signature already seen in the sector name field and in WldxEntry +0x0c. +0x08 is 8 for the near cluster and {0,8} for the far one, which is the already-refuted flags field (row 259).

column4: stop looking for interior/exterior in the world data -- go behavioural, drive the retail game through a door
column5: Data archaeology has now produced eight consecutive negatives on this question: items.pak fields (281), items.pak names (279-280), static.pak +0x08 and +0x14 (259), static.pak grouping (284), triggers.pak (262), the sector tail (264), and floor.pak chain shape (270). Each was a reasonable reading of one artefact and a wrong reading of the game -- the same pattern the plan's opening section already names for the first six wrong assumptions of this project. The one method never tried is the one that cannot be fooled by a plausible data reading: autopilot.so can drive the retail game and already supports the mouse wheel, so load the shipped save, walk the character through a door, capture before and after, and diff. That tells us WHAT changes on screen before anyone guesses WHERE it is stored. Only then go back to the data, with a known answer to check against.

column4: BEHAVIOURAL GROUND TRUTH captured: the building cutaway is a hard swap, fires from OUTSIDE, and affects a whole complex at once
column5: Drove the retail game headlessly with autopilot.so: menu -> Load Game (512,415) -> save (460,326) -> Load (882,300) -> OK (420,438) into the shipped autosave, then walked the character up the steps toward an arched doorway with click verbs and captured at five timestamps (analysis/tools/shot.sh door1). Frames at /tmp/shot-door1/. Findings: (1) the roof CENTRE is removed leaving the tiled ring and the outer walls, revealing interior floor, benches, an altar and a lectern -- a cutaway, not a fade, and not a whole-building swap; (2) the transition is INSTANT between captures, no intermediate blend; (3) the trigger fires while the character is still OUTSIDE, standing on the steps below the door -- it is proximity/region, not "is inside"; (4) BOTH the octagonal hall and the separate colonnade building lost their roofs simultaneously, so one trigger covers a whole complex, which is what finally ruled out per-object and per-building properties as the mechanism.

column4: sector streams carry a REGION TABLE with per-region sub-grids -- this is the interior structure
column5: Layout: [4096 x 32 B cells][region table][region grids]. The table starts at tail offset 32 with stride 36; 2231 records exist across the 361 sectors that have anything past the 324-byte footer (5689 sectors have none). Record: +8 u32 region cell x, +12 u32 region cell y (absolute, inside the owning sector), +16 u16 w, +18 u16 h, +20 u32 type = 6 (constant -- and a scan for this constant returns exactly 2231, independently confirming the coordinate-anchored count), +24 u32 offset into the DECOMPRESSED SECTOR STREAM (not the tail), +28 u32 byte size. The size field is exactly w*h*32 in every case, verified arithmetically: 13x8 -> 0xd00 = 3328, 13x13 -> 0x1520 = 5408, 50x55 -> 0x157c0 = 88000. So each region owns a w x h array of 32-byte cells -- an interior floor plan. The first grid begins at tail offset 284, exactly where the 7-record table ends (32 + 7*36 = 284), confirming the layout.

column4: the sector tail is NOT 99.6% padding -- it is these region grids, and they account for essentially all of it
column5: Results row 264 called the town tail a large sparse reserved array and used that to kill it as a lead. The zero measurement was right and the interpretation was wrong. Sector 64,39 has four co-located 50x55 regions plus a 13x8 and a 13x13: 4*88000 + 3328 + 5408 = 360736 bytes against a 361276-byte tail, i.e. the grids account for essentially the whole thing. They read as 99.6% zero because interior floor plans are sparse, not because they are padding. The four regions sharing one cell coordinate (4110,2505) are almost certainly the STOREYS -- matching the DCTower innenunten / innenmitte / innenoben naming found in items.pak.

column4: decode the region grid cell format -- it is not the WldxEntry layout
column5: Region cells are 32 bytes like WldxEntry but do NOT carry a static.pak index at +4: zero of 104, 169 and 2750 cells resolve to an art-bearing object under that reading. Raw dumps show cells that are almost entirely zero with a single non-zero byte at cell offset 31 (values 0xd0, 0xd1 observed). So the interior grid uses a different, much thinner per-cell record than the terrain grid. Next: dump the non-zero cells of the 13x8 region (2.2% non-zero, the densest of the six and the smallest, so the best specimen), determine what the +31 byte indexes, and check whether interior OBJECTS live in a parallel list rather than in the grid itself. The behavioural captures in /tmp/shot-door1 are the oracle -- the 50x55 region is the octagonal hall whose benches and altar are visible in sacred-50000.png.

column4: region grid cell format DECODED: 32 bytes of which only two are used -- byte31 = cell class, byte30 = door attribute
column5: Method note: this is the first positive result after eight consecutive negatives on the interior question, and it came from DUMPING BEFORE HYPOTHESISING. A per-byte-offset non-zero census over the 13x8 region showed only offsets 30 and 31 are ever set, which collapsed the search space before any guess was made. Laying byte31 out on the 13x8 grid renders a floor plan by eye: 0xd1 traces a closed perimeter, 0xd2 fills the inside, one 0xd9 sits IN the wall carrying an extra byte, and three 0xda sit immediately outside it. Walls, floor, door, threshold.

column4: cell class codes confirmed across all 1870 region grids, with a sharp falsifiable test on the door attribute
column5: Class histogram over every region in the world: 0x00 empty 143806, 0xd1 82866, 0xd0 21064, 0xe0 18580, 0xd2 16302, 0xda 2420, 0xe2 1802, 0xd9 566, 0xe9 385. Border cells are 87.3% 0xd1 (20305/23250), supporting wall. Interior cells are only 13.1% 0xd2 because regions bound more area than the building occupies, so most interior cells are empty -- expected, not contrary. The decisive test was a sharp prediction made BEFORE measuring: if low-nibble 9 means door, byte30 should attach to those classes and nowhere else. Result: 0xe9 80.3% (309/385), 0xd9 30.9% (175/566), 0xd1 0.0% (3/82866), 0xd0 0.0% (4/21064). Five orders of magnitude separation. byte30 only ever holds the value 4.

column4: determine what separates the 0xd0-family from the 0xe0-family, then wire regions into the port
column5: The class codes split into two parallel families with matching low nibbles: 0xd0/0xd1/0xd2/0xd9/0xda and 0xe0/0xe2/0xe9. Same structure, so the high nibble is likely storey or an inside/outside distinction -- which matters because sector 64,39 has FOUR co-located 50x55 regions that are almost certainly storeys (matching items.pak innenunten/innenmitte/innenoben). Test by rendering one region's class grid as an image and comparing against /tmp/shot-door1/sacred-50000.png, where the octagonal hall interior is visible. Then the port can use the region table directly: a region gives the building footprint, the wall ring, and the door cell, which is everything needed to reproduce the retail cutaway -- remove roof art inside the footprint when the player is near the door cell.

column4: region reader wired into the port and VISUALLY CONFIRMED -- the decode renders as a floor plan
column5: Sacred.Regions added to sacred.gd (RefCounted, matching the existing Pak/Tiles/World/Statics/Mixed/Items data-class pattern; Resource was considered and rejected because .tres serialisation is unusable here -- retail data is read at runtime, never authored or shipped). main.gd gained --regions, which draws one flat diamond per classified cell. Result at sector 64,39: a closed red wall ring, blue floor filling it including the L-shaped notch that matches the raw 13x8 byte dump, a single yellow DOOR cell in the wall, and green STEP cells immediately outside it -- correctly positioned on the terrain. This is independent visual confirmation of rows 290-291. Regression 50,50,1 unchanged at 28672 quads / 63 textures.

column4: the region table field offsets in row 287 were 8 bytes early
column5: Row 287 gave x at +0x08, y at +0x0c, w/h at +0x10/+0x12, type at +0x14, grid offset at +0x18, size at +0x1c. Those came from a Python analysis that framed the stream as starting at the cell array, ignoring the 32-byte sector NAME header that Sacred.World.entries already accounts for. The clean framing is: table starts at NAME + 64*64*32 = 131104 exactly, stride 36, with x at +0x00, y at +0x04, w/h at +0x08/+0x0a, type at +0x0c, grid offset at +0x10, size at +0x14, remainder zero padding. Found because the first GDScript render produced no overlay at all; a scan for the type-6 marker located the true boundary at stream 131096 under the old framing, i.e. 8 bytes before where the record actually starts.

column4: region floor cells are NOT the general interior/exterior discriminator
column5: Hypothesis: an object standing on a region FLOOR cell is interior furnishing, one on a WALL cell is structure, so hiding floor-standers reproduces the retail exterior. Measured across all 361 sectors that have regions: 45188 art objects, of which 13137 (29.07%) fall inside a footprint, but only 1509 stand on a FLOOR cell and 4307 on a WALL cell. 1509 world-wide is far too few to be every interior furnishing. Enabling the rule also leaves the sector 64,39 test building pixel-unchanged, because that building has no region at all -- the overlay shows its footprints lie elsewhere in the sector. Only 1870 region grids exist for the whole world, so regions cover SOME enterable buildings, not all of them. Shipped as opt-in --cutaway rather than default, so the port does not silently hide 1509 objects on an unverified rule.

column4: roofs are still unclassified -- that, not the region table, is what blocks the dark-voids fix
column5: The region work is real and verified but does not touch the original artifact. What is still missing is a way to identify ROOF art specifically. Two angles not yet tried: (a) the retail captures in /tmp/shot-door1 show the same building with and without its roof centre, so diffing those two frames isolates the roof pixels, and the roof sprite can then be identified by correlating against composited mixed.pak candidates -- this is the labelled-example route and it needs no new format guesses; (b) the 0xd_ versus 0xe_ class families in the region grids are still undecoded and may be storey levels, which would matter for multi-floor buildings.

column4: roof frames diffed successfully by solving the camera translation -- the removed art is isolated
column5: No two captures in /tmp/shot-door1 share a camera (it follows the character; all ten frame pairs differ by 47-56% of pixels). The scroll is a pure 2D translation, so it is solvable rather than a reason to re-capture: a coarse-then-fine search for the integer offset between sacred-32000 (roof on) and sacred-44000 (roof off) converged at dx=84 dy=-74, dropping mean absolute difference from 33.29 to 9.85. Diffing the aligned overlap at threshold 60 and masking the HUD band leaves 135209 changed pixels. Artefacts written to /tmp/shot-door1/al_before.png, al_after.png, al_mask.png, al_removed.png -- the last being the removed pixels drawn from the roof-on frame, i.e. the cutaway art in isolation.

column4: the cutaway removes MORE than roofs -- it removes everything that occludes the interior, which reframes the whole search
column5: al_removed.png shows the vanished art is not just roof tiles: it includes the octagonal tower's tiled roof AND its upper wall face complete with the tall arched window AND the entrance arch, plus the colonnade's roof. Meanwhile the tower's FAR-side wall ring survives and is visible behind the benches in al_after.png, as does the near-side low wall. So the removed set is precisely the geometry that would be drawn over the interior floor in screen space, and nothing else. HYPOTHESIS (not yet verified): the mechanism is a screen-space occlusion test against the region footprint, not a per-object roof property. This would explain why eight consecutive searches for a per-object flag failed (rows 259-284) -- there may be no such flag, because the engine does not need one.

column4: roofs are not identifiable by name either -- only 4 items.pak entries contain "dach"
column5: Searched all 17408 named items.pak entries for roof vocabulary. German Dach: 4 hits, all one tower (Wb_turm2_Dach, Wb_turm2_Dach_oben, plus .tga duplicates, mapping to mixed ids 4608/4656/4707/4757). English roof: 0. For comparison: wand 348, innen 272, mauer 155, aussen 18, aussen-with-sharp-s 11. So naming is an inconsistent authoring convention across the board and cannot classify roofs, closing the last name-based avenue.

column4: test the occlusion hypothesis in the port, where the geometry is already available
column5: The port already has everything the test needs: object sprite bounding boxes in screen space (computed in _build_objects from the mixed.pak dst rects) and region footprints with per-cell classes (Sacred.Regions). Test: hide any object whose screen-space sprite rect overlaps the projection of a region's FLOOR cells AND which sorts in front of them, then compare against /tmp/shot-door1/al_after.png. Pick a building that HAS a region -- sector 64,39's test building does not, which is why the floor-cell rule appeared inert there (row 295). If this reproduces the retail cutaway it also explains the dark voids without any per-object classification, and the --cutaway flag becomes the real implementation rather than the placeholder it is now.

column4: occlusion cutaway implemented; the DEPTH condition is what makes it viable, and omitting it is fatal
column5: Implemented in main.gd as _occludes_interior: project the sprite's screen rect to a cell-space AABB, count region FLOOR cells inside it, skip the object's own footing, and hide it past OCCLUDE_CELLS (4). Test specimen chosen by measurement rather than convenience -- sector 20,23, region 1299,1491, 45x44, which has 127 objects standing on floor cells, the most in the world, and carries three co-located regions (127/115/20 objects) matching the storey pattern. Attempt 1 without a depth condition stripped nearly the entire fortress: almost every sprite covers 4+ foreign floor cells, so the rule fired on everything. Attempt 2 added the condition that only cells strictly BEHIND the object's own footing count (iso depth cx+cy), which is required by the retail evidence -- a far wall covers interior floor in screen space too, but is drawn behind it and survives in al_after.png. With depth in, the fortress keeps its walls, towers and bridge while overhead planes are removed. Regression 50,50,1 unchanged at 28672 quads / 63 textures.

column4: the occlusion rule is PLAUSIBLE but NOT VERIFIED -- removing the roofs on the test fortress reveals bare terrain, not an interior
column5: With the depth condition the output is structurally sensible, but what appears under the removed roofs is snow terrain, not the furnished interior retail shows in /tmp/shot-door1/al_after.png. Two readings, not yet separated: either this fortress genuinely has no modelled interior and its region serves some other purpose, or the rule is also removing the interior objects along with the occluders. This cannot be settled from the current captures because there is no retail screenshot of sector 20,23 -- the door1 capture is somewhere else and its world coordinates are unknown. Recording this as unverified rather than claiming the cutaway works: the picture looks better, which is exactly the condition under which a wrong rule gets adopted.

column4: locate the door1 capture in world coordinates so the cutaway has a reference to be judged against
column5: Every remaining question about the cutaway -- does it remove too much, does it reveal the right interior, is OCCLUDE_CELLS = 4 right -- needs one retail screenshot matched to one port render of the same place. The capture shows an octagonal hall with benches and an altar, a colonnade with bookcases and beds, a statue in a courtyard and a stone well, at the shipped autosave near Valor's Fortress. Options: drive the retail game to a landmark whose sector is already known; read the player position out of install/save/game01.pak (a blind coordinate scan produced 3504 candidates in the first 400 KB, so it needs an anchor rather than a scan); or render candidate sectors in the port and correlate against the capture. Until then the cutaway stays behind --cutaway and is not the default.

column4: the retail debug log records per-object world positions and type ids -- Ref[1] Type[1] Fam[3] is the hero
column5: cObjectManager::load() emits one line per object: "Ref[N] Type[T] Fam[F] wp[a,b,c] size[S]". The door1 capture log carries 1211 such lines, 864 with a non-zero wp. Ref[1] Type[1] Fam[3] wp[2579,173827,135544] is the player. Field ranges over the 864: f0 min 0 med 2581 max 5938; f1 min 9418 med 166014 max 338549; f2 min 4320 med 137196 max 336993.

column4: the log's wp[] is NOT in static object coordinate space, and the log cannot locate the capture
column5: Decisive evidence: NO field is ever negative across all 864 entries, but static ox = 48*(cx-cy) must be negative over half the world, so f1/f2 cannot be ox/oy. Every field ordering was scored by how many objects land in a sector that actually has content (361 of 6050): (2nd,3rd) 1%, (1st,2nd) 9%, (1st,3rd) 17%, (3rd,2nd) 1% -- and the apparent "top sectors" in each are diagonal runs like 44,43 / 45,44 / 46,45, which is the artifact you get when cx is approximately cy, not a real cluster. An offset search over f1 peaked at O=134400 with 23%, placing the hero at cell 3234,2413; rendering there shows a ploughed field, not the captured fortress courtyard. Separately, the log's Type[] ids share ZERO values with the static object types of all 361 content sectors, because cObjectManager loads DYNAMIC objects (NPCs, items) whose type and coordinate spaces are both distinct from the static scenery. Sector 72,15, the first candidate, is a filler sector: one tile id across all 4096 cells, no statics, uniform light 255.

column4: locate the capture by region SHAPE, not by coordinates
column5: Coordinate decoding has now failed five ways and should be dropped. The capture shows a distinctive octagonal hall roughly 12-15 cells across, and the region table (row 287) stores exactly that: per-region grids whose FLOOR cells give the room outline. Searching the 1870 region grids for a floor area with octagonal outline and the right size is cheap and needs no coordinate space at all. Two fallbacks if that misses: render the 361 content sectors from Python using the existing mixed.pak compositor (much cheaper than Godot renders) and correlate against the capture; or decrypt scripts/us/global.res, which the game decrypts at load -- the log prints crypted[1060098] decrypted[102355], so both sizes are known and the region name table ("Valor's Fortress", from the autosave name) is inside it but not plaintext.

column4: no octagonal hall exists in the region grids -- and the search revealed the grids are not what I called them
column5: A shape search over all 1870 grids for an octagonal FLOOR outline (near-square bbox, fill 0.62-0.95, empty corners, full mid-edges) returned ZERO candidates. Dumping the largest regions as ASCII instead of testing a guessed signature shows why: class 0xd2 does not outline rooms. In sector 20,23's 45x44 region it fills a large irregular OUTDOOR courtyard, with wall runs threading through it and small rooms as separate enclosures. The capture's octagonal hall is not there.

column4: the region grids are a NAVIGATION / collision map, not building interiors -- this revises rows 290, 291 and 293
column5: The class vocabulary reads correctly as walkability, not architecture: 0xd1 blocks (walls, and it traces closed perimeters as observed), 0xd2 is walkable open ground (which is why it covers courtyards, not just rooms), 0xd9 is a door (a passable gap IN a blocking run, which is exactly where a door sits), 0xda is a step or threshold (a level transition, and it appears immediately outside doors). The two co-located 45x44 regions in sector 20,23 differ in their room layouts -- one has an enclosure at rows 17-26, the other at rows 26-35 with a door and steps -- which fits multi-LEVEL navigation and also explains the four co-located regions in sector 64,39. The earlier reading was not wrong about the codes, only about what they describe: I saw a wall ring around a walkable area and called it a floor plan. This also explains row 302 cleanly: the occlusion cutaway at sector 20,23 removed roofs and revealed bare terrain because the "interior floor" under them was an outdoor courtyard all along.

column4: the interior/exterior mechanism is still unfound; the region table is a navmesh and should be reused as one
column5: Consequences: the --cutaway rule keyed on FLOOR cells is testing walkability, not interiority, so it cannot be the mechanism regardless of tuning, and it should not be promoted to default. The region table remains valuable -- it is a shipped navigation and collision map with doors, level transitions and multi-storey layers, which the port will need for movement, and it is fully decoded. For the interior question the untried routes are unchanged: decrypt scripts/us/global.res (crypted[1060098] decrypted[102355]) for the region name table, or render the 361 content sectors from Python and correlate against /tmp/shot-door1 to locate the capture.

column4: global.res is NOT encrypted -- rows 306 and 309 misread a save-loading log line as being about it
column5: The debug.log line "crypted[1060098] decrypted[102355]" sits between "* Team/AllianceInfo" and "* Objects", both SAVE-file sections, so it describes save decryption (install/save/game01.pak, 2.6 MB), not scripts/us/global.res. Measuring global.res directly settles it: byte entropy 3.73 bits over 2760574 bytes, 46.1% printable, and the top bytes are 0x00, space, e, a, t -- that is plain data, not ciphertext. Encrypted content would sit near 8 bits.

column4: global.res decoded: "SZ" indexed UTF-16LE string table, 23122 records, 1195303 characters
column5: Layout: magic "SZ\0\0" at 0, then 16-byte index records {u32 key, u32 offset, u32 reserved, u32 length} from offset 4, with the string data beginning at 0x5a530. Payloads are UTF-16LE, which is why an 8-bit search for "Valor" returned nothing earlier -- decoded properly the file yields Valor x202, Treville x64, Fortress x20, Bellevue x97. Record 0 onward concatenates to the hero class list (Seraphim, Gladiator, Battle Mage, Dark Elf, Wood Elf...), confirming the parse. Keys start at 49 and are mostly but not strictly sequential, and the index slices strings slightly off their boundaries, so read by record POSITION and expect a leading fragment until the 4-byte length prefix is handled.

column4: sectors.keyx +0x2d8 is not a global.res string id, so it does not name regions
column5: +0x2d8 looked like the region field: 26 distinct values across 6050 sectors (6560 x663, 6510 x524, 6561 x467, ...), the right cardinality for Sacred's region count and in range for global.res. Resolving those as record positions returns spell and quest-book descriptions ("The Elf hurls rolling thorn shrubs...", "Ground poison description for quest book"), not place names, so the id space is different -- probably a separate per-category .res. Also mapped while there: keyx +0x298/+0x2a0/+0x2a8/+0x2b0 (167-177 distinct) pair with +0x29c/+0x2a4/+0x2ac/+0x2b4 (about 20 distinct, values 10/20/25/30/40) -- four (id, percentage) pairs per sector, i.e. a spawn table.

column4: locating the capture now needs the region NAME table, which is not in global.res's id space
column5: global.res holds the region names as text (Valor x202) but nothing maps a sector to one. Remaining routes: (a) find the per-category .res or script that sectors.keyx +0x2d8 indexes -- 26 distinct values matching Sacred's region count is a strong signal and only the target table is missing; (b) render the 361 content sectors from Python with the existing mixed.pak compositor and correlate against /tmp/shot-door1 -- brute force but bounded and needs no further format work; (c) drive the retail game to its map screen, which names the current region on screen.

column4: the door1 capture location is identified BY NAME: the Fortress of Urkenburgh
column5: Searching the decoded global.res string table for the autosave's character rather than its place name found position 9002: "Noble Seraphim! Go and find Sergeant Treville at the Fortress of Urkenburgh." Corroborated at position 7677, "The Fortress of Urkenburgh is the last bastion against the Orcs of Khorad-Nur", and position 1155 holds the bare place name "Urkenburgh" (20 bytes = 10 UTF-16 chars, exact). So the shipped autosave -- and therefore every frame in /tmp/shot-door1 -- is at Urkenburgh. The save's own title mentions Valor's Fortress, which appears to be a different or adjacent naming; Treville's posting is unambiguous in the quest text.

column4: sndprofiles.pak is not what keyx +0x2d8 indexes either
column5: sndprofiles.pak looked like a strong fit: magic "SPF", 8192 entries of uniform 184 bytes, comfortably containing the +0x2d8 value range 6504..6714, and an ambient profile per region would plausibly have about 26 distinct values across 6050 sectors. Falsified by the obvious discriminator: all 24 referenced entries are entirely zero, and so are 296 of 300 randomly sampled unreferenced entries. The table is shipped essentially unpopulated, so it cannot be carrying per-sector data. Note for future passes: check that a candidate table is POPULATED before reasoning about its index range -- an empty table accepts any id.

column4: global.res is a FLAT string pool, not grouped by category, so there is no contiguous region-name block to index
column5: Place names do not cluster. Position 1155 is "Urkenburgh" and 1158 is "Dryad Forest", but between and around them sit weapon names (Diablo's Gallant Saber), quest text and NPC barks. The 178 records containing "Valor" spread from position 203 to 23022. So sector -> name cannot be a small offset into a name table, and whatever keyx +0x2d8 indexes is a separate per-category table that has not been located in install/. Only one .res file ships (scripts/us/global.res); install/global.txt exists but is 0 bytes.

column4: with the location named, correlate rendered sectors against the capture -- the name gives a cross-check the brute force lacked
column5: Locating Urkenburgh in the 100x100 grid no longer needs the +0x2d8 table. Render the 361 content sectors from Python with the existing mixed.pak compositor and correlate against /tmp/shot-door1/al_before.png; the capture's landmarks are specific enough to score against -- an octagonal hall with benches and an altar, a colonnade with bookcases and beds, a courtyard statue, a stone well. Bounded work, no new formats. The name is the cross-check: whatever sector wins should be a fortress, and Urkenburgh is described as bordering the Orcs of Khorad-Nur, so it sits near an orc region.

column4: the door1 capture location is SECTOR 39,28 -- found by asset-family localisation, not by coordinates or pixels
column5: Method: build mixed-id -> name from items.pak, reduce each name to a family prefix, and map families to the sectors that use them. Of 242 families, 116 appear in 4 or fewer sectors and are therefore location-specific. The capture shows benches in rows facing an altar, beds, bookcases, a courtyard statue and a well -- monastic, not military -- which points at the family KLOSTER (German: monastery), present in exactly two sectors, 39,28 and 50,39. Rendering 39,28 shows the octagonal tower with conical tiled roof, the arched doorway at its base with stone steps, the colonnade and the grass courtyard -- the scene the character walked into. Sector 50,39 is a villa courtyard instead (Hof, BUSH_VILLA), so it is not the match. Confirmed structurally: sector 39,28 contains KLOSTER_KAPELLE01 parts -- Kapelle is German for chapel, which is exactly the octagonal hall with benches and altar.

column4: pixel cross-correlation cannot verify a port-vs-retail location match, and a control is what showed it
column5: Correlating the port render of sector 39,28 against the retail capture scored 0.047. That looks like a clean refutation until you run the control: the same search against an unrelated port render (the sector 20,23 snowy fortress) scores 0.050 -- indistinguishable. So the test has no discriminating power here and neither confirms nor refutes; differing time of day, camera offset and zoom defeat raw pixel correlation between the two engines. Without the control arm I would have recorded a false negative and abandoned a correct identification. Structural evidence (asset names present in the sector) is the right instrument for this comparison.

column4: building art is split BY LEVEL in the asset names, with an explicit both-levels form -- a far better interior classifier than "innen"
column5: Names follow <BUILDING>_<level>_<part>: across all 17408 named items.pak entries the level token frequencies are _1_ 455, _0_ 299, _2_ 249, _3_ 27, _4_ 17, plus combined forms _0U1_ 87, _0U2_ 63, _0U4_ 40, where U is German "und" (and) marking a piece that belongs to two levels at once. KLOSTER_KAPELLE01 alone has 157 parts split 0:25, 1:27, 2:72, 0U1:33. This is a general convention rather than one artist's habit, unlike innen (272 entries) and dach (4), both of which were refuted as classifiers in rows 279-280 and 299. If the engine shows one level and hides the others according to where the player stands, that IS the cutaway, and it is encoded in the name.

column4: test the level hypothesis against the capture, which can now be rendered side by side
column5: Everything needed is in place: the capture is at sector 39,28, the chapel is KLOSTER_KAPELLE01, its 157 parts carry explicit levels, and /tmp/shot-door1 holds the same building with and without its roof. Test: render sector 39,28 with each level set hidden in turn and compare against al_before.png (roof on) and al_after.png (roof off). The prediction to state before measuring is that hiding level 2 -- 72 of the 157 chapel parts, the largest group -- reproduces the cutaway, and that _0U1_ pieces survive in both states because they are marked as belonging to two levels. If that holds, the classifier is a name parse and the mechanism is finally identified.

column4: THE CUTAWAY MECHANISM IS THE LEVEL TOKEN IN THE ASSET NAME -- both retail states reproduced in the port
column5: Implemented Sacred.Items.levels(): parse <BUILDING>_<level>_<part> with RegEx _(\d)(?:U(\d))?_\d+$ into a level BITMASK, so a _0U1_ piece sets bits 0 and 1 and survives whichever of those two levels is hidden. 4333 of the mixed.pak sprites carry a parseable level. main.gd gained --hidelevel=N[,N]. Rendered at sector 39,28, the located capture site: --hidelevel=2 produces clean unbroken roofs with no interior showing, matching the retail exterior (/tmp/shot-door1/al_before.png); --hidelevel=0,1 removes the roof CENTRE while the tiled ring and outer walls remain and the octagonal chapel interior and colonnade floor become visible, matching the retail cutaway (al_after.png). Pixel deltas: baseline vs hide-2 10.3%, baseline vs hide-0,1 18.2%, and the two states differ from each other by 28.4%. Regression 50,50,1 unchanged at 28672 quads / 63 textures, no errors or leaks.

column4: the level->role direction was the OPPOSITE of my logged prediction
column5: Row 321 predicted, before measuring, that hiding level 2 would produce the cutaway because 72 of the chapel's 157 parts sit at level 2 and that was the largest group. The opposite holds: hiding level 2 gives the CLOSED exterior, so level 2 carries the interior content, while levels 0 and 1 carry the roofs and outer shell. The size argument was the error -- interior furnishing is more numerous than roof panels, so the largest group was always more likely to be the inside. The hypothesis under test (that the level token drives the swap) is confirmed; only my guess at the mapping was wrong, which is exactly what stating a prediction in advance is for.

column4: drive the level swap from player position and settle the numbering
column5: Remaining work is no longer discovery. (1) The port has no player, so choose a trigger -- the camera centre is the natural proxy until there is one, and the retail captures show the swap fires while the player is still OUTSIDE, on the steps below the door, so the test is proximity to the building not containment. (2) Confirm the level numbering on a second, multi-storey building rather than generalising from the chapel; the _0U2_ (63) and _0U4_ (40) forms imply buildings with more than two levels and should be checked against a case that has them. (3) Retire the --cutaway occlusion rule from row 301 -- it was keyed on navmesh walkability, is unverified, and is now superseded. (4) The dark voids in other sectors should resolve for free wherever the art carries a level token; sectors whose buildings have no parseable level (4333 sprites of 16255 with art do) will still show the artifact and are the next thing to look at.

column4: the reported "terrain boxes" are NOT terrain and NOT a renderer bug -- they are interior art drawn over exteriors
column5: Investigated in three steps, two of which refuted my own hypotheses. (1) Terrain is clean: rendered --noobjects at sector 39,28 and at the sector 20,23 snow, no boxes in either, so the artifact is entirely in the object layer. (2) Hypothesis "linear filtering bleeds across atlas tile edges" -- object sprites really are chopped into 64x64 tiles packed 16 to a 256x256 page, and tiles adjacent IN THE SPRITE are not adjacent in the atlas (sprite 24471 tile0 and tile1 stack vertically on screen but sit side by side in UV), so linear sampling really does pull wrong content into a 1px fringe. Switched to filter_nearest, which is also what the retail software blitter does. It did NOT remove the boxes. (3) Hypothesis "duplicate objects compound alpha" -- refuted, sector 39,28 has 184 art objects and zero exact duplicates yet shows the artifact. The answer came from compositing the same 184 objects independently in Python: the boxes appear IDENTICALLY, so this is not a Godot rendering fault at all. It is the same defect as the dark voids -- upper-level interior art drawn on top of the exterior shell.

column4: I called the Python composite "clean" from the wrong crop
column5: Having generated the Python ground truth I inspected a crop of the COURTYARD, which has few overlapping roofs, saw no boxes, and concluded the port was at fault. Aligning the composite to the port render properly (correlation 0.362 at scale 2.0, the composite having been saved half-size) shows the boxes in the same places in both. The lesson is narrow and worth keeping: when using an independent implementation as ground truth, compare the region that actually exhibits the artifact, not a convenient one.

column4: level tokens cover BUILDING parts specifically -- props correctly have none
column5: Sector 39,28 breakdown: 184 art objects, 80 carry a level token, 104 are named without one, 0 unnamed. The 104 are FENCE001-003, FLOWER003-011, MARKET21/22, PFAHL -- fences, flowers, market stalls, posts. A fence has no storey, so their absence is correct rather than missing data. Globally 4333 of 16255 art sprites (27%) are levelled, and those are the building parts. So the level mechanism has full coverage of the thing it needs to cover.

column4: hide level 2 does NOT generalise -- level numbering is per building, not a global convention
column5: Row 324 asked whether the chapel's numbering holds elsewhere. It does not. Across 192 building families with level tokens, the highest level present is 1 for 110 families, 2 for 54, 3 for 16, 4 for 3, and one family each at 6, 8 and 9. STALLUNG alone spans 0U4, 1U5, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6. So a building with only levels 0 and 1 cannot have its interior hidden by dropping level 2. Consequence: --hidelevel stays an explicit tool and the swap CANNOT yet be driven automatically from camera position, because the port does not know which level index is the interior for a given building. That mapping is the next thing to establish.

column4: the superseded occlusion cutaway is removed from the port
column5: Deleted _occludes_interior, _on_interior_floor, OCCLUDE_CELLS, the _cutaway flag and its CLI parsing. It was keyed on region FLOOR cells, which are navmesh walkability rather than interiority (row 308), and it was never verified. The region overlay (--regions) and Sacred.Regions stay -- the table is a genuine shipped navigation map. Regression 50,50,1 unchanged at 28672 quads / 63 textures, no parse errors, no leaks.

column4: row 328 was wrong -- "highest level = interior" DOES hold; my test was broken, not the hypothesis
column5: Row 328 concluded the numbering does not generalise, on the strength of rendering sector 32,54 (BLACKSMITH) and seeing hide-level-0 and hide-level-1 look nearly identical. The building was not in frame: the sector centre is not where BLACKSMITH stands. The tell was in the numbers I had already computed and did not act on -- baseline vs hide-0 changed 1.23% of pixels, baseline vs hide-1 1.74%, hide-0 vs hide-1 2.97%. Single-digit deltas mean the thing under test is not on screen, and I should have checked that before drawing a conclusion. Locating the family properly (83 objects centred on cell 2096,3493) reversed the result.

column4: a building family's HIGHEST level index is its interior -- verified on two structurally different buildings
column5: BLACKSMITH, levels 0 and 1: --hidelevel=0 opens the roof onto a stone floor with anvil on its block, barrel, forge and armour rack; --hidelevel=1 leaves the exterior intact. So interior = 1 = the top level. KLOSTER_KAPELLE01, levels 0, 1 and 2: --hidelevel=0,1 opens the roof onto the chapel floor and benches; --hidelevel=2 leaves a clean unbroken roof. So interior = 2 = the top level. Two buildings with different level counts, same rule, and it needs no per-building index -- which matters because 110 of the 192 levelled families top out at level 1 and 54 at level 2.

column4: --exterior implemented: hides each building family's top level, reproducing the per-building result exactly
column5: Sacred.Items now tracks family -> highest level and sprite -> its own level, where family is the name up to the level token (DCHOUSE01_FINAL_1_07 belongs to DCHOUSE01_FINAL), and exposes is_top_level(). main.gd gained --exterior. Cross-checked against the manual flags: on the chapel --exterior and --hidelevel=2 differ by 0.00% of pixels; on the blacksmith it matches --hidelevel=1. Regression 50,50,1 unchanged at 28672 quads / 63 textures, no parse errors, no leaks.

column4: interior PROPS are not covered by the level rule and remain visible
column5: The blacksmith's anvil, forge, armour rack and barrels are separate objects carrying no level token, so --exterior leaves them drawn over the roof. This is consistent rather than contradictory: props legitimately have no storey, which is why FENCE, FLOWER, MARKET and PFAHL have none either (row 327). But retail plainly hides the props that sit INSIDE a building, so a second, positional mechanism covers them -- most likely the same footprint test the building itself uses. This is now the largest remaining piece of the interior problem.

column4: resolve DAREETHIANER1 and find how retail hides interior props
column5: Two open items. (1) DAREETHIANER1 has levels 0-3 and neither hiding 3 nor hiding 0,1,2 yields a clean exterior; it is a cliff dwelling with a rock face behind, so its wooden decks may be legitimate exterior balconies rather than a counterexample to row 331. Deciding needs a retail capture of sector 17,11, which autopilot.so can now produce. (2) Interior props (row 333) need a positional rule. The region navmesh gives building footprints with walls and doors, so the natural test is whether a prop stands inside a footprint whose building is currently showing its exterior -- which would finally give the navmesh a role in the interior problem after it was ruled out as the mechanism itself in row 308.

column4: my brief to the tech mapper wrongly named Pillow and numpy as dependencies
column5: I primed the agent with "Python 3 with Pillow/numpy for the analysis tools". The agent checked and pushed back: all nine analysis/tools/*.py are stdlib-only (struct, zlib, json, hashlib, collections), and preview_terrain.py deliberately emits raw PPM piped to ImageMagick precisely to avoid an image library. Verified independently -- zero PIL or numpy imports in the checked-in tools. I had conflated throwaway heredoc scripts written during this session, which did use both, with the committed tooling. Worth keeping as a caution: priming a fresh-context agent propagates the orchestrator's errors as readily as its knowledge, and this one only surfaced because the agent verified rather than accepted.

column4: Sacred uses GRANNY 1.x, UNCOMPRESSED -- not Granny 2. The project's largest assumed risk collapses
column5: models.pak (434 MB, magic MDL v3, 4993 entries) carries 4991 embedded exporter blocks naming "RAD 3D Studio MAX 4.x / 3.x, (C) 1999-2000 RAD Game Tools". Verified independently: 4369 MAX 4.x + 622 MAX 3.x = 4991 exactly, zero GR2 section signatures, and payload entropy far below the ~7.99 that compressed data measures. Every public "Granny is impossible" account concerns GR2 -- Oodle section compression, pointer fix-up tables, type trees, the licensed SDK -- and none of it applies to 1.x, which is a sequential tagged-chunk stream with plaintext bone names. Difficulty estimate drops from months to days-to-low-weeks. Also found: models.pak holds ANIMATIONS as well as meshes (index kind 64 = mesh, 65 = animation), and motions.pak is 678 KB of motion parameters that embeds 434340164, the exact byte size of models.pak, as a pairing check.

column4: the research agent's GRN chunk offset was wrong -- magic is at +0x4EA, not +0x40
column5: The agent reported that each GRN begins with a 64-byte high-entropy preamble to skip, with 0xCA5E0000 at +0x40. That does not reproduce. Measured over 400 entries: the first 64 bytes of a models.pak entry are the ASCII NAME ("BAT.GRN\0..."), +0x40 is zeros, and the first 0xCA5E0000 sits at a CONSTANT +0x4EA in 399 of 400 entries, followed by a u32 chunk type. The high-entropy region the agent saw is real but sits between the name and the magic, not at the start. An implementer following +0x40 would fail on the first file. Its entropy figures also did not reproduce -- reported 4.88 bits/byte and 47% zeros, measured 6.65 and 21% on a different slice -- though both are far below the compressed threshold, so the conclusion stands and only the numbers are slice-dependent.

column4: THIRD recovered formula: the damage equation, from the German Loesungsbuch p.128
column5: Damage = PD*[PD/(PD+PR)] + MD*[MD/(MD+MR)] + FD*[FD/(FD+FR)] + GD*[GD/(GD+GR)], summing the four channels Physical/Magic/Fire/Poison, each attenuated by the defender's matching resistance. It uses exactly the BalCharPD/PR/... key names already mapped in analysis/balance-keymap.tsv. The book's five worked examples were re-checked: four reproduce exactly and the fifth is an arithmetic error in the book. Joins the to-hit formula and the skill-bonus curve as the third rule recovered without decompilation.

column4: the skill-bonus formula in docs/manuals-knowledge.md is a factor of 2 too small
column5: That write-up recorded bonus% = w*L/(L+50), fitted against a guide column assumed to be skill level 44. The Gold Loesungsbuch p.11 labels its columns literally "Wirkung Stufe 1 / Stufe 15 / Stufe 30", so the assumed level was wrong. Refitting with the stated levels gives 2w*L/(L+50), which reproduces the level-30 column exactly for all four families (Waffenkunde 150.0, Schwertkunde AW 112.5, SP 75.0, magic schools 75.0) and the level-15 column within 2 points -- the displayed bonus uses twice the stored coefficient. This matters immediately: Weapon Lore is the Gladiator's most important skill and it raises ALL FOUR damage channels together, not physical alone, so a 2x error there would corrupt every damage number in the vertical slice.

column4: the Gladiator slice is fully specified by the Loesungsbuch, and building interiors are a PREREQUISITE not polish
column5: LB p.15 gives the start quest step by step: the Gladiator begins in the CELLAR of the arena at Silberbach (Silver Creek); talk to the overseer, who tasks you with fighting; loot the cellar chest and equip; go out and kill two arena fighters; return to claim pay, at which point the boss betrays you. LB p.17 gives an unmodified level 1-30 stat table (level 1: STR 35, END 20, DEX 20, HP 149, Attack 27, Defence 23, weapon 12-22, 300 XP to level 2) -- a free oracle for validating the balance.bin read. LB p.19 gives all 11 combat arts at CA levels 1 and 5, including the counter-intuitive detail that regeneration time INCREASES as an art levels (Hard Hit 4s -> 11s). LB p.16 gives opening-region enemy stat blocks, all dealing pure Physical. Consequence for sequencing: the quest is offered INDOORS, so interiors are a hard prerequisite, which collides with the open interior-props defect in rows 331-334. At level 1 there is exactly one combat-art quickslot, so the slice needs Hard Hit only and combos are structurally out.

column4: actor state persistence is MECHANISM, not respawn POLICY -- the current never-resets behaviour is an unimplemented rule, not a retail-validated decision
column5: Raised by the user 2026-08-07 against the Phase 1 summary wording "a wounded monster stays wounded". Correct framing: Phase 1 fixed WHERE actor state lives (registry, not parented to the sector node), so the renderer no longer decides monster lifetime. It did NOT implement WHEN state resets. The bug it removed was state reset caused by the streamer queue_free-ing a sector at ~370 cells within seconds -- an artefact of memory management, not a game rule. Sacred DOES respawn normal enemies by design, and research already found the rule is coupled to quest state: clearing all side quests in a region dries respawn up ("region pacification", Loesungsbuch p.130, research/FEATURES.md line 78), with the character speaking a line and trader stock improving. Because respawn is quest-coupled, it MUST be able to consult quest state -- which is only possible now that the renderer does not own actor lifetime; under the rejected sector-parented design, pacification would have been unimplementable and respawn would have been an accident of player movement. OPEN AND UNVALIDATED: Sacred respawn timers/conditions for normal enemies are not decoded; which stats reset on respawn is not decoded; player death/respawn is LOW confidence and flagged verify-against-the-binary-first (research/FEATURES.md line 242, SUMMARY.md line 190). The current "state persists indefinitely" behaviour is therefore a PLACEHOLDER and must not be cited as faithful-to-retail. Project rule reaffirmed by the user: reproduce retail defaults including disliked ones (Sacred was criticised for its respawn settings -- that criticism is not licence to change them); mods/tuning/bug-fixes are a later opt-in layer on top of a finished canonical engine.

column4: PITFALL: texture.pak entry headers lie OUTSIDE the index-recorded size -- a naive read(offset, size) truncates every inflate
column5: Cost a wrong-turn while implementing the cursor (2026-08-07). The texture.pak index record gives {flags, offset, size}, but `size` counts only the DEFLATE payload; the 80-byte header (name[32], w u16 @32, h u16 @34, kind u8 @36) sits before it and is NOT included. Reading exactly `size` bytes from `offset` therefore yields header + payload-minus-80, and zlib fails with "incomplete or truncated stream" -- which reads like a corrupt or unsupported entry rather than a short read. Correct read is (offset, size + 80). This is already encoded in the port: Sacred.Pak.blob(i, extra) takes an `extra` parameter for exactly this reason and Sacred.decode_texture passes 80, with the header comment "The texture header lies outside the recorded size, hence the parameter." Recorded here because the port had it right and an independent Python reader still got it wrong -- any future out-of-engine tooling over texture.pak will hit the same wall.

column5: Found during Task 2 (02-01-PLAN.md), testing --bands=100000 (clamped to BAND_MAX=4096) at sector 64,39 zoom 1 against /tmp/p2/base_6439.png. _band_depth(p) depends only on pos.y, and at near-1-object-per-band granularity, two adjacent objects sharing an exact pos.y (common in a grid-aligned world, tie-broken only by ascending pos.x within the objs sort) land in different bands with an IDENTICAL sorting_offset. Inside one mesh this was never a problem -- triangles in a single surface draw strictly in submission/index order regardless of any sort key -- but two DISTINCT MeshInstance3D nodes with tied sorting_offset have no such guarantee. Visible result: 5447 mismatched pixels (magick compare -metric AE, 0.0073 of the 64,39 zoom-1 frame) as thin slivers along a handful of overlapping sprite edges (a tower silhouette, one roof corner), not a gross failure. Fix: sector_view.gd._build_objects now runs a forward strict-monotonic pass over band_repr after the object loop (BAND_TIE_EPS := 0.001), nudging any band whose representative depth is <= its predecessor to predecessor + BAND_TIE_EPS, restoring index order (matching the old single-mesh submission order) for tied bands. A first attempt at EPS=0.000001 barely changed the artifact (5447 -> 4920 mismatched pixels) because sorting_offset is a 32-bit real_t internally and float32 ULP at this scale's worst-case magnitude (640, per DEPTH_STEP's own comment) is ~7.6e-5 -- an epsilon below that rounds away to nothing when added. 0.001 (>10x the ULP floor, still <DEPTH_STEP/HH ~= 0.0021 per real world-unit of pos.y) resolved it: --bands=100000 is now byte-identical to base_6439.png, with --bands=1/2/0/64 re-verified unaffected (still byte-identical) and two independent --bands=64 process runs identical to each other (tie-order is stable run to run).

Result: 4 of 9 positions (1310,1502 / 1311,1502 / 1310,1503 / 1309,1501) show a diagonal/zigzag notch cut into the cube's top edge, NOT touching any image border, whose angle and position tracks the same jagged rock/gap silhouette visible in the background of every shot -- this is genuine partial occlusion, distinct from the previously-documented frustum-clipping trap (straight cut exactly at image edge, seen and correctly excluded in this same session as cube_fix_2524_1822_b64.png / cube_fix_2526_1820_b64.png from the earlier sector-39,28 sweep). Note: object.gdshader documents that objects DO get real per-pixel depth-testing against opaque terrain (depth_draw_opaque) but NOT against each other (object-vs-object order is submission-order only) -- the occluding jagged silhouette here is plausibly terrain/rock geometry rather than another sprite-object, which would explain why bands (an object-submission-order mechanism) has zero effect on it: banding only changes the order objects are submitted in relative to each other, it cannot change how objects are depth-tested against opaque terrain, and terrain-vs-object occlusion was already correct before bands existed.

column5: Evidence assembled for Phase 2 Wave 4 (02-04). PORT side: --bands=64 is byte-identical to --bands=1 in every comparison made across four sectors -- 64,39 (exhaustive, 1-cell resolution, ~80 captures, rows 375/376), 39,28 KLOSTER_KAPELLE01 (9-cell fine sweep), 51,42 arena, and 20,23 courtyard (rows 378/380 incl. the corrected centered recapture). RETAIL side (row 379): across ~50+ real gameplay screenshots and ~15 distinct close-contact hero/NPC-vs-architecture positions, the retail 2005 engine never once cut a sprite mid-body with a wall, pillar or roof edge -- it renders characters wholly in front of or wholly behind adjacent geometry. Not conclusive (the roof-overhang/loggia crossing was never achieved) but one-directional: no counter-example found. MECHANISM (from object.gdshader): objects depth-test per-pixel against opaque terrain (depth_draw_opaque) but resolve only by submission order against each OTHER; banding reorders object-vs-object submission, which is not the axis a character-vs-building case turns on. CONSEQUENCE: shipping --bands=N as "the fix" would ship a knob that provably changes no pixel; scheduling the SubViewport fallback would add partial occlusion that retail itself does not exhibit, violating the projects canonical-first rule (reproduce retail exactly, including its flaws). The dark-voids defect is therefore a separate object-vs-object ordering bug, not the character-integration problem R2 assumed, and Phase 4s shape should be revisited on that basis.

Shown able to fail, not vacuous: row 370's A3 closure experiment found /tmp/look/port-223921.png differs from /tmp/p2/base_wide.png at byte 1096647 when the engine's default sorting_use_aabb_center=true replaced the explicit sort-property assignment -- the same rule that reports 'identical' throughout this decision has demonstrated it can report 'different' when a real behavioural change is present. SORTING_OFFSET SIGN (row 367): positive band_repr, determined empirically by byte-comparing both signs against a captured baseline, not assumed from documentation. DRAW-CALL NUMBERS (each printed as a `drawcalls\tN` line by a command run in this phase, row 373), all eight, pixel-gated against the Plan-01 baseline before being trusted (all 8 captures /usr/bin/cmp exit 0 first): sector 64,39 zoom=1 (single sector): bands=1 -> 6, bands=8 -> 10, bands=16 -> 13, bands=64 -> 21. sector 64,39 zoom=2 (wide, multi-sector): bands=1 -> 9, bands=8 -> 12, bands=16 -> 17, bands=64 -> 32. Both views rise monotonically but sub-nominally (3.5x and 3.56x, not the nominal 64x), consistent with sparse sectors leaving many bands empty and skipped before _mesh_of. FOUR CUBE-PAIR COMPARISON RESULTS (row 375, sector 64,39, x=4128, y=2518/2522/2526/2530, walking the cube north-to-south through the test building): d1, d2, d3, d4 -- all four bands=64 vs bands=1 pairs byte-identical (/usr/bin/cmp exit 0 in every case). Cube-present gate passed first: all 8 captures (4 depths x 2 band counts) differ from the no-cube baseline /tmp/p2/nocube64.png, so the cube renders in every shot and the null is not an absent-cube artifact. Corroborated by a ~20-point sweep the same session and by the exhaustive ~90-position 1-cell-resolution search in row 376 -- no partial-occlusion transition exists anywhere in sector 64,39 under any camera framing. HUMAN VERDICT FROM 02-03-PLAN.md TASK 3 (quoted, not paraphrased): the Task 3 checkpoint's first review found the original 4-cell capture inconclusive (the cube was fully in front at all four depths in both series, never testing the 'behind' case) and issued the explicit instruction 'Extend the test -- option 1 -- with oracle live tests' (02-03-SUMMARY.md key-decisions), rather than approving past the gap. That instruction drove the exhaustive extension (rows 376-380) that this decision rests on. Applying the checkpoint's own three-question rubric to that extended evidence: (1) at 64 bands, is the box correctly ordered at all four depths -- moot, because no depth anywhere in the scene ever produced a partial-occlusion case to grade; the box was fully drawn at every depth tested. (2) at 1 band, is the control confined to wholly-in-front-or-behind at every depth -- yes, and indistinguishable from the 64-band series, which is the same null result stated the other way round. (3) is any depth worse at 64 bands than at 1 band, a new artifact or a dark-voids reappearance -- no, every pair compared byte-identical, not merely visually similar. RETAIL EVIDENCE (row 379), stated with its honest limitation: across ~50+ real retail gameplay screenshots and ~15 distinct close-contact hero/NPC-vs-architecture positions (tutorial-NPC pillar approach, arena-alcove doorway corner, iron wall-spikes), the 2005 engine never once cut a sprite mid-body with a wall, pillar or roof edge -- always wholly-in-front or wholly-behind. This is SUGGESTIVE, NOT CONCLUSIVE: the one geometry type most likely to force a true roof-edge partial cut in a 3D-depth-buffered engine -- walking the hero fully under a loggia roof overhang -- was never reached in three attempts, blocked by click-to-move and tutorial-NPC-gating issues unrelated to the occlusion question itself. What would settle it: a save or script that reaches a roof-overhang/loggia crossing and captures the hero mid-crossing (row 379's own stated recommendation). MECHANISM (godot-port/object.gdshader, cited in row 381): objects depth-test per-pixel against opaque terrain (depth_draw_opaque) unconditionally, but resolve only by submission order against each other. Banding is an object-vs-object submission-order mechanism; it cannot change object-vs-terrain depth-testing, which was already correct before banding existed. This is why the null result is clean rather than ambiguous: banding was never capable of affecting the axis (object-vs-terrain occlusion) a character-vs-building case turns on in every scene tested. SUBVIEWPORT FALLBACK'S REAL COST, recorded per the plan's own requirement so it is not treated as a drop-in swap (02-RESEARCH.md Pitfall 3, restated in 02-04-PLAN.md Task 1 context): transparent_bg=true plus render_target_update_mode=UPDATE_ALWAYS on the character's SubViewport, because an animating character cannot be a one-shot bake; a premultiplied-alpha compositing shader on the receiving quad to avoid the documented colour-bleed artifact when a transparent-background viewport texture is blended over another blended surface; and, the expensive part, re-inserting the compositing quad into whichever sector mesh currently owns it every frame it moves -- there is no incremental per-frame sector-mesh update path today (object meshes are built once and cached), and object build already costs roughly 54 ms mean / 186 ms worst per sector, with no spare frame budget. DECISION: ship-bands. --bands=N ships as a knob; the SubViewport fallback is NOT scheduled as its own phase. Rationale: shipping SubViewport would add partial-occlusion capability that neither the port's own exhaustive search nor retail's own observed behaviour exhibits -- a fidelity regression under this project's canonical-first rule (reproduce retail exactly, including its flaws; tuning/fixes are a later opt-in layer). Banding, by contrast, is a proven-safe, zero-observed-cost mechanism (pixel-identical at every tested band count, modest measured draw-call cost) that gives Phase 4/5 a working per-instance sort-key placement model matching what retail's all-or-nothing behaviour actually requires -- a character that sorts as a whole unit among sector objects, not one that needs per-pixel compositing. CARRIED FORWARD, NOT RESOLVED HERE: this decision does not explain the dark-voids defect that originally motivated R2. Row 381's synthesis (already recorded) concludes the defect is more likely a separate object-vs-object submission-order bug than the character-integration problem R2 assumed, and recommends Phase 4's shape be revisited on that basis before Phase 4 is planned. This decision record does not re-litigate that recommendation; it is carried forward as an open item for whoever plans Phase 4. REVERSIBILITY: rated 'costly' by the plan, not 'trivial' -- reversing ship-bands to schedule SubViewport later would mean replanning Phase 4 and Phase 5 and rebuilding the character-rendering path, though no data migrates and no published contract breaks. This decision was made under autonomous execution authority granted for this session and is explicitly open to the user's review and reversal.

Cause, from verify.gd lines 74-83: the hash is over "tag,off,len" triples from Sacred.Models.walk(), which excludes the terminator; those 9 tags sit at identical relative offsets and sizes in every kind=64 entry, so the hashed text is byte-identical corpus-wide. Note this is a DIFFERENT and weaker definition than grnwalk.gd --grn-index= produces (b818fc52 for 589, 44c399e4 for 1, which do discriminate) -- verify.gd deliberately uses a simpler plan-specified definition, and that choice is what made it non-discriminating. This is the THIRD occurrence of this defect class in this project (row 269 tiles.pak u16; row 383 the Wave-1 walk md5; now this), and it sits inside the phase verification gate, where a column that looks like content verification but is constant is actively misleading. RECOMMENDED FIX (assigned to plan 03-05, which parses the per-model-varying bulk region): extend the fact-line hash to cover per-model-varying bytes, and assert as an acceptance criterion that the md5 for index 589 differs from index 1. Not a blocker for 03-04, which met its stated criteria.

column4: The dense post-preamble tag-chunk run (0xCA5E0F00-0xCA5E0F06 and related families) carries no informative payload for the highest-frequency tags -- it is a corner/topology reference stream, not vertex attribute data
column5: Per-tag payload census (Python, GLADIATOR.GRN=589, 1272 chunks in the dense run): 0xca5e0f01/0f02/0f06 occur 235 times each with byte-8 field (the second payload u32) CONSTANT at 2/0/1 respectively across every occurrence -- pure tag-family discriminators, zero varying content. Byte-4 field (first payload u32) is a monotonically-increasing value (range 16684-20152 across the 235 occurrences, step ~12-15 bytes) inconsistent with being either a plausible float (denormal bit patterns, e-41 magnitude) or a small bounded index -- read at face value as an entry-relative byte offset it does not land on a chunk boundary (mod-12 remainder 2, not 0), so its role (cross-reference into the same stream, or leftover exporter memory-address garbage) is UNRESOLVED, not asserted. 0xca5e0f00/0f05 occur 83 times each (~1/2.83 ratio vs 0f01/02/06, not the clean 1/3 a per-triangle-of-3-corners reading would predict), with 0f00's second payload field varying 4-10 (real content, unlike the others) -- role also UNRESOLVED. This run is provably NOT vertex position/normal/UV data: every payload is 8 bytes (2 x u32/float), too small to hold a Vector3 (12 bytes), and the two informative fields found (0f00's varying int, the growing offset-like field) do not resolve to plausible model-space floats.

The span ends with a run of small u32s (0x9f,0,0x26e,1,...) immediately before a large near-file-size-magnitude value (0x0012ed54) and the trailing final 0xCA5E-tag at bulk_len-12 -- read as an index/offset table into the string table, UNCONFIRMED. CONCLUSION: this plan's Task 1 goal (mesh_arrays() returning decoded positions/normals/UVs/indices from this file's bulk region) cannot be met without fudging -- no per-vertex float32 array of plausible size exists anywhere in the entry (every byte from magic_offset to true_len is accounted for by the fixed header chain, the exporter-tool preamble, the dense topology-tag stream, this bone-name string table, and one trailing tag -- zero unaccounted bytes). column3: New structural table found: fixed-width index/reference array immediately before the terminator tag
column4: In GLADIATOR.GRN (idx589), bulk-rel [179216, 185400) -- immediately before the final 0xCA5EFFFF terminator at bulk-rel 185400 -- is a clean, unambiguously little-endian u32 array of 1546 values. Stated-before-measuring: if this were unstructured/incidental data, no consistent record stride or monotonic key column would appear. Programmatically confirmed structure: first 2 values are a header (0, 385); remaining 1544 values decompose into 385 fixed 4-field records (record[i] = [i, a, b, c]) where field 0 of every record equals the record's own ordinal 0..384 (verified across the full table, not just the eyeballed head/tail), and fields a/b/c are small integers in range 0-624ish. This is a strong structural match for a triangle/face index buffer: 385 records = 385 triangles, referencing a vertex set of roughly 625 elements (max observed index was 623). Three anomalous large trailing values (1240404, 1240404, 1240760) sit just past this table, right at the terminator, and are not yet explained -- they are far larger than the entry's own true_len (186842) and their meaning (absolute pak offset? unrelated counter/checksum?) is unresolved.
column5: This is the strongest new lead of the session: a genuine, decoded, non-trivial data table consistent with topology (face/triangle indices), found by structural analysis rather than a permissive statistical filter.  Confidence: high

column3: Isolated float32 triple (1.0, 1.0, 1.0) immediately precedes the index table
column4: At bulk-rel ~179200-179212 in GLADIATOR.GRN, three consecutive 4-byte words decode as IEEE-754 float32 0x3f800000 = 1.0 each, immediately preceding the [0,385] header of the index table in V3. This confirms genuine float32 data exists near this table (plausibly a default/identity normal or scale vector), but it is a single isolated triple, not the start of a large flat per-vertex array -- the 8000 bytes immediately preceding it (bulk-rel 171216-179216) were examined by eye and match the same dense 12-byte tagged-record pattern seen throughout the rest of the bulk region, not raw vertex floats.
column5: Confirms float data is present in the file but does not by itself locate a vertex array; the preceding region reads as more tagged records, not geometry.  Confidence: medium

column3: Whole-bulk sliding-window spatial-coherence sweep is not a valid discriminator at the thresholds used
column4: A systematic sliding-window scan (700-point xyz float32 windows, 1024-byte stride, 3 byte alignments, band [-2000,2000], bbox span 0.01-500, mean_step < span*0.2) over GLADIATOR.GRN's full 185412-byte bulk region returned 379 "candidate" windows out of 537 tested. Stated-before-measuring (the test-that-cannot-fail check required by project convention): before trusting this hit rate, the same filter was run against a region known NOT to be vertex data (the ASCII bone-name string-table region) and, more decisively, the base rate of the identical filter across ALL windows in the bulk was measured directly: 276/537 = 51.4% of windows pass, regardless of position. This means the filter's thresholds are too permissive to mean anything -- most of the bulk's dense tagged-record byte patterns coincidentally reinterpret as "plausible" small float32 triples. The 379-candidate result from this sweep is noise and must not be reported as evidence of located vertex data.
column5: Do not reuse these threshold values for future spatial-coherence tests; a real discriminator needs either a much tighter band/step constraint calibrated against a genuine positive control, or a non-statistical (structural) approach like the one that worked in V3.  Confidence: high

column3: Vertex position/normal/UV float32 array not located in GLADIATOR.GRN kind=64 entry despite full-bulk testing; open question, not fabricated
column4: Combining all tests this session (10 largest binary runs at 3 alignments each via /tmp/binary_run_analysis.py, the full-bulk systematic sweep in V5 -- shown to be unreliable -- and manual inspection of the region surrounding the newly found index table in V3/V4): no span of the bulk region produces a convincing large-N (hundreds+), moderate and consistent magnitude, smoothly neighbor-coherent point cloud consistent with genuine mesh vertex positions. The one new structural win (V3, a topology/index table) narrows the search: if 385 triangles reference ~625 vertices, a genuine position array would be ~625*12=7500 bytes (xyz float32) or ~625*4=2500 bytes if indices only reference a separate smaller unique-vertex set -- neither size range was pinpointed this session. This is an honest "still unknown after real effort" result, not "vertices provably absent from models.pak" (V3's topology table is strong evidence real mesh data of some kind IS in this entry) and not "vertices located."
