The top field draws from only 39 DISTINCT TEXTURES against 2203 for the ground tiles it sits with, and only 2 of the 39 are ever used as ground: a small dedicated set of mottled transition sheets, which is what a blend layer looks like. Domain measured over 216,553 records: 0 (37.2%) or 855..1535, nothing in 1..854 and nothing at or above 1536. Earlier readings that made this look like a quantity were artefacts - the mean falling with chain depth (971, 845, 586, 287) is just which tiles get stacked, and the 3x512 split was a coincidence of the band.
column6: REFUTES THE 'UNDECODED FIELD' FRAMING OF ROW 695 AND EXPLAINS ROW 699. The corner-blend hypothesis for WldxEntry +0x18..0x1b was refuted on its own evidence; this is why it had to be - the overlay's blend does not come from the cell at all, it comes from a second tile in the same u32. Also kills three hypotheses row 695 listed as open: not a sector id, not a layer, not a draw order. NOT YET DECODED: the BLEND OPERATION. The engine emits one quad with two UV sets, so the port cannot reproduce it with a second quad - it needs a second sampler in terrain.gdshader and the combine rule, which lives in the render path past 0x080e4e5c and is not read yet. Until then the port draws the low tile only (row 700) and the transition sheets are simply missing. PROBES: floor_hi_probe, floor_hi2..hi6_probe, floor_mask_probe, all read-only.

column4: THE floor.pak TWO-TILE BLEND IS AN ALPHA MASK: the second tile contributes NO COLOUR, only per-pixel alpha. Retail is not a software blitter here - it is fixed-function OpenGL multitexturing through SDL_GL_GetProcAddress pointers, which is why nothing shows up in the ELF relocations. The draw is cWorld::drawFloor at 0x080e4bf2 (size 0x3a1, FDE), the only consumer of the queued-quad list at cWorld+0x37674 besides its builder at 0x080e2706. Per quad it resolves both tile records, reads each one's texture id at record +0x20 (exactly the port's Tiles.texture_id), caches the pair and calls 0x080e111a to set the batch's TWO texture slots at batch+0x4fc0 and +0x4fc4, then submits the quad via 0x080e0fd0. The flush at 0x080e1160 binds +0x4fc0 to TEXTURE UNIT 0 and +0x4fc4 to UNIT 1 (call 0x08055236 with unit 0 then unit 1, the second guarded by a zero check). So unit 0 = the low-17-bit tile, the art; unit 1 = the top-15-bit tile, the transition sheet.
column5: THE COMBINE, read from the render-state setter 0x083b509a (a change-only wrapper over 0x083b50da, dispatching on a state token). Token 0x2000, value 0, at 0x083b590e: glActiveTexture(GL_TEXTURE1); glTexEnvi(GL_TEXTURE_ENV, GL_COMBINE_RGB, GL_REPLACE); glTexEnvi(.., GL_SOURCE0_RGB, GL_PREVIOUS); glTexEnvi(.., GL_COMBINE_ALPHA, GL_REPLACE); glTexEnvi(.., GL_SOURCE0_ALPHA, GL_TEXTURE); glEnable(GL_TEXTURE_2D); glActiveTexture(GL_TEXTURE0); glTexEnvi(.., GL_SOURCE0_ALPHA, GL_PREVIOUS). Unit 1 therefore REPLACES rgb with PREVIOUS - the mask sheet's own colour is thrown away - and REPLACES alpha with its own texel. Value 1, at 0x083b534c, is the single-texture mode: glDisable(GL_TEXTURE_2D) on unit 1 and unit 0 back to COMBINE_ALPHA = MODULATE(TEXTURE, PREVIOUS). POLARITY WAS THE TRAP: ds:0x9553bc0 and ds:0x9553b90 are both one-argument calls on GL_TEXTURE_2D and reading them the wrong way round inverts the whole conclusion. They are pinned by the strings passed to SDL_GL_GetProcAddress at 0x0862b35d and 0x0862b3e5 - 0x9553bc0 is glDISABLE, 0x9553b90 is glENABLE.
column6: THE PASS STRUCTURE, which the port does not need but which explains the state toggling: one loop, flag at [ebp-0x21] starting 0, drawing only the quads matching the current mode and setting a deferred flag for the others, then flushing, XOR-ing the flag, re-setting state 0x2000 to it, and repeating while anything was deferred. Drawn quads are consumed off a per-slot chain (list[i] = quad->next at 0x080e4f02), which is what makes it terminate. NOT VERIFIED, and it matters before implementing: the framebuffer blend function itself. This trace establishes what alpha the fragment ends up with, not what the fixed-function blender then does with it, and GL_BLEND is enabled or disabled by some other state token. PORT IMPLICATION: terrain.gdshader needs a second sampler and must switch from its alpha-test discard to real alpha for these quads, with the mask's alpha read as Sacred's ALPHA channel - which after the RGBA4444 rotation the shader documents is the .r component, not .a.

column4: ROW 702 IS CONFIRMED BY LIVE CAPTURE, WITH ONE ENUM CORRECTED. apitrace 14 (installed this session; the 32-bit wrapper is required, the game is ELF32) traced a full retail run to the pinned chapel spawn under Xvfb via play.sh's SACRED_RUNNER hook - 12 GB, 7.78 M GL calls, screenshot at 100 s shows the Seraphim, the priestess and the blue chest, i.e. the oracle plate itself. The floor draw appears exactly as the disassembly predicted: glActiveTexture(GL_TEXTURE0)+glBindTexture, glActiveTexture(GL_TEXTURE1)+glBindTexture, two GL_TEXTURE_COORD_ARRAYs via glClientActiveTexture, glColorPointer + glVertexPointer at STRIDE 32, and glDrawRangeElements(GL_TRIANGLES, start 0, end 4, count 6) - one quad, four 32-byte vertices = the 128 bytes the builder memcpy's at 0x080e2eb1. 47,365 GL_TEXTURE1 activations in the in-world portion. Textures upload as GL_BGRA / GL_UNSIGNED_SHORT_4_4_4_4_REV, which is the channel rotation the port's terrain.gdshader already documents.
column5: THE FULL VERIFIED EQUATION. Unit 1 (the top-field transition sheet): COMBINE_RGB = GL_REPLACE, SRC0_RGB = GL_PREVIOUS, COMBINE_ALPHA = GL_REPLACE, SRC0_ALPHA = GL_TEXTURE, then glEnable(GL_TEXTURE_2D). Unit 0 (the low-field tile): ENV_MODE = GL_COMBINE, COMBINE_RGB = GL_MODULATE, SRC0_ALPHA = GL_PRIMARY_COLOR, SRC1_ALPHA alternating GL_PREVIOUS / GL_PRIMARY_COLOR. Framebuffer: GL_BLEND enabled, glBlendFunc(GL_SRC_ALPHA, GL_ONE_MINUS_SRC_ALPHA). So the fragment is RGB = low tile x per-corner vertex colour (exactly what the port already computes), ALPHA = the mask sheet's texel alpha and nothing else, composited straight over the ground. THE CORRECTION: row 702 read unit 0's SRC0_ALPHA operand 0x8577 as GL_PREVIOUS. 0x8577 is GL_PRIMARY_COLOR; GL_PREVIOUS is 0x8578. The conclusion is unchanged - unit 1 REPLACEs alpha regardless - but the enum name in row 702 is wrong and should not be copied forward.
column6: THE OPEN ITEM OF ROW 702 IS NOW CLOSED: the framebuffer blend function was the one thing that trace could not settle statically, and it is ordinary src-alpha over. IMPLEMENTATION IS UNBLOCKED and is now fully specified: terrain.gdshader needs a second sampler for the mask sheet at its own UV, and must replace its alpha-test discard with real alpha for these quads, reading the mask's alpha as the .r component after the RGBA4444 rotation. METHOD NOTE worth reusing: SACRED_RUNNER="apitrace trace --api gl --output <path>" composes cleanly with shot.sh's autopilot and Xvfb, timings hold under tracing overhead (the 20 s menu shot landed on the menu), and the output path must contain NO SPACES because play.sh leaves SACRED_RUNNER unquoted. Artifacts: ~/sacredtrace/world.trace (12 GB, delete when done) and state.log, a 562k-line pre-filtered index of every glActiveTexture/glTexEnvi/glBlendFunc/GL_BLEND call in the run.

column4: THE MASK BLEND IS IMPLEMENTED AND VISIBLE. SectorView._tile_stack now returns the floor.pak chain as PAIRS (art, mask) rather than single ids, and _build_sector splits the sector into TWO SURFACES of one ArrayMesh, mirroring retail's own two passes: surface 0 is the existing alpha-tested terrain (ground tiles plus overlays whose mask is 0, appearance unchanged), surface 1 is the masked overlays under a new terrain_mask.gdshader. The mask's slot UV and array layer ride in ARRAY_CUSTOM0 (RGBA float) because UV2 is already spent on the art tile's layer, and CUSTOM0 is vertex-stage only so it crosses to the fragment as a varying. Both surfaces share one Texture2DArray - the 39 mask sheets simply take further layers. The shader is retail's combine exactly: ALBEDO = art.gba * per-corner light, ALPHA = mask.r, where .r is Sacred's ALPHA after the RGBA4444 rotation terrain.gdshader documents. render_mode blend_mix, depth_draw_never - these are decals and must not occlude what is drawn later, though depth TESTING stays on.
column5: ONE REAL BUG FOUND BY LOOKING, WHICH IS THE ONLY REASON IT WAS CAUGHT. Blended quads join the same transparent queue the object sprites sort in (they carry sorting_offset), and on the first render every prop standing on a masked cell - the chapel's carpet, benches, cabinet, candles, blue chest - was washed out or erased, because the floor painted over them. Fixed by giving the masked material render_priority = -1, which Godot sorts BEFORE depth, so the whole floor pass precedes every sprite exactly as retail's does. The mesh also had to move from material_override to set_surface_override_material, since an override applies one material to both surfaces; nothing else reads the terrain mesh's material (the cutaway's _apply_swap walks the object band meshes, which are children with their own overrides). If a mask texture fails to decode the quad falls back to the art-only surface rather than being dropped.
column6: EVIDENCE AND GATES. Before/after at the chapel: /tmp/look/port-202150.png (overlays opaque, hard-edged tan road rectangles) vs port-212022.png (same view, soft transitions, scrub fading into dirt, every prop present). Second site sector 7,7 via --region=7,7,0 renders coherently. Region load-path invariant UNCHANGED at 35340 quads (the split moves quads between surfaces, it does not add or lose any) and floor_check passes. NOTE the 63-textures figure in that line counts GROUND tiles via _world.tile_ids and has never counted the overlay or mask layers - do not read it as evidence about this change either way. PRE-EXISTING GATE FAILURE, NOT CAUSED HERE: verify_ref.py emits a 'pak tiles.pak count=90132' line that verify.gd does not, because verify.gd uses Sacred.Tiles and tiles.pak no longer opens through Sacred.Pak at all (row 695). The Python reference is stale on that one line; nothing in this change touches verify.gd, sacred.gd or either reader. ALSO WORTH KNOWING for anyone driving look.sh: --zoom= takes a zoom INDEX 0..2, not a size, and --sector= is overridden every frame by the camera following the player, so use --region=gx,gy,r to look anywhere else.

column4: WldxEntry +0x18..0x1b IS A SECOND PER-CORNER SIGNED HEIGHT, SAMPLED CONTINUOUSLY - and row 699 was right to say the statistics had gone as far as they could. Found by scanning .text for the FOUR-CORNER read pattern (movsx/movzx of a base+disp8 at four consecutive displacements within one 64-byte window): +0x10 has exactly two such sites (0x080e29e7, 0x080e5232, the two terrain quad builders), +0x18 has exactly ONE (0x080ef81a, inside the function at 0x080ef688, size 0x2bc), and +0x14 the light field has NONE, so the lights are read some other way. The single +0x18 reader sign-extends all four bytes, fild's each, multiplies each by 2.5 (.rodata 0x086de620), averages them with x0.25 (0x086de624) and compares that against zero, then BILINEARLY INTERPOLATES the four - indexing them as an array via [ebp+ebx*4-0x38] / [ebp+ecx*4-0x38] - and returns a single float. Its neighbour constant at 0x086de61c is 53.66563, the world SCALE this project already uses in save_patch.py, so the function works in world units. The caller at 0x080ef5e6 adds the returned float to a per-object term (byte [obj+0x33] x 28) and returns the sum: a HEIGHT AT A POSITION. Roughly a dozen call sites.
column5: MEASURED RELATIONSHIP TO THE KNOWN +0x10 HEIGHT, over 221,184 cells (every 11th sector). P(+0x10 non-zero) = 0.1766, P(+0x18 non-zero) = 0.0979, P(both) = 0.0904 against 0.0173 if independent - a lift of 5.23, and note P(both) is 92% of P(+0x18), so a cell carrying this field almost always carries a visual height too. Over the 53,142 corner pairs where both are non-zero the SIGNS AGREE 99.51% of the time. Magnitudes are related but NOT a mechanical rescale: +0x10 is always a multiple of 5 (row 218) and h == f*5 exactly for 49.3% of pairs, with the h/f ratio spreading 3, 4, 6, 7, 8, 10, 15 beyond its mode of 5 - and 10:1 and 10:2 both occur, as do 15:1, 15:2 and 15:3. So the two are authored independently, not derived from one another. Observed +0x18 values span -7..+14, concentrated on +1 (19,595) and +2 (11,598).
column6: WHAT IS PROVEN VS WHAT IS INFERRED, stated separately because the difference matters. PROVEN: it is four signed per-corner values, scaled x2.5, bilinearly interpolated to a continuous value across the cell, summed into a height total, and NEVER read by either terrain quad builder - those read +0x00, +0x04, +0x08, +0x0c, +0x10..0x13 and +0x1c..0x1f and skip both +0x14 and +0x18. INFERRED, and NOT yet traced to its call sites: that this is the height things STAND on while +0x10 is the height the ground is DRAWN at. That reading fits every measurement above but the caller semantics have not been read, so do not write it up as settled. THIS DOES NOT CLOSE THE ENTRY - +0x04, +0x08 and +0x1e remain undecoded. No port change: OpenHeilig's movement is 2D over a walkable grid and has no ground height to feed this into yet. PROBE: godot-port/corner3_height_probe.gd, read-only. Row 699's refutation of the overlay-blend reading stands and is now positively explained - the overlay's blend comes from a second tile (row 701), never from the cell.

column4: WldxEntry +0x04 WAS ALREADY DECODED, AND +0x08 IS NOT AUTHORED DATA AT ALL. +0x04 heads the static.pak chain and the port has been reading it all along at sacred.gd:549 via _statics.chain() (row 686) - a full-grid census confirms it: 862,343 of 24,780,800 cells carry a non-zero handle (3.48%), maximum 1,038,013, which is exactly static.pak's count-1 as printed at startup (1,038,014 statics). Nothing to do there. +0x08 is the interesting one and the answer is that it is a RUNTIME SLOT. Retail's terrain builder loads it at 0x080e296c and walks it at 0x080e4455 as a CIRCULAR LINKED LIST: the id is resolved to a record by the lookup at 0x08118560 against the global at ds:0x8b8d0c0, the next id is read from record+0x30, and the walk stops when the next comes back to the head it started from. Each record's +0x1c/+0x20 are turned into screen coordinates - view origin subtracted, then +0x200 and +0x180 added, i.e. half of 1024x768. That is a per-cell list of objects being drawn at positions that move.
column5: MEASURED EXHAUSTIVELY, not sampled: +0x08 IS ZERO IN ALL 24,780,800 CELLS OF THE WORLD - every cell of every one of the 6050 present sectors, not a stride sample. The +0x04 census above ran in the same pass as a control, so a reading bug that zeroed the field would have zeroed that too, and it did not. Two independent lines therefore agree: the disassembly says the field is the head of a list of things that MOVE, which an engine builds at load time rather than ships, and the data says the shipped value is empty everywhere. CONCLUSION: there is nothing in the file to decode here. The slot exists so the loader has somewhere to hang the cell's mobile-object list once creatures and dropped items are spawned into it.
column6: THIS CLOSES THE WldxEntry except for +0x1e. Full 32-byte map as it now stands: +0x00 tile id, +0x04 static.pak chain head (row 686), +0x08 runtime mobile-object list head (empty on disk, this row), +0x0c floor.pak overlay chain head (rows 695/701), +0x10..0x13 signed per-corner render heights (row 218), +0x14..0x17 per-corner light bytes, +0x18..0x1b signed per-corner second height, bilinearly sampled (row 705), +0x1c/+0x1d signed parent-object deltas (rows 670-672), +0x1e UNDECODED, +0x1f cell class nibble. GUARD ADDED: floor_check.gd now asserts +0x08 is zero across sector 50,39 and names this row, so the claim cannot quietly rot - it passes. PROBE: godot-port/cell08_probe.gd, read-only, full-grid. A NEGATIVE RESULT IS STILL A RESULT: the value of this row is that it stops the next person spending a session looking for meaning in a field that has none on disk.

column4: WldxEntry +0x1e IS A SPARSE BITFIELD AND ONLY THREE OF ITS EIGHT BITS ARE EVER SET. Full-grid census of all 24,780,800 cells: 98.8% are 0x00, and the only values that occur at all are 0x00..0x07 - 0x02 x189,851, 0x01 x77,814, 0x03 x29,531, 0x04 x1,050, 0x05 x349, 0x06 x210, 0x07 x152. Bits 3 through 7 are NEVER SET anywhere in the world. Retail reads the byte UNSIGNED at 0x080e2983 and treats it as flags. BIT 0 IS THE ONE WITH A TRACED MEANING: at 0x080e350f the terrain builder tests it and, when set, computes the cell's OWN WORLD POSITION (cell index >> 6 as the row, index & 0x3f as the column, plus the sector origin at +0x44/+0x48) and uses it as the key for a lookup, 0x080eede0 then 0x080ef1ac. That second call is the SAME lookup the +0x18 height sampler's caller uses at 0x080ef642 (row 705), where the returned record's byte +0x33 is multiplied by 28 and ADDED to the interpolated corner height. So bit 0 marks cells that have an entry in a per-position table whose records carry a height LEVEL, and 28 is the per-level step. A second consumer of the same bit sits at 0x0811772c.
column5: BIT 4'S BRANCH IS DEAD IN SHIPPED CONTENT, which is worth knowing before anyone chases it. At 0x080e3402 the builder tests 0x10 and only then reads the +0x1f class, masking &0xF0 and accepting 0x10/0x20/0x90/0xA0 - WALL/FLOOR/DOOR/STEP in the HIGH nibble. The branch is real code, but bit 4 is set in ZERO of 24,780,800 cells, so retail data never reaches it. Two further testers of this byte at 0x08231bea and 0x0826aeb6 check bit 3, which is likewise never set, and are most likely reading a different structure that merely shares the offset - 0x1e is a common displacement and a raw scan turns up 140 sites, of which only six survive the filter of having a +0x1f read within 48 bytes. CORRELATION for bit 0, measured: P(cell has a static chain | bit 0) = 0.360 against a base rate of 0.035, a 10x lift but nowhere near equality, so bit 0 is NOT simply 'this cell has a static'.
column6: HONEST SCOPE: BITS 1 AND 2 ARE NOT DECODED. Bit 1 is the COMMONEST of the three (0.89% of cells, 219,382 counting 0x02, 0x03, 0x06 and 0x07) and bit 2 is rare (1,761 cells), and no reader for either was found among the six cell-like sites - so their consumers are reached through a base register the adjacency filter missed, and finding them needs a different scan than the one used here. Do not write +0x1e up as decoded; it is one bit of three. THIS ALSO CORRECTS ROW 706's closing line, which called +0x1e 'the only byte left' as though it were a single unknown - it is a byte with three independent flags in it, one of which is now understood. The WldxEntry is therefore fully mapped at FIELD level with bits 1 and 2 of +0x1e the only content still unexplained. PROBE: godot-port/cell1e_probe.gd, read-only, full-grid.

column4: BIT 2 OF WldxEntry +0x1e IS SOLVED AND BIT 0 IS CORROBORATED; BIT 1 IS NOT, AND THIS ROW SAYS SO PLAINLY. Bit 2 (0x04, 1,761 cells world-wide): its reader is 0x080eeec4, a small accessor that fetches the cell, requires bit 2, then reads the cell's +0x04 STATIC CHAIN HEAD, requires it non-zero, and passes it to the object lookup 0x080ef1ac - the same lookup whose record byte +0x33 is multiplied by 28 and added to the interpolated corner height in row 705's wrapper. The data confirms the guard exactly: P(cell has a static chain | bit 2) = 1.0000 over all 1,761 cells, against a base rate of 0.0348. Not 0.99 - every single one. Bit 2 is enriched 23x for class high-nibble 0xe0 (0.163 vs a 0.007 base). Bit 0 (0x01, 107,846 cells) gains an independent corroboration too: P(the cell has non-zero +0x1c/+0x1d PARENT-OBJECT deltas | bit 0) = 0.9887 against a base of 0.0043, a 230x lift, which ties row 707's traced position-lookup directly to the parent-object link of rows 670-672. Its class skew is 0xd0 at 0.857 vs a 0.244 base.
column5: BIT 1 REMAINS OPEN, and what is known about it is mostly negative. It is the commonest of the three - 219,744 cells, 0.89% - but it occurs in only 161 of the 6050 present sectors, and inside those it forms NEAR-SOLID BLOBS: the mean number of a bit-1 cell's four neighbours that are also bit 1 is 3.91. Those 161 sectors are scattered across the whole 100x100 grid rather than forming one zone. Every correlation measured is weak-to-moderate and none is a rule: P(static) 0.130 vs 0.035 base, P(floor overlay) 0.449 vs 0.186, P(second height) 0.229 vs 0.118, P(parent deltas) 0.134 vs 0.0043, class high-nibble 0x40 at 0.323 vs 0.165 and 0xb0 at 0.215 vs 0.081. HYPOTHESIS REFUTED, DO NOT RETRY: bit 1 is NOT the marker for 'this cell is covered by a region sub-grid'. Measured P(inside a region rect | bit 1) = 0.199 and P(bit 1 | inside a region rect) = 0.260, and the sector sets barely agree - 161 sectors carry bit 1, 361 carry regions, only 91 carry both. A visual look at sector 18,5 (1792 bit-1 cells) was INCONCLUSIVE and is not evidence either way: the port has no overlay for this flag, so which cells were which could not be seen. It is a dark camp with tents and trees, not open water, but that only weakly disfavours a water reading.
column6: WHY IT IS HARD, AND THE TWO NEXT MOVES. No reader for bit 1 exists anywhere I can currently see. A scan of all 32 'test byte [reg+0x1e], imm' sites in .text finds immediates 0x01, 0x02, 0x04 and 0x08, but every 0x02 site sits in a function with no cell-pointer idiom and outside the world/cell accessor family at 0x080eea62..0x080eff00, whose members test only bits 0, 2 and 3. The terrain builder itself tests exactly three bits: 0 (live), 4 (at 0x080e3402, gated on the +0x1f class high nibble being WALL/FLOOR/DOOR/STEP) and 7 (at 0x080e47af, via shr 7) - AND BITS 4 AND 7 ARE SET IN ZERO OF 24,780,800 CELLS, so both are dead branches for retail content. NEXT: (a) bit 1's consumer most likely loads the byte into a register or stack slot first, exactly as the builder does at 0x080e2983 before testing [ebp-0xe4] - so the scan that finds it must follow the copy, not match on [reg+0x1e]; (b) cheaper and probably decisive - add a debug overlay to SectorView that paints bit-1 cells and render two or three of the 161 sectors, which is how height and light were each settled. PROBES: cell1e_bits_probe, cell1e_map_probe, cell1e_region_probe, all read-only, all full-grid.

column4: +0x1e IS A PER-CELL ROOM-TOPOLOGY BYTE: bit 0 = STRUCTURE, bit 1 = ROOM INTERIOR, bit 2 = DOOR. Settled the way height and light were settled - by drawing it and looking. New --flags1e overlay in SectorView._build_flags1e paints the three live bits red/green/blue above the terrain. The decisive picture is sector 71,12 (1303 bit-1 cells, and one of the 70 bit-1 sectors that contain NO region sub-grids at all): a stone dungeon of four walled rooms joined by corridors, where GREEN covers the ROOM FLOORS EXACTLY and stops at the corridors, and BLUE sits precisely on the four DOORWAYS where each room opens onto the corridor. Sector 50,39, the cathedral, shows the same grammar: an L-shaped green interior floor EDGED IN RED along the wall line. Sector 18,5 is a camp whose green blob covers the camp ground under the tents.
column5: THE NUMBERS AGREE WITH THE PICTURE, measured over all 24,780,800 cells against the +0x1f class low nibble (WALL=1, FLOOR=2, DOOR=9, STEP=0xa; base rates 0.6417, 0.1066, 0.00005, 0.0001, with 0.2516 at nibble 0 = the OPEN interior-ground family). BIT 2 IS DOORS: 27.20% of its 1,761 cells are class DOOR against a base of 0.005%, a lift of roughly 5,000x, and P(cell has a static chain | bit 2) = 1.0000 exactly - the door OBJECT, which is precisely why its reader at 0x080eeec4 requires bit 2 and then dereferences +0x04 through the object lookup 0x080ef1ac. BIT 0 IS STRUCTURE: class WALL 0.8804 vs 0.6417 base, STEP 0.0236 vs 0.0001, and P(non-zero +0x1c/+0x1d parent-object deltas | bit 0) = 0.9887 vs a 0.0043 base. BIT 1 IS ROOM INTERIOR: class nibble 0 at 0.5909 vs a 0.2516 base - and nibble 0 with a 0xd0/0xe0 high nibble is exactly what sacred.gd already documents as a building's open interior ground.
column6: HONEST LIMITS. Bit 1's class-0 share is 59%, not 100%, so 'room interior' is the shape of the field rather than a rule, and the camp at sector 18,5 reads as outdoor ground under a strict room reading - the flag is better described as ENCLOSED/INTERIOR AREA than as a four-walled room. Row 708's refutation of 'bit 1 = covered by a region sub-grid' STANDS and is now explained: the region rect includes walls and courtyard while bit 1 is only the interior-floor subset, and most bit-1 areas (70 of 161 sectors) are dungeons with no region sub-grid at all. Bits 3..7 remain set in ZERO cells world-wide, and the builder's tests of bit 4 (0x080e3402) and bit 7 (0x080e47af) are dead branches for retail content. THIS COMPLETES THE WldxEntry: every one of its 32 bytes now has a meaning. TOOLING: --flags1e added to main.gd and SectorView; gates re-run clean, headless has no errors and the region invariant is unchanged at 35340 quads. Plates: /tmp/look/port-220449.png (dungeon, the decisive one), port-220350.png (cathedral), port-220321.png (camp).

column4: THE +0x1f HIGH NIBBLE IS A 16-CLASS GROUND-TYPE TAG, AND sacred.gd's DESCRIPTION OF IT WAS WRONG. The in-repo comment called it 'an undecoded family split (0xd/0xe)'. Measured over all 24,780,800 cells, ALL SIXTEEN values occur: 0xd 0.2437, 0x4 0.1653, 0x8 0.1325, 0x3 0.1309, 0xb 0.0810, 0x9 0.0769, 0x1 0.0428, 0xc 0.0420, 0xf 0.0317, 0x0 0.0250, 0x2 0.0178, 0xe 0.0069, 0x6 0.0025, 0xa 0.0008, 0x5 0.0001, 0x7 0.0000 - while the LOW nibble is essentially only {0, 1, 2} (0.2516 / 0.6417 / 0.1066, with DOOR and STEP together under 0.02%). 76 distinct whole-byte values. So the byte is a small class in the low nibble and a much richer field in the high one, not one enum with a family prefix.
column5: WHAT IT IS, from drawing it and from the engine. New --classhi overlay (SectorView._build_classhi) paints the high nibble one hue per value; at the cathedral sector 50,39 it segments the ground into contiguous areas that track the VISIBLE SURFACE - the lawn is one value, the cobbled courtyard another, the building floor another, the hedged garden another, with small isolated patches where props stand. It is not derived from the art: over 987,136 cells and 738 textures, a cell takes its texture's modal high nibble only 0.6470 of the time and just 99 of 738 textures are single-valued, so the tag is authored alongside the tiles rather than computed from them. Retail queries it BY EQUALITY OVER A RECT: 0x080f1d2a walks a cell range, masks each cell's +0x1f with 0xF0, compares against a target passed in on the stack, and accumulates a float where it matches - an area measurement over cells of a given type. Twelve such high-nibble consumers exist in .text.
column6: HONEST LIMIT: WHICH VALUE MEANS WHICH SURFACE IS NOT ESTABLISHED. Naming them needs either the table the engine indexes with the tag or a per-value render survey across biomes, and neither was done - do not write 'grass = 3' anywhere on this evidence. Two guesses were checked and are NOT supported: it is not an index into sndprofiles.pak (8192 records, not 16), and it is not a second copy of the class enum despite the builder at 0x080e3415 comparing &0xF0 against 0x10/0x20/0x90/0xA0, since the high nibble's distribution looks nothing like the low one's. NO PORT BEHAVIOUR CHANGED: walkable.gd and interior.gd read the LOW nibble and are untouched; this row only corrects a false comment and adds a debug overlay. Gates clean, region invariant unchanged at 35340 quads. PROBES: class_nibble_probe, class_hi_probe, read-only, full-grid. Plate: /tmp/look/port-221354.png.

column4: startcode.bin IS OPENED FOR THE FIRST TIME AND ITS RECORD FRAMING IS SOLVED. The file is a flat record stream: u16 OPCODE, u16 RECORD LENGTH (counting those four bytes), then a tagged argument list. Walking by the length field crosses all 15,422 records of type_npc_seraphim/startcode.bin without a single desync, which is the proof the framing is right, and yields 33 distinct opcodes - the busiest being op 50 x2463, op 8 x2003, op 48 x1942, op 108 x1595, op 23 x1427, op 94 x1267, op 40 x1021 (always 80 bytes) and op 114 x906 (always 10 bytes). All eight class files are within 3 KB of each other in size (575,477..578,356), so they are the same script with per-class edits and DIFFING THEM is an obvious lever nobody has pulled yet. Tool: analysis/tools/startcode.py.
column5: THE ARGUMENT GRAMMAR IS ONLY PARTLY SOLVED, and the row says so rather than dressing it up. Three tags are certain because the fixed-length opcodes close on them exactly - opcode 114's 10-byte body is precisely `0b <u32> 02 <u32>`: 0x01 = NUL-terminated string, 0x02 = u32, 0x0b = u32. 8,450 of 15,422 records parse under that partial table. The rest need tags not yet identified, and a size-solver that maximised clean parses DRIFTED INTO NONSENSE, assigning ASCII letters (0x42 'B', 0x4d 'M', 0x52 'R') as tags - the signature of landing inside a string, so at least one string-bearing tag is still mis-sized. Do not trust a parse that reports letter-valued tags. NEXT METHOD, and it is the one that worked for the fixed opcodes: group records by (opcode, length) and find the byte positions that are constant across the group; that reads a schema off the data instead of guessing sizes.
column6: WHAT IS ALREADY VISIBLE, and it bears directly on the blocked threads. 17,490 embedded strings, 10,202 distinct: chestTrigger x2273, GRABSTEINMOUSEOVER x1022, BRUNNENMOUSEOVER, PanelTrigger, WWTrigger, Versteck_1..111 (hiding places), Abuecherstaender, plus 170 NPC-related names including NPC_Dialog_Farmer / _Citizen / _Noble / _Soldier / _Magician - so DIALOGUE ROUTING BY NPC TYPE is authored here. AND THE TEXT CHAIN RESOLVES: the scripts carry 335 references of the form res:N and cres:N (135 distinct, range 17,085..22,008), and install/scripts/us/global.res is the English string table they point into - magic 'SZ', a 16-byte-per-slot index ending at the first data offset 0x5a530, 23,122 slots. Slot 17,466 reads "Mother's Powder Contain..." and slot 22,008 "These stones with runes on them are said to strengthen the magic power of the herbs growing her...". CAVEAT, MEASURED NOT GUESSED: the index arithmetic is ~2 bytes out (slot 1 renders as '\x1a\x00Seraph' where the text is 'Seraphim'), and the first u32 of each slot is NOT an id - it rises past 2 billion. The offset/length pair is right, the alignment needs finishing.

column4: THE startcode TAG TABLE IS SOLVED TO 96.5%, AND funkcode.bin IS THE SAME FORMAT. Fourteen tags, read off the data by grouping records on (opcode, length) and marking the byte positions that are constant across the group - not guessed: 0x01/0x09/0x1e/0x29/0x41 are NUL-terminated strings, 0x02/0x0b/0x1f are u32, 0x03/0x28 are u16, 0x04/0x0c/0x0d/0x2a are TWELVE-byte payloads (almost certainly 3 x u32; the tool currently prints them as one 96-bit integer, which is ugly but not wrong), and 0x10 is a ZERO-LENGTH marker. That last one is why the first solver stalled - 0 was not among the candidate sizes it tried. 13,855 of 15,422 startcode records parse under this table. Opcode 40 (1,021 records, always 84 bytes) accounts for most of the rest and is NOT a tag stream at all but a FIXED 80-BYTE STRUCT beginning ffffffff with bytes 30..67 always zero. 13,855 + 1,021 = 96.5% of the file explained.
column5: funkcode.bin USES THE IDENTICAL FRAMING: 3,962,707 bytes, framed 100.000% end to end with no desync, 125,055 records, 102 opcodes. So the 3.8 MB file that has never been read by anything is the same u16-opcode / u16-length record stream as startcode, just with a wider opcode vocabulary - 47.6% of its records already parse under the startcode tag table, and the remainder need the same (opcode, length) treatment. vectoren.bin is a DIFFERENT format and should not be run through this parser: 2,172,600 bytes, header u32 23,494, then fixed-stride entries (dominant delta 84 bytes) whose payload is a NAME - dq_belohnung, super_kiste, Dialog:MP_Romata_99, trigger99, ok_hq, QIS_Trigger99. That reads as the SCRIPT SYMBOL TABLE, i.e. plausibly the name-to-id map the bytecode's numeric operands refer to, which would make it the key to reading funkcode semantically rather than structurally. Not confirmed - the 84-byte stride does not divide the file exactly, so the record layout is not yet pinned.
column6: METHOD WARNING, LOGGED BECAUSE IT COST TIME TWICE. A greedy solver that assigns tag sizes by maximising cleanly-parsed records DRIFTS AND MUST NOT BE TRUSTED past its first few large jumps. Both runs began assigning ASCII letters as tags (0x42 'B', 0x4d 'M', 0x60-0x75 'a'..'u') and flip-flopping sizes for the same tag (0x31 -> 12 then 1; 0x32 -> 12 then STR; 0x11 -> 12 then 4), each change buying only a handful of records - the signature of the parser landing inside string data and rationalising it. The trustworthy method is positional: same opcode, same length, look at which bytes never vary. Every tag in the table above was confirmed that way or by a record closing exactly on it. TOOL: analysis/tools/startcode.py carries the table and refuses to guess - unknown tags are reported as ('?tag', N) with the offset, never silently resynced.

column4: vectoren.bin IS funkcode.bin's SYMBOL TABLE, AND THE SCRIPTS ARE NOW READABLE BY NAME. Layout, pinned: u32 count = 23,494 at +0x00, then fixed 84-BYTE RECORDS from offset 0x58 - char name[64], then five u32s. The proof is arithmetic and exact: the second and third u32s are OFFSET and LENGTH, they chain perfectly (a[i+1] == a[i] + b[i] for 23,492 of 23,493 consecutive pairs), sum(length) = 3,962,707 and max(offset+length) = 3,962,707, which is EXACTLY the byte size of funkcode.bin. The 23,494 named ranges therefore TILE funkcode contiguously with nothing left over. 23,461 of 23,494 names are printable. The file also carries a 199,016-byte tail section after the table (at 0x1e1d50) that is not yet looked at. Name prefixes: QIS x2317, ToDo x1870, fillchest x1810, Dialog x1021, DQ x903, setvar x438.
column5: A NAMED SCRIPT DUMPS CLEANLY, end to end. Dialog:NPC_Dialog_Novizin - the chapel priestess, the same novizin1 that DefPos.bin places at (3239,2525) in row 698 - occupies funkcode[0x1c4be..0x1c57e], 192 bytes, and decodes to: op105 ['Zufallsdialog', 0, 5]; op105 ['Zufallsdialog4', 0, 8]; op22 ['AllgemeinesPool']; op26 ['NOVIZIN_0+Var(Zufallsdialog)']; op60 ['res:1024', 'npc_dialog_ok']. That is a random-dialogue variable over 0..5, a text key built by CONCATENATION (NOVIZIN_0 .. NOVIZIN_5), and a resource string plus a button id. One record of the eight does not parse yet. So the chain name -> symbol -> bytecode -> res:N -> global.res text is now walkable end to end.
column6: IMPORTANT NEGATIVE, and it redirects row 692: THE SCRIPTS DO NOT CARRY NPC APPEARANCE. funkcode.bin's 3.9 MB contains ZERO occurrences of '.grn', '.GRN', 'model', 'creature' or 'kreatur'. The only novizin strings are 'Novizin' and 'novizin1', i.e. the DefPos name. So the 'what to draw' link is NOT in the script bytecode and looking for it there is now a closed avenue - it must live in the creature/model binding instead. FUNKCODE OPCODE SWEEP, partial: same framing as startcode (125,055 records, 102 opcodes, framed 100.000%). Three new tags pinned positionally from op 115, whose 32-byte body is exactly 02 <u32> 87 <u32 u32> 88 <u32 u32> 89 <u32 u32>, giving 0x87/0x88/0x89 = 8 bytes and lifting funkcode from 47.6% to 58.5% of records parsed. Remaining blockers, in order of records: 0x1c x9350, 0x8b x7444, 0x20 x5808, 0x36 x5360, 0x7d x2112, 0x48 x1985 - each addressable by the same (opcode, length) mask method. startcode stays at 89.8%; those tags do not occur there.

column4: FUNKCODE'S TAG TABLE IS SWEPT TO 84%, startcode TO 90%, ON 39 TAGS - all pinned POSITIONALLY, none by the drifting size-solver row 712 warns about. Method for every one: take the records where the parse first fails on tag T, group by (opcode, body length), dump the raw bytes from the tag to the end of the dominant group, and read the size off a record that closes exactly. Added this round: 0x1c=4 (op122 closes as 1c <u32> 38 <u32> in 10 bytes), 0x8b=1, 0x20=12, 0x7d=STR, 0x48=4, 0x38=4, 0x7e=4, 0x1d=4, 0x34=8, 0x16=STR, 0x53=4, 0x49=4, 0x12=1, 0x67=STR, 0x33=8, 0x44=STR, 0x7c=0, 0x52=STR, 0x64=4. Zero-length marker tags now number three (0x10, 0x7c, and 0x2b from the earlier pass) - a size the first solver never tried, which is what stalled it.
column5: PROGRESSION, measured at each step so a wrong assignment would show as a zero or negative gain: funkcode 47.6% -> 58.5% (0x87/0x88/0x89 = 8) -> 75.3% -> 79.7% -> 84.0%; startcode 89.8% -> 90.0%. THREE ASSIGNMENTS ARE UNCONFIRMED BY SCORE and are flagged rather than trusted: 0x36=4, 0x35=12 and 0x19=4 were read off op 51's bytes but each bought ZERO extra records, because those records still fail later on another tag in the same body. They are positionally plausible and harmless, but nothing has actually tested them. 0x64=4 is also weak - op 51's 31-byte body leaves a 7-byte tail after it, which 4 does not divide cleanly, so the byte after its u32 is doing something unexplained.
column6: WHAT THE TAG PAYLOADS REVEAL, which is worth as much as the parse rate: the string tags carry the game's own vocabulary, and the NPC TYPE names live here - 0x7d holds TYPE_NPC_FARMER_MAL and 0x52 holds TYPE_NPC_DARKELVE, the same TYPE_NPC_* namespace as the bin/ directories. 0x16 holds quest ids (DQ1_BRINGE_ITEM), 0x44 holds variable names (Q_NUM), 0x67 holds effect names (ECS_HEALING, ECS_LIGHT...). REMAINING BLOCKERS, all addressable by the same method: funkcode 0x00 x4186 (a null/void tag, the single biggest), 0x42 x748, 0x32 x727, 0x3c x711, 0x75 x708; startcode is dominated by opcode 40's fixed 80-byte ffffffff struct (1,021 records) which is NOT a tag stream and needs its own schema. TOOL: analysis/tools/startcode.py now carries all 39 tags and still refuses to guess - unknown tags surface as ('?tag', N) with an offset.

column4: TAG 0x00 IS A 2-BYTE FIELD AND IT WAS THE SINGLE BIGGEST REMAINING WIN. Found positionally: opcode 51's 31-byte body parses to 36 <u32> 35 <12> 19 <u32> 64 <u32> and then has exactly THREE bytes left, 00 00 00 - and the same three bytes recur mid-record in its 88-byte bodies, immediately followed by a valid 0x19. Both readings are satisfied by tag 0x00 carrying a 2-byte payload. Confirmed BY SCORE against its alternatives rather than assumed: size 2 lifts funkcode to 85.9% while size 1 gives 84.1% and size 4 gives 84.4%, a gain of 2,339 records. Continuing the same (opcode, length) method through the tail added 0x32=8, 0x42=0, 0x75=4, 0x3c=8, 0x14=8, 0x2b=0, 0x0a=8, 0x3a=STR, then 0x0f=4, 0x39=0, 0x54=STR, 0x11=4, 0x1b=0. FUNKCODE IS NOW AT 89.0% (111,306 of 125,055 records) AND startcode AT 90.2%, on 53 tags. Zero-length marker tags now number seven: 0x10, 0x2b, 0x39, 0x42, 0x7c, 0x1b and (from the earlier pass) 0x6-family entries were dropped as unverified.
column5: TWO ASSIGNMENTS ARE WRONG OR CONTEXT-DEPENDENT AND THE EVIDENCE IS IN THE FAILURE LIST ITSELF. 0x02 is in the table as 4 bytes - pinned hard by opcode 114's fixed 10-byte body, which is exactly 0b <u32> 02 <u32> - yet 572 records still fail ON 0x02, in one case with only THREE bytes left in the body. A tag cannot be four bytes wide and also fit in three, so in those records a PRECEDING tag is mis-sized and the parser arrives at 0x02 off by two. The same pattern indicts 0x0a=8, which bought only 14 records when added and now reappears as a blocker on 648. Do not 'fix' either by changing 0x02 or 0x0a; the error is upstream of them, in whichever neighbour tag is short. Finding it needs the (opcode, length) mask on the records that fail this way, not another size guess. Likewise 0x36=4, 0x35=12, 0x19=4 and 0x64=4 remain positionally plausible but score-unverified from row 714.
column6: DIMINISHING RETURNS ARE NOW VISIBLE AND WORTH STATING SO THE NEXT PASS IS BUDGETED HONESTLY. The last five tags bought 701, 225, 593, 164 and 0 records respectively, against 2,339 for 0x00, and the remaining blockers are a flat tail - 0x0a x648, 0x79 x587, 0x02 x572, 0x5f x542, 0x31 x516, 0x8f x447 - so the next several tags are worth roughly half a percent each. The structural payoff is already banked: with 89% of funkcode parsed, any named symbol from vectoren.bin can be dumped and read (row 713), which was the point. What is NOT yet touched: startcode's opcode 40 fixed 80-byte struct (1,021 records, the bulk of its residue), vectoren's 199,016-byte tail section, and the OPCODE SEMANTICS - every number in this work is a record shape, and no opcode has been given a meaning beyond the handful legible from their string payloads. TOOL: analysis/tools/startcode.py, 53 tags.

column4: ROW 715 IS WRONG ABOUT TAG 0x00: IT IS A ZERO-LENGTH MARKER, NOT A 2-BYTE FIELD. Row 715 stated the size was 2 and said it was 'confirmed BY SCORE against its alternatives' - but the alternatives tested were 1, 2 and 4. ZERO WAS NEVER TRIED, which is the same blind spot that stalled the very first solver in row 712 and which row 714 explicitly noted had already bitten twice. Three times now. The score cannot separate the two readings: 0x00=0 gives funkcode 89.1% and 0x00=2 gives 89.0%, a difference of 74 records out of 125,055, so the aggregate metric is effectively blind here and only the positional evidence decides.
column5: THE POSITIONAL EVIDENCE IS DECISIVE AND POINTS AT ZERO. The record that exposed it is opcode 1, 46-byte body: 01 'res:DQ1_BRINGE_NPC_ZIEL10' 00 | 04 <12 bytes> | 00 | 02 82020000. Under 0x00=2 the parser eats two bytes and then arrives at 0x02 with only THREE bytes left, which a 4-byte tag cannot fit - that is the contradiction row 715 flagged and misattributed to an unknown upstream tag. Under 0x00=0 the record closes EXACTLY at 46 with 0x02 taking its full u32 (642). The op-51 evidence that originally motivated the value of 2 - a trailing 00 00 00 after 64 <u32> - is satisfied by BOTH readings, since three zero-length markers close the record just as well as one 2-byte field plus one stray byte, so it never discriminated in the first place. THERE WAS NO MIS-SIZED UPSTREAM TAG. The bug was 0x00 itself, and row 715's diagnosis pointed the next reader in the wrong direction.
column6: EFFECT, MEASURED: records failing on 0x02 drop from 572 to 110, and funkcode goes from 89.0% to 89.1% (111,380 of 125,055). The residual 110 are a genuinely separate problem and still unexplained. 0x0a=8 remains suspect on its own terms - it bought 14 records when added and still blocks 656 - and should be re-derived positionally rather than trusted; 0x64=4 is also now explained differently, since its 7-byte tail reads as 64 <u32> followed by three zero-length 0x00 markers. LESSON, and it is the same one three rows running: WHEN SOLVING A FIELD WIDTH, ALWAYS INCLUDE ZERO IN THE CANDIDATE SET, and never let an aggregate parse rate arbitrate between two readings whose scores differ by less than a percent - go back to a single record and make it close. Tool updated to 0x00=0.

column4: 0x0a=8 IS WRONG - BUT MORE IMPORTANTLY, THE CLOSURE METHOD CANNOT DETERMINE IT, AND THAT INVALIDATES PART OF THE TABLE. Re-derived positionally: the tightest cases are opcode 3 bodies where 0x0a sits 3 bytes from the end as 0a 00 00. Scoring the candidates, sizes 0, 1 AND 2 ALL GIVE EXACTLY 112,688 of 125,055 (90.11%) - byte-identical results - while 4 gives 89.74% and the table's current 8 gives 89.06%. So 8 is definitively wrong and costs 1.05 points, but WHICH of 0, 1 or 2 is right cannot be decided this way. The discriminating record, opcode 1 with 0a 01 00 00 as its last four bytes, CLOSES UNDER ALL THREE readings.
column5: THE ROOT CAUSE IS THAT THE GRAMMAR AS MODELLED IS AMBIGUOUS, and this is the real finding of this row. Row 716 established 0x00 as a ZERO-LENGTH marker; the payload bytes are also overwhelmingly zero. A trailing run of 00 bytes can therefore be read as a marker, as part of a preceding field, or as an empty string after 0x01 - all of which close the record. Any tag whose evidence rests only on records where it is followed by zeros is CONSISTENT rather than ESTABLISHED. That covers an unknown fraction of the 53-tag table: the tags pinned by non-zero payloads (0x87/0x88/0x89 from op 115's 02 <u32> 87 <u32 u32> 88 <u32 u32> 89 <u32 u32>, 0x1c from op 122, the STR tags read off their own text) are solid; the ones derived from zero tails are not. Parse rate is a WEAK metric here and rows 712-716 leaned on it more than it can bear.
column6: THE DECISIVE SOURCE IS THE ENGINE, AND THE ENTRY POINTS ARE NOW FOUND. The filenames are CamelCase in .rodata, which is why an earlier lowercase search reported zero hits: '%s\\StartCode.bin' at 0x086f3cb0 referenced once from 0x08266c6f, '%s\\FunkCode.bin' at 0x086f3cc1 from 0x08266d2c, '%s\\Vectoren.bin' at 0x086f3d05 from 0x0826749a - each an sprintf building the per-class path. Following the loaded buffer to the routine that switches on the tag byte would give the widths authoritatively instead of by inference, and that is the correct next step rather than more closure fitting. 0x0a set to 2 in the tool as the simplest reading of the 0a 00 00 tail, EXPLICITLY FLAGGED as undetermined among {0,1,2} - do not cite it as decoded. funkcode now 90.1%, startcode 90.2%.

column4: THE SCRIPT INTERPRETER IS FOUND AND THE TAG WIDTHS ARE NOW AUTHORITATIVE INSTEAD OF INFERRED. The filenames are CamelCase in .rodata ('%s\\FunkCode.bin' at 0x086f3cc1), which is why a lowercase search found nothing; its one xref at 0x08266d2c is an sprintf building the per-class path. The interpreter itself is the record loop at 0x0826af24: it reads the record LENGTH as movsx eax, WORD PTR [ebx+0x2] - INDEPENDENTLY CONFIRMING the u16-opcode/u16-length framing of row 711 - compares a cursor at [esi] against it, reads the tag byte at record_base+cursor, bounds-checks against 0xa1 and dispatches through a 162-ENTRY JUMP TABLE at 0x086f3fbc with 52 DISTINCT HANDLERS. Each handler ends in add DWORD PTR [esi], N, so the width of every tag is N-1, readable directly. Shared handlers prove equal widths: 0x33/0x87/0x88/0x89 all land on 0x0826d008, and 0x53/0x54/0x55/0x56/0x57/0x86 all land on 0x0826dd5c.
column5: VERIFIED BY DISASSEMBLING THE HANDLERS, four of them read in full. 0x0a at 0x0826e30a reads a u16 and adds 3, so WIDTH 2 - the guess row 717 flagged as undetermined among {0,1,2} was right, and the 8 in the table before it was wrong. 0x53/0x54 at 0x0826dd5c read a u32 and add 5, so WIDTH 4 - which means 0x54 IS NOT A STRING, and row 714's STR assignment for it was wrong; the 'mp' text it appeared to carry was a mis-parse. 0x28 at 0x0826dac2 reads a BYTE and adds 2, so WIDTH 1, not the 2 in the table since row 712. 0x00 at 0x0826e8b2 does NOT advance the cursor at all - it sets the return value and exits, the same target the out-of-range bounds check jumps to, so 0x00 TERMINATES the record rather than being a zero-length field. Row 716 got its behaviour right for the wrong reason.
column6: AND THE FIXED-WIDTH MODEL IS ITSELF WRONG FOR SOME TAGS. 0x04's handler at 0x0826d1e9 begins cmp DWORD PTR [eax+ebx*1+0x1], 0xfffffffe and branches: when the u32 after the tag is the SENTINEL -2 it computes a pointer at cursor+5 and reads a STRING there, otherwise it takes a different path entirely. So 0x04 is a VARIANT record, not a 12-byte field - which is exactly why 'aaa' appeared inside what row 713's parse showed as a 96-bit integer. Any tag with a branch in its handler needs the variant read, and a flat width table cannot express it. STATUS OF THE 53-TAG TABLE against the engine, using a first-add heuristic that is itself unreliable for branching handlers: 26 agree, 9 disagree, and 44 TAGS EXIST THAT THE SERAPHIM DATA NEVER EXERCISES. NEXT: disassemble all 52 handlers properly rather than heuristically, and rebuild the table from them - do not extend the closure-fitting approach, it has now been shown wrong on at least three tags.

column4: THE 52 HANDLERS ARE MAPPED BUT THE BULK EXTRACTION IS NOT TRUSTWORTHY, AND THE TABLE IS NOT REBUILT. The jump table at 0x086f3fbc was read in full - 162 tag slots, 52 distinct handlers, 66 slots pointing at the default 0x0826e0bc. Handler classification by disassembling the whole switch body once (0x0826af50..0x0826e900) and slicing each handler's extent as [start, next_start) gives: 37 STR, 22 four-byte, 7 END, 7 two-byte, 7 eight-byte, 5 twelve-byte, 4 VARIANT, plus singletons. FOUR HANDLERS READ BY HAND ARE AUTHORITATIVE AND STAND: 0x0a reads a u16 and adds 3 so WIDTH 2; 0x53/0x54/0x55/0x56/0x57/0x86 share 0x0826dd5c which reads a u32 and adds 5 so WIDTH 4 (0x54 is NOT a string); 0x28 at 0x0826dac2 reads a byte and adds 2 so WIDTH 1; 0x00 at 0x0826e8b2 does not advance at all and exits, so it TERMINATES the record. String handlers are identifiable by a strcpy from record_base+cursor+1 into a 256-byte slot array at +0xa46c.
column5: THE EXTRACTION IS FLAWED AND THE EVIDENCE IS THAT IT SCORES WORSE. Applying the engine-derived table wholesale drops startcode from 90.2% to 63.3% and funkcode from 90.1% to 87.8%. A table read from the actual interpreter cannot be worse than one fitted to the data unless the READING is wrong - and it is: slicing handlers by address range assumes the switch cases are laid out contiguously in tag order, so a handler with no add of its own silently inherits its neighbour's. Proper extraction has to FOLLOW CONTROL FLOW from each handler entry to the shared epilogue at 0x0826e8b9, not slice by address. That is the outstanding work. A second attempt applying only the four hand-verified corrections ALSO scored worse (60.4% / 84.1%), for a different and more interesting reason: 0x04's non-sentinel branch jumps to 0x0826d8b4, which is not modelled, so shortening 0x04 from 12 to 4 bytes shifts every later field in the record and surfaces new blockers (0x27 x1950, 0x0e x1341). The variant must be modelled fully before any of the four corrections can be applied.
column6: STATE LEFT BEHIND, deliberately conservative: analysis/tools/startcode.py carries the EMPIRICAL 53-tag table, restored and re-measured at startcode 90.2% / funkcode 90.1%, with a header naming the four confirmed engine corrections and explaining WHY they are not applied yet. Nothing in the tool now claims to be engine-derived. This row exists so the next reader does not repeat either mistake: do not re-fit widths by closure (rows 712-717 showed the grammar is ambiguous once zero-length tags and zero payloads are in play), and do not bulk-extract handler widths by address slicing (this row). The correct method is per-handler control-flow following, and the entry points are all listed in the jump table at 0x086f3fbc.

column4: THE TAG TABLE IS REBUILT FROM THE INTERPRETER AND startcode.bin NOW PARSES 100%. Method, replacing the address-slicing that failed in row 719: analysis/tools/tagwidths.py walks the CONTROL FLOW from each handler entry in the jump table at 0x086f3fbc to the shared epilogue at 0x0826e8b9, accumulating the cursor advance along every path - add DWORD PTR [esi],imm adds imm, inc [esi] adds 1, add [esi],reg means a computed length, and a strcpy on the path means the payload is a NUL-terminated string. Width is advance minus one, the one byte being the tag itself. Paths are kept SEPARATE rather than merged, so a handler that copies a string on one branch and takes a fixed field on another is reported as the VARIANT it is instead of collapsing to STR - which is exactly what row 719's version did to 0x04.
column5: THREE RULES COMPLETE IT, AND THE MISSING ONE WAS WHY THE ENGINE TABLE HAD SCORED WORSE THAN A FITTED ONE. First: 66 of the 162 tag slots point at the DEFAULT handler 0x0826e0bc, which is nothing but `inc [esi]; jmp epilogue` - so EVERY UNLISTED TAG BELOW 0xa2 IS A ZERO-WIDTH MARKER. Row 719 excluded the default handler as uninteresting and thereby dropped 66 real tags, which is why startcode collapsed to 63% there; adding them took it from 71.1% to 100%. It also independently confirms the empirical finding that 0x10, 0x1b, 0x2b, 0x39, 0x42 and 0x7c are zero-width. Second: a tag at or above 0xa2 fails the interpreter's own bounds check and exits the record. Third: VARIANT tags (0x04, 0x0c, 0x0d, 0x3c fixed 12; 0x37, 0x4b fixed 1; 0x71 fixed 0) read a u32 and, when it is the sentinel 0xfffffffe, take a string instead - which is the 'aaa' that appeared inside a supposed 96-bit integer in row 713.
column6: RESULT ACROSS ALL EIGHT CLASSES: startcode.bin parses 15,408..15,494 records with ZERO unparsed in every one; funkcode.bin parses 124,931..125,236 records with EXACTLY 358 unparsed in every one. That constant is itself evidence - the same shared construct fails in all eight files, so it is one unmodelled record shape rather than corruption. Those 358 cluster on tags 0x02/0x03/0x04 at 110 each plus 0x36 at 10, i.e. almost certainly one opcode whose 0x04 variant has a third branch. CORRECTIONS TO EARLIER ROWS NOW CONFIRMED BY THE ENGINE: 0x28 is 1 not 2 (row 712), 0x54 is 4 not STR (row 714), 0x0a is 2 not 8 (rows 715/717), 0x00 terminates rather than being zero-width (row 716), and 0x04 is a variant not a flat 12 (row 713). analysis/tools/startcode.py now carries the engine-derived table and says so.

column4: THE SCRIPT BYTECODE NOW PARSES 100% - ALL SIXTEEN FILES, 1.12 MILLION RECORDS, ZERO UNPARSED. The residual 358 that were identical across all eight classes turned out to be TWO separate constructs, neither of them corruption. FIRST, tag 0x3a TAKES TWO STRINGS, not one: its handler at 0x0826be72 contains TWO strcpy calls, so two NUL-terminated strings follow with no tag byte between them - 3a 'HERO' 00 'res:17562' 00. The CFG walk had collapsed it to a single STR because it recorded the first string outcome and stopped. Modelled as STR2, it accounts for the op-58 and op-66 failures (28 records).
column5: SECOND, AND MORE INTERESTING: THE ENGINE TOLERATES A PAYLOAD THAT OVERRUNS THE RECORD, and my parser was treating that as failure. The interpreter's loop test at 0x0826af30 is `cmp DWORD PTR [esi], eax / jge end` where eax is the record LENGTH - it checks the cursor BEFORE reading a tag, never after reading a payload. So when opcode 41's 2-byte body holds `02 00`, the 0x02 handler reads a u32 that runs four bytes past the record end into the next record, stores the garbage, advances the cursor to 9, and the loop then exits because 9 >= 6. The engine does not care. That single behaviour accounts for all 330 op-41 records (bodies exactly 0200, 0300 and 0400, 110 each). Treating an overrun as 'consume what is there and end the record' rather than as an error is therefore FAITHFUL to retail, not a fudge - though it does mean those records' final operand is whatever happened to follow in the file, which the engine also reads.
column6: VERIFIED ACROSS EVERY CLASS: startcode.bin 15,408..15,494 records and funkcode.bin 124,931..125,236 records, ZERO unparsed in all sixteen files. Regression check on the named scripts still reads cleanly - Dialog:NPC_Dialog_Farmer dumps as op22 'IsInRgn', op105 'Zufallsdialog' 0..6, op75 'NPCGeklickt' 1, op67 'NPCGeklickt' 0, op26 'FARMER_+Var(atmos_rgx)+_+Var(zufallsdialog)', op60 'res:1024' 'npc_dialog_ok' - i.e. a region test, a random-dialogue variable, a clicked flag, a text key built by concatenation, and a resource string with a button. THE FORMAT IS DONE. What remains is SEMANTICS: 102 opcodes, none of which has a verified meaning beyond what its string payloads suggest, and the 66 zero-width tags are presumably operators whose identity is in the handlers already located.

column4: THE OPCODE DISPATCHER IS LOCATED - SEMANTICS WORK NOW HAS ITS ENTRY POINT, BUT IS NOT STARTED. Architecture, established: the record parser at 0x0826aed6 (rows 718-721) only PARSES a record's tagged arguments into slots and returns; it does not execute anything. It has 110 CALL SITES, and those are the per-opcode handler functions - each opcode's implementation calls the parser to fetch its own operands. The dispatcher that routes to them is the function at 0x0826e8ce (size 0x381e, ending 0x082720ec), which begins immediately after the parser. Its switch is at 0x0826ea49: `jmp DWORD PTR [eax*4+0x086f4298]`, bounded by a cmp against 0x8c and a ja to the default at 0x082720dd. So the OPCODE JUMP TABLE IS AT 0x086f4298 WITH 141 ENTRIES, opcodes 0..140 - which matches the data exactly, since the highest opcode observed in startcode.bin is 140.
column5: WHY THE EARLIER GUESS AT THE STRUCTURE WAS WRONG, noted so it is not repeated: a scan for a dense table of function pointers containing the 110 handler addresses found NOTHING, because the dispatch is not a pointer table - it is a switch whose cases CALL the handlers, so the handler addresses appear as E8 call displacements inside the dispatcher rather than as words in .rodata. The right way to enumerate them is to read the 141-entry jump table at 0x086f4298, follow each case, and record which of the 110 handler functions it calls.
column6: SCOPE OF WHAT REMAINS, stated honestly because it is large: 102 opcodes occur in the seraphim files (103 in gladiator) and NONE has a verified meaning. What can be inferred cheaply from payloads alone is suggestive but unproven - op22 takes names like 'IsInRgn' and 'AllgemeinesPool', op105 declares a variable with a range, op75/op67 set and test 'NPCGeklickt', op26 builds a text key by concatenation, op60 pairs a res: string with a button id. Turning those into decoded semantics means reading 141 dispatcher cases and their handlers, which is a substantially bigger body of work than the format decode was. The 66 zero-width tags are the other half - they are presumably operators, and their handlers are already enumerated in the tag table at 0x086f3fbc.

column4: ALL 141 OPCODE SLOTS ARE RESOLVED TO HANDLER FUNCTIONS AND 30 OF THEM ARE NAMED FROM THE ENGINE'S OWN STRINGS. Method (analysis/tools/opcodes.py): read the 141-entry jump table at 0x086f4298, then walk each case body - every live case is a stub that pushes the parsed slot array (ebp-0x818) and the dynamic_cast'd target, CALLs one function and jmps to the shared tail, so opcode -> handler is 1:1 and readable. 124 slots are live, 17 point at the default case, and the 124 resolve to 121 DISTINCT handlers (37/38, 65/67, 88/134 and 35/51 pair up). Handler extents come from .eh_frame; the .rodata literals inside each handler are what name it. Named from strings, not guessed: 1 CreateNPC, 8 CreateOBJ, 24 group-alive test, 37/38 SOUND_, 44 NPCUWR_, 46 Teleport, 58 IsNotVarBit, 60 RES:%d, 63 QuestkompassPos, 64 QuestkompassOBJ, 65/67/75/76/105 atmo_rg, 78 chest, 91 blacksmith UI, 92 teleport-without-listener, 94/140 versteck, 98 weather (rain/regen/thunder/snow per sector), 104/127/128 SOUND_FX_, 108/109/113/133 GetPoolPos, 119 region pool, 130 cInterpretSQW::Teleporter, 138/139 UI_WND_TASKBAR. The dispatcher's class name falls out of opcode 130's format string: cInterpretSQW.
column5: TWO STRUCTURAL FACTS THE TABLE SETTLES. First, the DEFAULT CASE AT 0x082720dd IS NOT AN ERROR PATH - it is `mov ecx,1; ret`, i.e. success - so an opcode with no case is SILENTLY IGNORED, not rejected. That matters because OPCODE 42 OCCURS 4950 TIMES IN THE SHIPPED SCRIPTS AND HAS NO CASE: the engine reads those records and does nothing. Alignment is not the explanation - 41 and 43 flank it with real cases and identical counts (4950/4961), and every other data opcode has a case, so 42 is a genuine no-op. Second, opcode 0's case is the only one that sets ecx=0 instead of 1 before the shared return, so 0 is the halt/false result the dispatcher's caller tests on.
column6: NOT DONE, AND THE LIMITS ARE SPECIFIC. 91 of the 121 handlers carry no naming string and are still unnamed; the operand samples in analysis/script-opcodes.md narrow them but do not settle them. Four handlers (40, 47, 59, 66, 88/134) fell outside .eh_frame so their extent defaulted to a 0x400 window and their strings are UNRELIABLE - 59/66 reporting the wincompat '%s/%s' is that artifact, not a finding. Handlers are not virtual, so RTTI gives nothing: analysis/rtti/lgp_linux_vmethods.tsv has zero of the 121. Next lever, untried: the handlers call virtual methods on the object they receive, so resolving even one call site per handler to a class from lgp_linux_vtables.json would name the SUBSYSTEM each opcode drives.

column4: THE VTABLE LEVER RUNS BUT IT IS WEAK: IT NAMES A SUBSYSTEM FOR 18 OF THE 91 UNNAMED HANDLERS AND NOTHING FOR THE OTHER 73. Method, now in analysis/tools/opcodes.py: build typeinfo/vtable/vslot maps for sacred_orig directly (typeinfo = [__*_type_info vptr, name*], vtable starts one word past a pointer to a typeinfo, then walk slots), and flag every immediate in a handler that equals a typeinfo (dynamic_cast), a vtable (construction) or a vtable slot (direct call to a member function). Across all 120 handlers only 15 DISTINCT CLASSES appear at all, and five of them - cEvent, cEventNetwork, cObject, cCreature, cFile_ram - occur in 13 to 66 handlers each, so they carry no information and are filtered. What survives: 2 cObject3D/cObjectFX/cEventFX, 7/35/51 cItemBase, 18/70/79/89/121/125/132 cEvent_engine, 62/72/74/93 cEvent_creature, 73/99 cEventFX, 49/93 cObject3D, and 132 cCommand_armaStop - an animation-stop command, the only handler the lever names outright. Column added to analysis/script-opcodes.md.
column5: WHY IT UNDERPERFORMS, measured rather than assumed: the handlers do not call virtual methods through resolvable statics. ZERO of the 121 handler addresses is itself a vtable slot, and direct calls to functions that ARE vtable slots number in the single digits across the whole set. The dispatcher's own dynamic_cast is the shape of the whole subsystem - `dynamic_cast<cCreature*>` from typeinfo 0x872e260 (cObject) to 0x872e320 (cCreature) at 0x0826e900 - so nearly every handler receives an already-cast cCreature and does its work through non-virtual calls and raw field offsets, which RTTI cannot see. A depth-1 sweep (harvest strings from every callee with an .eh_frame extent under 0x3000) was tried alongside and added only opcode 58's condition vocabulary (if IsDead/IsFighting/IsLocked/IsNotLocked/IsInRgn) and TYPE_OBJECT_DOOR on 2/49.
column6: A METHOD WARNING PAID FOR IN LOST WORK. analysis/rtti/extract_vtables_elf.py WRITES ITS OUTPUT TO A FIXED PATH (analysis/rtti/lgp_linux_vmethods.tsv and .json) regardless of which binary is passed in, so running it on install/sacred_orig SILENTLY OVERWROTE the artifacts built from analysis/lgp-2010/sacred-1.0.02-final. It was restored by re-running on that binary and re-checked (0x872e2c0 is cUI_CDKey there, as before). During the window where the two were confused the sacred_orig addresses looked like MISLABELLED CLASS NAMES - a cUI_CDKey where the code plainly holds cObject - and that read was wrong: the extractor is correct, the two builds simply do not share addresses. The maps in analysis/rtti/ are for the lgp-2010 build ONLY and must not be used against sacred_orig; opcodes.py now builds its own.

column4: THE BEHAVIOURAL LEVER NAMES 20 MORE OPCODES AND CRACKS global.res OPEN AS A NAMING ORACLE. Tool: analysis/tools/opsem.py, output analysis/script-opcodes-behaviour.md. For every opcode across all 16 script files it profiles the TAG SIGNATURE (startcode.parse now takes with_tags=True), the operand NAMESPACE histogram (res:, pos_, DQ_, TYPE_NPC_, POOL_, Dialog:, SOUND_ ...), the neighbouring opcodes, and the ENGLISH TEXT its res: operands resolve to. global.res decoding, which nothing had done correctly: u32 'SZ' magic, then 16-byte index entries [id, offset, 0, size], text is UTF-16LE at offset+4 running size bytes, and `res:N` IN THE SCRIPTS IS THE SLOT INDEX, NOT the id field - the id field is non-monotonic and runs past 2^31. Checks: slot 49 'Seraphim', 50 'Gladiator', 18101 'Settler', 19554 'Save... Vilya...', 17562 'My Daddy is much stronger than you!'. Named this way: 3 say(res:TEXT, dialogue label), 23 named-position table, 26 label/entry point, 48 declare-trigger, 50 trigger payload, 53 quest-log line, 58 IF, 59/62 block markers, 66 second conditional family, 67/68/86 set-variable, 20/21 quest-id-only, 22 reference-by-name, 100/115 bulk data.
column5: THE BIGGEST STRUCTURAL RESULT IS THAT OPCODE 58 IS `IF` AND ITS PREDICATE IS CHOSEN BY THE TAG BYTE, NOT BY THE OPCODE. Its handler at 0x82a8672 holds the vocabulary - if IsNotVarBit:%s=%d, if IsDead:%s, if IsFighting:%s, if IsLocked:%s, if IsNotLocked:%s, if IsInRgn:%s - and the corpus shows the operand tag selecting among them: tag 0x52/0x7d/0x8f carry TYPE_NPC_* (25,974 records), 0x47 carries quest variables and PoolEmpty, 0x40 carries res: text, 0x3a carries the HERO/res: pair. Opcode 66 has the same shape and is the second half of the conditional family. Every claim in the table is a measured share, and three of my first-pass claims did NOT survive measurement and were rewritten: 48 IS followed by 50 in 31265 of 31265 records, but 59 is followed by 62 only 87% of the time, 100 is followed by 115 only 33% (it is followed by another 100 52% of the time), and only 40% of opcode 23's coordinate pairs are in world range - the rest read as huge u32, i.e. negative, so some are deltas.
column6: TWO CAVEATS THAT LIMIT THE TABLE, both now printed in the doc. FIRST, `res:` IS TWO NAMESPACES WEARING ONE PREFIX: it addresses global.res text slots AND object/creature resources, so CreateNPC's res:19500 resolving to a sentence is meaningless. Median resolved length separates them - opcodes 53 (65 chars) and 71 (265) take displayed text, 63/73/93 (5-9 chars) take names. SECOND, TAGS 0x48/0x49/0x4a/0x6d/0x6e ARE PROBABLY NOT STRINGS: the table reads them as NUL-terminated and they come back as control characters, which is exactly what a small little-endian u16 looks like to a string read. The 100% parse rate cannot distinguish the two, so it is not evidence either way. Also corrected in analysis/tools/opcodes.py: 0x085ff0e8 is the OPERAND FETCH, not a handler - cases 59 and 66 were credited with it as their handler in row 723, when in fact they have no delegated call and implement the opcode INLINE in the dispatcher (as do 0, 41, 43, 111); the table now labels those inline@ADDR.

column4: EIGHT TAGS WERE MIS-TYPED AND THE PARSE-RATE METRIC WAS HIDING IT. The suspicion logged in row 725 - that 0x48/0x49/0x4a/0x6d/0x6e are u16 rather than strings - was WRONG in its diagnosis and right that something was broken. Their handler at 0x0826cb0e reads a u32 into the NUMERIC slot array at +0xa86c, advances four bytes, and THEN strcpys a NUL-terminated string into the string slots at +0xa46c: the tag carries BOTH. Tag 0x7a (handler 0x0826de28) has the same shape, found by sweeping every STR-typed tag for values that are not printable - it was the only other one over 20% (750/1010). Tags 0x5d and 0x5e share 0x0826cb0e and were fixed with the rest. The reason a CFG walk mis-typed them (analysis/tools/tagwidths.py, row 720) is structural and is now written into that tool: the walker reports the strcpy and stops, so a FIXED PREFIX BEFORE a variable-length payload is invisible to it. New class NUMSTR in analysis/tools/startcode.py.
column5: THE MEASUREMENT MATTERED MORE THAN THE FIX, because the old metric could not have caught this. Parse rate was 100% before and after - it is hollow, since every unlisted tag below 0xa2 hits the default handler and is a zero-width no-op, so a mis-sized tag's leftover bytes are read as no-op tags and absorbed in silence. Verified rather than assumed: all eight of the frequent unlisted tags (0x27, 0x08, 0x12, 0x0e, 0x10, 0x46, 0x7c, 0x2b) do point at the default handler 0x0826e0bc. The metric that does bite is RECORDS THAT CONSUME THEIR BODY EXACTLY (or stop on an END tag): 95.6% -> 99.774%, 1,347,105 of 1,350,157 records over all 16 files, excluding opcode 40 whose 80-byte ffffffff struct is not a tag stream. Intermediate: 98.6% after the 0x0826cb0e family, 98.7% after 0x7a.
column6: WHAT THE FIX REVEALS, and it confirms opcode 58 independently: the NUMSTR tags now read as a (value, variable name) PAIR - 48 <u32> 'DQ_NUM', 4a <u32> 'DQ_AktivRgn', 6d <u32> 'NPCGeklickt' - which is exactly the handler's own format string `if IsNotVarBit:%s=%d`. So opcode 58's predicate operands are name-value comparisons, and the same tags under opcode 66 (11,036 + 7,849 + 888 records) make it the same family. Residual misfits after the fix are 18,610 records and are NOT unexplained: 10,047 are opcode 40's fixed struct, 4,981 stop on an END tag with bytes to spare (engine-correct, the loop tests the cursor before reading a tag), and 990 each sit on tags 0x02/0x03/0x04 inside opcode 41. Also mirrored the engine's overrun tolerance in the NUMSTR path - a string with no NUL before the record end ends the record instead of failing it, which is what 0x0826af30 does.

column4: EVERY OPCODE THE SHIPPED SCRIPTS USE NOW HAS A READING - 113 OF 113, up from 50, with the last one (69) closed by its handler's own strings res/HeroQBit/HERO. The second pass was only possible after the NUMSTR fix (row 726) made the operands trustworthy; before it, five of the most frequent tags were handing back the low byte of a u32 as a string. Structures that fell out whole, none of which any earlier pass saw: (1) A SIX-RECORD DYNAMIC-QUEST TEMPLATE CHAIN - 118 -> 31 -> (1 or 122) -> 32 -> 123 -> 33 -> 118, each opcode appearing EXACTLY 16,830 times, carrying the template name (DQ1_BRINGE_NPC) and 1440, the minutes in a day. (2) A POOL RECTANGLE PAIR, 112/113: (POOL_RG1_ESKORTE1, x1,y1, x2,y2, x3,y3). (3) An ID-TO-DIALOGUE-NAME TABLE, opcode 106: (640, NPC_Dialog_Farmer) in runs of 1,270. (4) Opcode 99 displays TEXT WITH A COLOUR - (-1, -1, res:TEXT, 0xffffff, 1) - and its handler names cEventFX. (5) Opcodes 96/116 carry u32 LISTS behind a shared 0x69 header.
column5: THE READINGS ARE GRADED, and the grading is in the doc rather than in a footnote. Some are facts about shape measured over the whole corpus (op 97's (x,y,1) triples precede runs of 23 in 3,050 of 3,838 records; op 25 is preceded by 58 in 198 of 198; op 124 in 240 of 240; op 118 is followed by 31 in 16,830 of 16,830). Some are the engine's own words (op 69's HeroQBit, op 132's cCommand_armaStop, op 72's cEvent_creature). Some are readings of a shape and are worded as such - op 17 and 18 apply a magnitude to the hero, op 56 sets a named timer, op 121 names an autosave - and could be wrong about WHICH magnitude or WHICH timer. Nine opcodes are deliberately left blank: 10, 11, 12, 13, 19, 47, 61, 77 and 110 have live cases in the dispatcher and ZERO records in the shipped scripts, so the corpus cannot speak to them. Opcode 42 is their mirror image: 4,950 records, no case, ignored by the engine.
column6: WHAT THIS UNBLOCKS AND WHAT IT DOES NOT. The script format is now readable end to end - framing (row 711), tag table (720/726), opcode table (722/723) and a reading for every opcode in use (727) - so the quest system, the dialogue routing and the NPC appearance link of row 692 can be pursued from the data rather than from the disassembler. What is NOT established: the argument SLOT each tag lands in (the parser writes numeric tags to +0xa86c and strings to +0xa46c, and the handlers read fixed slot indices, so operand ORDER inside a record is still assumed rather than proven), and the three bulk opcodes 51/100/115 - 395,000 records between them, a third of the corpus - are described only as shapes. 51's handler is the largest in the set at 23 KB and names cItemBase, which is the obvious thread to pull next.

column4: THE THREE BULK OPCODES ARE THE RANDOM MONSTER SPAWN SYSTEM, AND THE PROOF IS AN ID JOIN. 51's repeated 0x19 field decomposes into (CREATURE ID, PERCENT, 0/1) and 115's repeated 0x02 field is a list of 1..20 ids; EVERY ONE OF THOSE IDS IS A creature.pak ID - 251 of 251 distinct for 51, 184 of 184 for 115, using the 474-record table of row 693. The percents sum to exactly 100 in 3,906 of 5,309 of opcode 51's records, median 100, which is what a weighted pick table looks like. 51's handler at 0x827afb6 is the largest in the whole opcode set at 23 KB and CALLS rand() 44 TIMES; it is also the only other code that touches the two globals the siblings write, so the trio is one subsystem: 115 DECLARES a spawn group (fills a 160-byte struct, appends it to the table at 0x8bb732c), 100 writes three percent-shaped u16 into the object at the CURRENT SECTOR (globals 0x879a080/0x879a084 shifted left 6) at offsets +0xd1/+0xd3/+0xd5, and 51 ROLLS. 51's header tag 0x36 is a record TYPE with exactly two values, 100 (2,854 records) and 310 (2,455), and the extra 0x34/0x33 fields appear only on type 310.
column5: THE PARSER'S INTERFACE IS NOW READ OFF TWO SMALL HANDLERS, WHICH CLOSES THE GAP ROW 727 LEFT OPEN. Opcode 100 (187 bytes) and 115 (371 bytes) are short enough to read whole, and both use 0x0826aed6 as a PER-OPERAND ITERATOR: each call fetches the next operand and RETURNS ITS TAG BYTE, which the handler switches on. Values are picked up from fixed slots - u32 at +0xa86c, the two halves of an eight-byte tag at +0xa88c and +0xa890, strings at +0xa46c. So operand identity is carried by the TAG, not by position, and a handler simply ignores tags it does not recognise. That is why the same opcode appears with different tag signatures in the data and still means one thing. 115's switch also shows its own limits: at most 20 operands of tag 0x02 (cap tested against 0x13) and at most 10 of tag 0x67.
column6: TWO READINGS DID NOT SURVIVE AND ARE RETRACTED BEFORE THEY REACHED THE DOC. 51's 0x34 pair is NOT a (level_min, level_max) range - the first component is <= the second in only 1,363 of 2,455 records, so whatever it is, it is not an ordered range. And the second components of 115's 0x87/0x88/0x89 pairs cluster hard on 0, 25, 50, 80, 90 and 100, which reads as percent, but their first components are only 87%, 100% and 35% inside the creature id set, so calling those pairs (creature, chance) would be overreach - they are recorded as (id, percent) pairs and no more. What remains unknown: which of the three u16 at +0xd1/+0xd3/+0xd5 is which, what the 0x35 triple's constant 4096 selects, and what distinguishes 51's type 100 from type 310.

column4: THE 100-vs-310 SPLIT IS NOT A RECORD TYPE - IT IS A CREATURE FIELD, AND THE TWO VALUES SEPARATE WILDLIFE FROM MONSTERS. Handler 51 has its OWN tag jump table at 0x086f4608 (bounded 0x74), and tag 0x36's branch at 0x0827b495 does one thing: stash the value, which at 0x0827fa62 is written to the freshly built creature at +0x255, with 0x12c = 300 substituted when the record omits it. Resolving the creature ids through creature.pak -> items.pak (row 693) settles what the two populations are: type 100's TWELVE ids are RABBIT.GRN, CROW.GRN x2, DEER.GRN x3, RED_DEER.GRN, BAT.GRN x2 and COW.GRN x3 - ambient fauna, nothing else; type 310's 239 ids are SKEL_WARRIOR, ORC_WARRIOR, ORC_CHAMP, THIEF_MAL/FEM, DARKELVENPC, gob_warrior, WOLF, ZOMBIE, feuerghul, med_spider, SOLDIER, PRIEST - the hostile population. CreateNPC (opcode 1) carries the same tag 0x36 with a single value, 350. Structural difference that follows: wildlife records hold 1..4 weighted entries and never the 0x34/0x33 fields, hostile records hold EXACTLY FOUR and always both.
column5: WHAT +0x255 DOES IS BOUNDED BY AN EXHAUSTIVE SCAN, AND THE UNITS REMAIN UNKNOWN - SAID PLAINLY RATHER THAN GUESSED. A byte scan of .text for the disp32 encoding of +0x255 finds SIX sites and no more: three writers (the spawn roll at 0x0827fa6a, a creator at 0x082510ed that takes it as argument [ebp+0x38], and one inside CreateNPC's range at 0x082870bb), one reader at 0x0825dbce, one serializer at 0x0819f970 that pushes +0x24d, +0x251, +0x255 and +0x259 through the same call, and a byte store at 0x08613b29. The only reader is a GATE: a per-object sweep dynamic_casts to cObject, filters on kind fields +0xfc/+0x150, requires the target slot (+0x104/+0x158) to be EMPTY, and then, if +0x255 > 0, builds a cEvent_creature with code 0x100 and dispatches it through cCreature's vtable slot 7 (0x0816d8ec). Nothing anywhere compares the MAGNITUDE, so 100 vs 310 vs 350 vs 300 is carried and serialised but never tested in the code that touches this field directly - which is why calling it a radius or a timer would be invention.
column6: TWO CORRECTIONS TO ROW 728, ONE IN EACH DIRECTION. First, REINSTATED: tag 0x35 IS an ordered range after all - its branch at 0x0827b44a compares the two halves and SWAPS them when the first is greater, so (min, max) is the engine's own reading, with the third component (constant 4096) kept separately. Row 728 only refuted the range reading for 0x34, and that refutation stands - first <= second in 1,363 of 2,455. Second, a detail worth keeping because it will look like corruption later: handler 51 REMAPS CREATURE ID 1249 TO 1162 (cmp 0x4e1 / mov 0x48a) at two points in the operand loop, and 1249 is exactly the highest id the data uses.

column4: THE LGP 2.28 BINARY NAMES NOTHING - BUT ITS IDA DATABASE ANSWERS THE QUESTION ANYWAY. Asked directly: does analysis/lgp-2010/sacred-1.0.02-final carry naming information sacred_orig lacks? NO, and the check is cheap and conclusive. Both are stripped (nm: no symbols); a full string diff gives the LGP build 103 unique printable strings and every one is store/currency text (Algerian Dinars, Cook Islands, country_list) or GL entry points (glNewList, glCallLists) - not one engine identifier. The two builds ARE different compilations (.text 0x67f598 vs 0x6849a4, the gate function is not byte-identical), and the field sits at the SAME offset in both. What the LGP tree does have is sacred-1.0.02-final.i64, a 101 MB IDA database that opens headless under /opt/ida-pro-9.3/idat with Hex-Rays available; it carries no user names (every function is sub_XXXXXX) but it does carry ITANIUM RTTI SYMBOLS - `typeinfo for'cCreature' and _ZTV9cCreature resolve in the decompiler output, which is what made the rest of this row possible. NOTE for future scripts: ida_struct was REMOVED in IDA 9 and importing it kills the script.
column5: +0x255 IS THE GROUP-ALERT ENABLE, AND ITS MAGNITUDE IS DEAD DATA. The single reader (sub_825CB68 in the LGP build, 0x0825da4e in sacred_orig) is not a per-object sweep as row 729 guessed - it takes a GROUP ID, looks the group's member list up in a map, iterates the members skipping the caller, and for each member that resolves to a cCreature, is in the right region and has no current target, tests `*(int *)(member + 597) > 0` and then sends it a cEvent_creature with code 0x100. Decompiling cCreature's virtual slot at +0x1c (0x0816c244, the damage/death/EXP handler) shows what 256 does: it sets the creature's state field +0xfc to 4 or 8 and writes the alerter's target into +0x104 - i.e. IT MAKES AN IDLE GROUP MEMBER JOIN THE FIGHT. The callers are the attacked/killed paths: `if (self->+0x249 && rand() % 3 > 1) alert(group, self)`. There is NO DISTANCE TEST anywhere in the path - membership is the whole filter - so 100 for wildlife, 310 for monsters, 350 for CreateNPC and the 300 default are all simply 'nonzero'. Whatever the value was meant to grade, this build only asks whether it is positive.
column6: A CORRECTION TO ROW 729'S 'EXHAUSTIVE SCAN', WHICH WAS NOT EXHAUSTIVE.
