THE BRIDGE BETWEEN THE BALANCE TABLE AND THE CODE THAT USES IT, WHICH IS WHAT THE COMBAT SYSTEM WAS WAITING ON. FUN_0812d25c in sacred_orig is the Linux balancing_parseKeys, and every key goes through one flat repeating shape -- push the key name, locate it in the loaded text, strrchr past the '=', strtod, then store to a fixed absolute address -- so the key's NAME and its RUNTIME ADDRESS fall out of the same instruction window. 348 keys extracted that way. Every one of them sits at global = 0x08b8d29c + its balance.bin file offset, 343 of 343 keys the two sources share, with no exception at all: balance.bin is loaded verbatim as a single struct and a tunable read is one absolute load. The two numbers came from different binaries by different means and neither knew about the other -- the file offsets from Sacred.exe via balance_keymap.py, the globals from the Linux parser's disassembly -- so the agreement is a genuine cross-source confirmation of both artifacts rather than a restatement of one. Xrefing the 348 globals then names the combat code by what it reads: FUN_081f686a reads 117 keys and is the creature stat builder, FUN_081f5ef6 the HP tables, FUN_08205cee the per-element resistance tables, and FUN_0820ef48 reads all four BalChar damage tunables and all four BalanceRes resistance tunables and is the derived-stat pass. Decompiled, it runs every attribute through one kernel, K(S) = (156 - BalStatOff)*S/156 + BalStatOff + 9, a line pinned at K(156) = 165 for any BalStatOff; damage accumulates as (K(attr) * weapon * 0.1 + flat) / BalChar<C>D into eight floats at +0xa6..+0xc2, and resistance as a bare quotient by BalanceResPh/Fe/Ma/Gi into four floats at +0x66..+0x72. The FD and GD channels ship divisors of 440 against PD and MD's 220 because they sum two weapon terms and count their flats twice, so they are a mean and not a halving. Claimed as read, not as confirmed: unlike to-hit this is single-source, the struct offsets are offsets and not attribute names, and the resolution step that consumes these numbers at the moment of a hit is still unread. 28 of the 348 keys are parsed and then read by nothing.

FUN_081f686a WAS SUPPOSED TO NAME THE CREATURE STRUCT'S FIELDS AND INSTEAD HANDED OVER SOMETHING BIGGER. It reads 117 balance keys, is called both from the derived-stat pass and from cUI_StatisticsChar::vf06 so it is what the character sheet displays, and it does almost nothing itself: 41 calls to FUN_081f64ac, once per stat family, passing that family's off/_s/_w triple and the level. FUN_081f64ac is four lines. Reduced, it is stat(L) = off + 2*(w - off)*(L - 1)/((L - 1) + s), a saturating hyperbola; the closed form and the decompiled expression agree to 1.6e-12 relative over 20000 random inputs, which is float noise. The three tunables are its geometry rather than free parameters: stat(1) = off, stat(1 + s) = w exactly, and the asymptote is 2w - off, never reached. Then the balance table settles what they mean -- every one of the 41 complete off/_s/_w families ships _s = 50.0 with NO exception while _w ranges 10 to 375, so _s is not a per-stat tunable at all. The entire game shares ONE curve shape pinned at level 51 and a stat is tuned by moving only its two endpoints. That also settles the German: _s is Stufe, the level, and _w is Wert, the value there, which is evidence rather than a guess about an abbreviation. Retail HP runs 4 at level 1 to 130 at level 51 toward 256; attack rating 9 to 150 toward 291. The SP suffix families were read the same way, from FUN_081f64e8, which applies the curve's output as record[+0x10] = base[+0x10]/(1 + pct/100) with a floor of 1.0 and a running minimum at +0x12, and formats it %+d%%: dividing a duration shortens it, so SP is a speed modifier. What this did NOT do is name the struct offsets, which was the reason for opening it; that stays open and the character-sheet strings printed beside each value are the next lead.

WENT AFTER THE STAT NAMES AND CAME BACK WITH HALF A BRIDGE, WHICH IS WORTH SAYING PLAINLY RATHER THAN DRESSING UP. FUN_081f64e8 is passed a resource id beside each stat family -- HM 0x24b8, FM 0x24c6, WM 0x24c7, EM 0x24c8, LM 0x24c9, MM 0x24ca, KO 0x24cb, BA 0x24d1, BL 0x24d3, ZK 0x24d4, HOM 0x24d7 -- so the engine plainly knows what to call each one, and resolving those would expand the abbreviations that name half the balance table. The labels themselves were found: global.res slots 1395 to 1410 are the character sheet in order, Hero Name, Damage, Resistance, Weapon, Spell, Combat Arts, Strength, Endurance, Dexterity, Physical Regeneration, Mental Regeneration, Charisma, Skills, Duration, Speed, New Skill, and the last of those has a balance key named after it, NewSkill, one of the five keys the Linux parser has that the Windows map does not. The id does NOT reach them. 0x24b8 is not a global.res slot -- slot 9400 is quest prose about an antidote at Faeries Crossing -- and it is not the id field either, which in that file runs to eight digits and is absent for every value tried. FUN_084c3806 resolves the id through FUN_084c2e06 against an in-memory resource TREE and then dynamic_casts the node to a string resource, so the namespace belongs to whatever builds that tree, and that is the thing to find next. Recorded as an open lead with both halves written down rather than guessed across: the German abbreviations remain unexpanded, and BalanceGeschick shows the table uses full German where it has room, so they are abbreviations of the same vocabulary and not a separate code.

CLOSED THE OPEN LEAD FROM ROW 857 IN THE SAME SESSION IT WAS OPENED, AND THE ANSWER WAS A HASH OF A NUMBER'S OWN SPELLING. The tree the character sheet reads is not built from .\SCRIPTS\RESOURCE.PAK at all: main sprintfs .\SCRIPTS\%s\global.res at 0x0809af0d and loads it into 0x0890ac48, and FUN_084c2d6c's RESOURCE.PAK literal is vestigial -- no such file ships in either the LGP Linux install or the extracted retail Gold Windows disc, both of which carry only scripts/us/global.res. The Armalion prerelease still has one, and it is a different and simpler format, RES 0x01 with 8192 twelve-byte slots direct-indexed by id and 376 populated, whose vocabulary is openly Das Schwarze Auge: COURAGE, INTUITION, DEFTNESS beside Rondrakamm and Thorwalder shield. Its ids stop at 8191 and retail's run past 9400, so it resolves nothing of retail's; it was a detour that paid in provenance rather than in answers. The real mechanism is FUN_080ae4d2: h = (h*0x71 + toupper(c)) % 0x3b9ac9f7, masked to 31 bits, applied to a resource's NAME -- and a caller holding a number prints it to decimal first, so resource 9400 is the entry whose name hashes like the four characters 9400. The mask is why FUN_084c2e06 branches on sign: a negative id is a key already hashed, a non-negative one is a number to be spelled and hashed, which is the two namespaces in one branch. Thirteen of thirteen ids resolve and every one is a stat name -- HM Heavenly Magic, FM Fire Magic, WM Water Magic, EM Earth Magic, LM Air Magic, MM Moon Magic, KO Vampirism, BA Ballistics, BL Bloodlust, ZK Weapon Technology, HOM Hellpower -- and a wrong hash returns nothing rather than thirteen coherent labels, which is the check. Two of them settle SP from the other direction: it was called a speed modifier because the code divides a duration by 1 + pct/100, and ids 1100 and 1107 are literally Attack Speed and Regeneration. Stated against the tool's own green: the MODULUS is unverified by the data, since h only exceeds it at five characters and nothing in the shipped file reaches that, so mutating it leaves the self-check passing while mutating the multiplier breaks it. Also fixed opsem.py, whose docstring claimed slot 49 Seraphim and 50 Gladiator as checks; the file gives Unicorn and Fire Troll there, and they are at slots 0 and 1 -- another line asserting something nothing had run.

CORRECTION TO ROW 858, WHICH READ A NAME OFF A SINGLE CALL SITE AND GOT ONE OF ELEVEN WRONG. Row 858 listed KO Vampirism among the resolved balance abbreviations. Counting the call sites rather than reading the first one shows bal_KOoff/_s/_w is passed FOUR different resource ids -- 9419 Vampirism, 9426 Trap Lore, 9430 Dwarven Lore and 1147 Special Move -- so it is not the abbreviation of a skill at all but a SHARED curve, the triple reused by skills that were never given one of their own. The other ten are each passed exactly one id and stand: HM Heavenly Magic, FM Fire Magic, WM Water Magic, EM Earth Magic, LM Air Magic, MM Moon Magic, BA Ballistics, BL Bloodlust, ZK Weapon Technology, HOM Hellpower. The rule that follows is now written into the format doc: count the call sites before naming anything. Going after the remaining weapon-skill families through cUI_StatisticsChar::vf06 did not find their ids -- its only literal in that range is 0x24b7 -- but resolving every literal it does carry gave the two contiguous blocks behind them. 9400 to 9432 is the WHOLE skill list in order, from Heavenly Magic through Weapon Lore, Sword Lore, Axe Lore, Dual Wielding, Ranged Combat, Agility, Parrying to Forge Lore, with each skill's in-game description at id+50; and 1070 to 1199 is the character sheet and item tooltips. That second block pays a debt from row 855: resources 1078 to 1081 are Physical, Fire, Magic, Poison in order, which independently confirms that BalCharPD/FD/MD/GD and BalanceResPh/Fe/Ma/Gi are physisch/Feuer/Magie/Gift, previously argued from the German key suffixes alone. So the skill names the unexpanded families must map onto are now all known, which makes the remainder a matching problem rather than a search -- and matching by plausibility is precisely what the KO case proves unsafe, so it stays open until an id or a second source decides it.

Every balance-table family prefix is resolved, and not by matching German abbreviations to skill names -- that route would have got four of thirteen wrong. The binary states the identity itself: a creature holds eight skill slots at +0x24, one byte each holding a SKILL TYPE; cUI_StatisticsChar::vf06 turns that byte into the skill's name with a literal `add $0x24b7, %eax` at 0x0854e99b, so resource id = skill type + 9399, and it passes the same byte unchanged to FUN_081f686a as its switch selector. FUN_081f686a's jump table at 0x086ed568 is therefore indexed by skill type, and case i reads exactly the balance globals of skill 9399+i. The table is a PERMUTATION, not the identity -- index 1 jumps to the tenth case body by address -- so reading the cases in address order gives a complete, self-consistent, entirely wrong answer, which is what the first attempt produced. The check is a coincidence that cannot survive being wrong: thirteen case bodies push their own skill's resource id as a literal and every one equals 9399 + that case's index, 13/13 with zero mismatches; shifting the base by one or the table pointer by one entry breaks 12-13 of them. The traps were real -- FK is Faustkampf (Unarmed Combat 9423) not Fernkampf, BK is Beidhaendiger Kampf (Dual Wielding 9405) not Bogenkampf, W is Wendigkeit (Agility 9407) not Waffe, R is Ruestung (Armor 9410) not Resistenz; three of those four would have put a weapon family on the wrong weapon. KO is Konzentration, shared by Concentration 9424, Vampirism 9419 and Trap Lore 9426; row 859's claim that it also serves Dwarven Lore was the address-order artefact and is withdrawn. Skill type 30 (9429 Two-handed Weapons) alone jumps to the default and has no balance family. tools/binary/skillmap.py regenerates research/formats/generated/skill-families.tsv and fails on a mismatch; only the resource ids are read from the binary, the German expansions are inference and are marked as such.

The 2001-12-11 Armalion prerelease is a DEBUG build, so its assert strings survived and they carry Sacred's original source tree: the C:\Projects\Armalion\armaSource\... path of every file that fired an assert, a cClass::method() naming the function, and the invariant text. The method-to-file association is not inferred -- the linker emits a translation unit's string literals together, so walking the string table in FILE OFFSET order and attributing each cClass::method() to the nearest preceding path recovers it, an ordering property of the object file. tools/binary/armasource.py does this and reports 76 source files, 259 methods and 80 classes; it exits non-zero if the ordering trick binds fewer than 40 files or 60 methods. The cross-build check is retail's own RTTI: 25 of the 80 classes are still there -- cCreature, cWeapon3D, cArmor3D, cArrow3D, cObject3D, cObjectFX, cSector, cWorld, cWorldView, cEngine, cResourceMgr, cParticleSystem, cFsFont, cFile_cached, cFile_memoryMapped, cEvent_idle, six cUI_* and two cCommand_* -- spanning every module, so the tree is retail's tree at module and class granularity. Method names are Armalion's alone and must not be transplanted onto retail addresses. The tree: kernel/, engine/{calendar,granny,kampaign,scenery,weather,object/{base,creature,items,inventory,sfx}}, scripts/, library/{dx7,file,formats,generic,math,resource,timer}, ui/{commands,controls,windows}, particle/, sound/, movie/. engine/object/creature/ is 53 of the 259 methods and names the whole simulation state machine -- state_Main_Idle, state_Attacking, state_Fighting, state_Dying, state_proc_Moving_{init,default,target_position}, state_proc_AngleMoving_*, state_proc_Jumping, state_proc_Magic_{Interpret,Send}, collision_detect, subtractLife, getStaminaRecovery, levelCreate/Enter/Exit. Combat is therefore a state machine split across creature_fighting.cpp and creature_collision.cpp, not one arithmetic function, which is why the still-open resolution step has not been found by looking for one. Written up in research/builds/armalion-source-tree.md.

The same assert strings give the script VM's own vocabulary and its invariants, from armaSource/scripts/: cScriptCompiler (parseStatement, parseArmaStatement, parseResource, loadScriptedSequenceR, save, saveResources, load), cScriptVM::load, cScriptInterpreter (load, interpreter, findScriptFunction), cScriptLoader::getResource. `fp->code[ip]<256` states that an opcode is a BYTE indexing a byte array with a frame pointer and an instruction pointer; `serialID<exportFunctions.size()` that the script API dispatches by INDEX INTO A VECTOR rather than a fixed switch; `chunk.type==CHUNK_TYPE_ACS` and `hdr.ver==2` name the compiled-script container and its version. cScriptCompiler shipping inside the game explains why cScriptLoader::getResource reaches RESOURCE.PAK, the Armalion-era container retail dropped. A NEGATIVE result worth recording: the Armalion script API id space does NOT join to retail's 141 opcodes. The binary's name table holds about 85 API names and armalion-script-api.tsv records 62 with handler addresses, but Armalion 67 is printTextResource while retail 67 is a variable setter, Armalion 60 is soundSFX while retail 60 takes res: text, Armalion 26 is item_createX while retail 26 is a label/entry point -- every sampled pair disagrees. The Armalion API is a vocabulary for naming retail opcodes, not a key to them, and a join needs a shared invariant rather than a shared index. Also ruled out this iteration: harvesting NAMED callees from the 141 retail opcode handlers (tools/binary/ghidra/Callees.java, written for it) returns zero at depth 3 with the caller cap raised to 400, because the handlers reach C++ objects only through vtable dispatch, which leaves no static call reference. The instrument works; the lever is absent for this table.

Row 862 reported that harvesting named callees from the 141 retail script opcode handlers returns nothing. That was measured against 0x086f3fbc, which is the 162-entry TAG table, not the opcode table; script-bytecode.md states the opcode jump table is 0x086f4298 and I did not read it before running. Against the correct table 26 of 141 handlers do reach named functions, so the instrument is not blind. The result is still weak for naming: nearly every one of the 26 resolves to the same shared pair (cEventNetwork, cCommand_armaStop), which is a utility rather than a per-opcode signature, so the conclusion that vtable dispatch hides the subsystem stands even though the number that supported it was wrong. Recording the mistake because a wrong address produced a plausible negative that would have closed off a lever.

The 2001-09-20 Armalion prerelease ships Scripts/SCRIPT.PAK together with the script0N.txt files it was compiled from -- the only place in any Sacred build where a script exists as both text and bytecode. The language is C-like with INLINE VM ASSEMBLY: `asm rsp` before most calls, `asm movi 1, 4`, `asm mov 1, 0`, so the VM has numbered registers and a stack pointer the author resets by hand, and -1 is a sentinel meaning the object just created. SCRIPT.PAK is magic ACS version 2, matching the debug build's chunk.type==CHUNK_TYPE_ACS and hdr.ver==2 asserts, and it is the ORDINARY .pak blob layout -- tools/formats/pak.py reads it unmodified, 256-byte header then a {flags,offset,size} index at 0x100, 59 entries, one per script function, entry 0 being the interpreter's own invalid_function stub. Each payload is char[32] name, a u32 that is NOT the code length (spTrigger5 stores 44 in a 212-byte payload), then a flat u32 code stream in which 0xff introduces a call and the next word is the script API id. spTrigger5 decodes line-for-line against its source: 0x3b trigger_chkState, 0x3d playSfx, 0x39 trigger_setState, 0x3a trigger_resetState, in the source's exact order with the source's exact arguments. Corpus-wide, tools/formats/armascript.py requires the source's call list to be a SUFFIX of the bytecode's and gets 26 of the 35 string-free functions; mutating the 0xff marker drops it to zero, which pins the marker and the id space and therefore CONFIRMS armalion-script-api.tsv's ids independently of how they were assigned. Three limits are recorded rather than hidden: every function opens with one call no source line asks for (usually 77, sometimes 59, 63, 9, 12, 30, 72) so the check is a suffix rather than an equality; a suffix comparison cannot pin the header layout, and a 28-byte name field scores the same as 32; and the 9 failures are all npcDialog* which also exist as localized copies in Scripts/us and Scripts/de. Functions with an inline string are excluded because the string length need not be a multiple of four and the u32 walk goes out of phase after it. This still does not name a retail opcode: retail re-encoded to u16 opcode plus u16 length with tagged arguments and renumbered -- its trigger opcodes are 4, 5 and 39 where Armalion's are 56-59. research/formats/armalion-acs.md.

DEBUG.LOG beside the 2001-12-11 build is one complete traced run, and three things in it are evidence. It dumps sizeof for 22 engine classes before doing anything else -- cWorld 132708, cCreature 1904, cGrnMdlChunk 1200, cSectorChunk 512, cSector 384, cObjectShared/cGrnMtnChunk/cSectorEnvironment 256, granny_transform_state 220, cObject3D 140, cSoundChunk/cCreatureInfo 128, sObjectNonstatic3D 86, cObject/sObjectStatic/cPatchSharedIso 64, sObjectNonstatic 53, cEvent_creature 52, cPatchIso 32, cTrigger 16, cTimerListener 12, cMutex 4 -- which is a hard constraint on any struct claim. It logs every container with version and entry count, so retail can be compared three years later: TEXTURES v3, MODELS v3, PATCHES v3, SOUNDS2 v1, STATIC v1, FLOOR v1, TRIGGERS v1 are unchanged in retail (TEX/MDL/ISO/SND v3,v3,v3,v1 and OBJ v1, TRG v1), while ITEMS went v2 to v5 and WORLD/SECTORS v4 to v5. A caution that came out of checking it: VERSION EQUALITY DOES NOT IMPLY RECORD EQUALITY. static.pak is OBJ v1 in both builds yet its stride is 76 bytes against Armalion's sObjectStatic of 64, so the version byte covers the container and not the payload. The one clean coincidence that does hold is cTrigger at 16 bytes against triggers.pak's 16-byte stride at TRG v1 in both. The engine's own asserts also name the pak header fields -- hdr.tag[0..2], hdr.ver, hdr.numEntries -- which is a fourth independent confirmation of a format already solved in pak-containers.md and the first source that gives the field NAMES rather than the offsets. Reader: tools/binary/armalog.py.

Correction to row 865. I claimed version equality does not imply record equality, on the grounds that static.pak is OBJ v1 in both builds while its stride is 76 and Armalion's sObjectStatic is 64. That compared an ON-DISK STRIDE to an IN-MEMORY sizeof, which are different objects -- the loader builds one from the other. Measuring the prerelease's own World/ directory instead settles it the other way: Floor.PAK is OBJ v1 with a 28-byte stride in Armalion 2001-09 and in retail; Static.PAK is OBJ v1 with a 76-byte stride in both; Triggers.PAK is TRG v1 with a 16-byte stride in both; and the one container whose version DID move, Sectors.key from WLK v4 to v5, is also the one whose stride moved, 512 to 768. Same version, same stride, three times; bumped version, changed stride, once. The version byte does track the record layout. Note the scale: the world grew from 1201 sectors to 6050 and from 2.59M to 6.71M floor records without the record layout moving, so prerelease world data is readable with retail's readers and is a second corpus for them. research/formats/pak-containers.md now carries the table and the warning not to compare a stride to a sizeof.

Supersedes rows 865 and 866, both of which were wrong from the same arithmetic slip. I divided static.pak's file size by its entry count and got 76, but these are BLOB containers: 76 is 12 bytes of index entry plus a 64-byte payload. 76 matches no class, which I first read as 'a frozen version can still change its record' (865) and then, after seeing the prerelease has the same 76, as 'an on-disk stride is not comparable to a sizeof' (866). Both explanations were invented to cover the same miscount. Measured correctly with pak.py, which reads the prerelease files unmodified: Floor.PAK payload is 16 bytes with flags 0x87 in Armalion 2001-09 and in retail; Static.PAK payload is 64 bytes with flags 0x86 in both; Triggers.PAK is 16 in both; and Sectors.key, the only container whose version moved (WLK v4 to v5), is the only one whose record moved, 512 to 768. Static.PAK's 64-byte payload IS sObjectStatic, which the debug build prints as 64 -- the engine's own name for the on-disk static-object record, and the first time a world record has a name rather than an offset. The practical consequence: OBJ v1 is frozen across three years and 2.6x growth in record count, so the prerelease World/ directory is a SECOND CORPUS for the retail world readers, which is worth more than either wrong caution was. The lesson to keep is to count a blob container's index separately from its payload before comparing anything to a struct size.

Six retail script opcodes named, from 102 unverified down to 96, using a second and explicitly weaker tier of evidence than the 34 already named. Those 34 come from strings inside the handler; these come from strings reachable within two calls of it (Impl2.java on the opcode table with the caller cap at 8), which is weaker because a shared callee's message can be read as the caller's purpose. Two filters make the tier usable: the string must be reachable from EXACTLY ONE opcode block, and opsem.py's independent behavioural profile must agree. 17 = award experience to the hero (addExperience(%d) level%d tmp%d, and its operands are Hero plus 10000/5000/1000); 20 = quest-in-sector trigger by number (QIS_Trigger%d, one u32 quest id); 25 = CreateDynamicQuest (Pool, Header, Typ, ToDo, and it follows opcode 58/IF in 198 of 198 records); 120 = play movie (a 25-byte trampoline reaching the 14-entry .\MOVIE\*.MPG table, one small index); 121 = AUTOSAVE (operand is a checkpoint name at tag 0x1d, e.g. uw_autosave_01); 126 = NPC refusal speech (SOUND_FX_REJECT*). They are marked [reached] in the generated table so they stay distinguishable. The second filter earned its place immediately: opcode 79 uniquely reaches `cCreature::equipment_reset() EquipmentRef unknown?!` and reads as 'reset equipment', but its operands are (res:TEXT, small id) carrying quest prose, so the string is a deeper callee's and 79 is left unnamed. Also corrected: the naming oracle doc records 108 cClass::method strings in the Armalion build, but relaxing the pattern from ^c[A-Z] to any identifier::identifier( finds 275, because the engine also asserts from dxDriver7, sState, BcCreatureQueue and granny_transform_state and from destructors; armasource.py binds 259 of them to a source file. The oracle has 2.5x the reach it was credited with.

Ten Armalion script API ids are now pinned INDIVIDUALLY rather than only as a sequence: 15 view_setLocked, 35 creature_setFacing, 39 creature_setDialog, 47 creature_setAlliance, 51 creature_morph, 52 creature_setLevel, 57 trigger_setState, 58 trigger_resetState, 59 trigger_chkState, 67 printTextResource. Each is an id that landed exactly where the source names that same function, inside a function whose entire call list aligned, so armalion-script-api.tsv's names for those ten are verified against the compiler's own output rather than against whoever assigned them in an IDA session. armascript.py now reports this and FAILS if any id maps to two names; none does. Kept separate as a weaker class: id 63, which the table has no entry for at all, lands where the source writes trigger_chkState. That is a PREDICTION from a gap, not a confirmation, and merging it into the confirmed set would be the same error as reading a shared curve off one call site. 35 distinct ids appear in the compiled corpus with a maximum of 77.

The floor.pak +0x04 17/15 split is right for retail, but the argument recorded for it in world-sectors.md and asserted in floor_check.gd is VACUOUS. The claim was that the two fields must partition the word with no shared bit so only 17/15 reconstructs the original u32. That is an identity: (v & ((1<<s)-1)) | ((v>>s)<<s) == v for every s, measured 6872 of 6872 at splits 13, 16, 17, 18 and 20 alike. The companion over16 test is circular the same way -- it counts values of the 17-BIT READ exceeding 65535, which only says bit 16 is sometimes set and is equally consistent with bit 16 belonging to the mask. Only the under18 test discriminated anything, and only against 18 bits. The real discriminator is which read FILLS THE TILE TABLE. The 17-bit read runs 0..90131, exactly tiles.pak's last index of 90132 entries, using its space to the final entry and stopping. The 16-bit read tops out at 65420, just under its own 65536 ceiling, and would leave tiles 65421-90131 -- 27 percent of the table -- unreachable as an art tile. floor_check.gd now asserts the fill ratio (a ratio not an equality, because at STRIDE=977 the sampled max is 90085 of 90131); mutating LOW17 to 0xffff makes that assertion fire first, at 64436 of 90131, while the other three still pass. The split is BUILD-DEPENDENT, which is how it was caught. The Armalion prerelease's tiles.pak holds 13402 tiles; there the 17-bit read reaches 67071 and is impossible while the 16-bit read tops out at 13400. Armalion packs 16/16, retail packs 17/15 -- the art field took a bit from the mask when the tile table outgrew 16 bits. Both files are OBJ v1 with the same 16-byte record, so the version byte covers a record's size and field offsets and NOT the bit packing inside a field, which narrows row 867's reading.

Row 867 said the prerelease World/ directory is a second corpus for the retail world readers. True for Floor.PAK and Static.PAK, which are OBJ v1 in both builds, and for Triggers.PAK at TRG v1. NOT true for the sector data, and the version byte says so in advance: Sectors.key is WLK v4 with a 512-byte directory record against retail's 768, and the cell layout differs -- the tile id sits at +0x04 with a flag word at +0x00, where retail has the tile id at +0x00. Retail's 32-byte WldxEntry decode therefore cannot be tested against it, and the world-sectors.md claim that all 32 bytes are accounted for stands on retail alone. Plumbing recorded so the v4 corpus is reachable if wanted: 1201 sectors, the block offset is the u32 at directory-record +92 (found by scanning every u32 position for monotonicity and in-range-ness across all records), blocks are 131360 bytes = a 288-byte prefix then 4096 32-byte cells, and the cells are stored UNCOMPRESSED -- retail's zlib came later, which is why 1201 sectors occupy 158 MB. A hazard for anyone using this corpus: the prerelease is a debug build and leaked uninitialised heap into shipped data. 4211 of its 4.92M cells contain 0xcdcdcdcd, MSVC's debug fill. An unfiltered pass over them reported a maximum tile id of 543162368, which is what prompted looking at the raw bytes and finding the layout difference.

static.pak's nextStaticId at +0x1f was taken from Resacred's rs_file.h and never tested; it is now pinned by structure, and the same 64-byte record decodes identically in the Armalion prerelease (OBJ v1 in both builds). Reading the value as a valid index proves nothing -- SIX offsets in the record are a valid index for every one of 1.04M records (0x00, 0x04, 0x07, 0x08, 0x12, 0x13, 0x1f). Two structural properties settle it. First, a chain is a LINKED LIST, so links minus distinct targets must be zero: +0x1f scores 0 over 174422 links in retail and 0 over 51224 in the prerelease, while the best rival carrying comparable traffic has 30973 excess over 31031 links. Second, A LINKED RECORD IS NEVER A HEAD -- none of those 174422 targets is among the 31752 chain heads the WORLD CELLS name at WldxEntry +0x04, two separate files partitioning the same records between them. tools/parity/static_next_check.py measures both; moving NEXT to 0x1e or 0x20 produces 3 failures, and moving the cell head field to +0x08 or +0x00 also fails. A metric error caught on the way, worth keeping because it looked convincing: counting 'targets hit more than once' scores a field that points 418026 times at a SINGLE record as one collision. +0x1a does exactly that and read as the closest rival at 1 collision until the measure was changed to excess. An empty result must also fail rather than skip -- reading the cell head from +0x08, which is zero in every cell of the world, yields no heads and would have passed the disjointness arm by having no work to do. Independent of the offset: the record's other fields agree across three years -- self-index 393765/393765 and 1038014/1038014, type ids in 0..12513 and 0..32095, and eight of the +0x08 flag values shared between builds.

The Armalion v4 cell record is retail's v5 record shifted by exactly one word, with an extra flag word in front, and three of the fields are pinned independently rather than by alignment. Each is pinned the same way: the field must fill its own table and carry no duplicate link. v4 +0x04 is the tile id, max 13395 against Tiles.pak's 13402. v4 +0x08 is the static chain head: 116832 links, ZERO excess (links minus distinct targets), max 393764 = Static.PAK count minus one exactly. v4 +0x10 is the floor chain head: 1969048 links, ZERO excess, max 2591135 = Floor.PAK count minus one exactly. Two fields landing on their table's final record with not one record linked twice between them is what makes the shift safe, and it makes the remaining row an inference worth stating: v4 +0x0c corresponds to retail's +0x08. That sharpens a documented negative. world-sectors.md said of retail +0x08 that it 'carries no meaning to recover, empty in every cell of the world'. It is empty in retail, but the prerelease populates the same slot in 73 cells with distinct values running to 170, so it is a LAYER THE SHIPPED GAME DROPPED rather than a field with nothing behind it. What it indexes is not identified: the prerelease's World/NonStatic.PAK, a file retail does not ship at all, holds only 106 records of 384 bytes, so the 73 values do not index it as an array. Those records also carry 0xAB and 0xCD MSVC heap fill, so the prerelease serialized raw memory images and their sizes should not be read as on-disk layouts.

parse_trg.py reads the Armalion prerelease's Triggers.PAK unmodified, and the 16-byte record is Armalion's own cTrigger, which the debug build prints as 16 bytes -- a name for a record that had none. Structure across both builds: word0 is the record's OWN INDEX in every populated record (209 of 209 in the prerelease, 1246 of 1246 in retail, the same self-index invariant static.pak and floor.pak carry); word3 is always zero; word1 is a varying high half over a low-half flag that retail fixed at 0x0010 while the prerelease also uses 0x0004 and 0x0040; word2 is bit 16 over a small code with 16 distinct values in retail and 6 in the prerelease. The file is sparse -- 209 of 1218 slots and 1246 of 2268. The small code is deliberately NOT named. trigger_setType exists in the script API and the reading is tempting, but the prerelease's single trigger_setType (1,1) call refers to trigger 1, whose record is ALL ZEROS. That is informative in the other direction: triggers.pak holds only authored triggers and scripts create the rest at runtime, so the file is not the complete trigger set. Naming word2 from the API would have been the KO error again -- an attractive name attached to a call site that does not support it.

tiles.pak is fully read, from 2 known fields of 16 words to all of them, and confirmed against the Armalion prerelease's own tiles.pak which is ISO v3 in both builds (13402 tiles against retail's 90132). The record is: char[32] SOURCE TGA FILENAME NUL-padded, 'iso00.tga' through 'iso999.tga'; u32 texture.pak id at +0x20; u32 orientation at +0x24; zero at +0x28; the constant 65536 at +0x2c; and four zero words to the end. The filename was not documented at all before and is a naming oracle for terrain art -- every tile now says which .tga it was cut from. Tiles.source_name() returns it. THE TABLE IS A PRODUCT. Eighteen consecutive tile ids share one filename and one texture id: 5008 of 5008 groups in retail, 745 of 745 in the prerelease. So tile_id = group*18 + orientation, and name, group and texture id are in bijection -- 5008 names, 5008 groups, and no name on two texture ids. The only content in 5.8 MB is 5008 texture ids and 5008 names. That settles a nuisance in floor_check.gd. orientation(i) == i %% 18 is an IDENTITY BY CONSTRUCTION rather than a property of the data, so the gate's note that it 'cannot fail' was right for a reason it did not know, and every test resting on it is permanently vacuous. The comment now says so and points at the fill-the-table ratio as the assertion that actually carries the 17-bit boundary. Both known fields are also uniquely determined: +0x20 is the only word in the record that is ever a plausible texture index and +0x24 the only one ever inside 0..17, in both builds. Incidental: the prerelease's TEXTURE.PAK is TEX v2 with 17146 entries against retail's v3 with 25535, so the texture container bumped version between the two builds while the tile container did not.

pak-containers.md listed mixed.pak's heterogeneous payloads as OPEN. They were never open: engine/formats/mixed.gd had already read them completely, down to the 16+64*n size formula, the u16 destination rect and the UV floats, and the open item was simply never struck. Recording the drift rather than quietly deleting the line, because a research doc lagging the engine is the failure mode the three-repo split exists to prevent. The payloads are also not heterogeneous -- every slot is populated and every one carries flags 0x63. What this iteration adds is a second corpus. The Armalion prerelease's MIXED.PAK is MIX v0 as well (8192 slots against retail's 32096) and every reading holds in both: size == 16 + count*64 for 32095/32095 and 8191/8191 records; every element name ends in .444, 209956/209956 and 24297/24297; the element's +0x20 texture id stays under texture.pak's count with a maximum of 25534 of 25535, filling the table to its last entry; all four element floats lie inside [0,1], 839824/839824 and 97188/97188; and the port's destination-rect field ORDER is confirmed by x1>=x0 and y1>=y0 holding 209956/209956 and 24297/24297, which a wrong order would fail constantly. The .444 extension is Sacred's own image format -- armaSource/library/formats/444.cpp in the recovered source tree, with the debug build asserting hdr.tag[0] through hdr.tag[2] all equal to '4'. Retail ships no .444 files, so the names are provenance for art that became texture.pak TGAs. Also noted: retail still ships the uninitialised 0xcccccccc word at record +0x0c that the debug-build tooling left there.

global-res.md's only open item is closed. It asked why the by-name namespace holds only numeric names and whether the Armalion build's non-numeric resources were carried over. There were none: the prerelease ships Scripts/us/resource.txt, the SOURCE that RESOURCE.PAK was compiled from, and every declaration in it is `#pragma resource <int>, 1, "text"` -- 376 of 376 with a numeric id, zero with a word, ids running 1..8191 with a type field of 1 throughout, which is exactly the 376 populated slots of 8192 the format doc already recorded. So resources were addressed by number from the start. Armalion indexed RESOURCE.PAK by that number directly; retail replaced the direct index with a hash of the number's decimal string. Nothing was ever word-named, so there is no missing vocabulary to hunt for and the question was malformed rather than hard. Colour worth keeping: the file is the Armalion hero list and it is Das Schwarze Auge throughout -- AMAZON, MAGE, ELF, WITCH, BORON PRIESTESS, PHEX PRIESTESS, WARRIOR, DRUID, BORON PRIEST, PHEX THIEF, with Boron and Phex being DSA deities. Retail's Seraphim and Gladiator replaced all of them, which is the same licence-loss story the RESOURCE.PAK vocabulary already told.

I built tools/binary/assert_names.py on the belief that the naming oracle had only ever been pointed at the Armalion build and that retail's own assert strings were unmeasured, and I wrote that into naming-oracle.md before checking. It is false. research/engine/decompilation-coverage.md already records the retail scan in detail -- 248 cClass::method strings in .rodata, 207 referenced exactly once, 131 distinct names across 53 classes, with the 11 percent frame-disagreement rate measured. My first run was also WORSE than the existing work, because I restricted it to the 50 strings shared with Armalion and got 33 functions where retail's own strings give 131. The doc edit has been rewritten. The lesson is the cheap one I skipped: read the document that owns the question before building the tool that answers it. The open-questions row pointed straight at decompilation-coverage.md and I did not open it until after the tool ran.

Two real additions survive that correction. FIRST, the scan pattern. The existing oracle looks for c[A-Z]\w+::\w+, which is Sacred's convention and not its rule; scanning for any identifier::identifier finds nine more real names -- TypeManager::loadItemTypes, ::loadWeaponInfo, ::loadSoundProfiles, ::getRandomItem, ::saveSpawnInfo, ItemTypeMgr::makeWeaponInfo, ::getDoorDirection, ItemDataMgr::saveHero, dxDriver::createSurface -- plus every destructor, which \w cannot match through a leading ~. The item and weapon TYPE LOADERS are in that list. Widening has a cost and the tool pays it explicitly. A run-on guard drops classes that are another class plus a stray leading character (BcEngine, AcInventoryEntry, BcStatsManager, CcWorldView2, GcEngine) while keeping cItemDataMgr, whose tail ItemDataMgr is a real class. Ambiguity and aliasing are separated: one name at several addresses is the known 11 percent inlining effect and is dropped (3 names), one address under several names is the engine spelling itself twice (cUI_Character::execAction vs ::executeAction, cUI_BlackSmith vs cUI_Blacksmith) and is merged (2), and one address under two different CLASSES is dropped with a note (2). Result 130 distinct functions, 130 of 130 landing on exact function entries per Ghidra, whose boundaries come from its own analysis rather than this tool's .eh_frame walk. Imported, so decompiled output now reads with them. SECOND, a second source that compares ADDRESSES rather than names. The existing second arm is the Armalion symbol catalogue, which agrees or not about a name. Comparing instead against the RTTI vtable walk at the same address pairs two oracles sharing no input -- one reads typeinfo, one reads strings -- and gives 18 agreements with 0 disagreements. Getting there needed two corrections that would otherwise have been false alarms: a vtable slot may hold an INHERITED method, so cWeapon3D's slot legitimately holds cItemBase::advanceTime and vmeth.py now emits each class's full ancestry; and the engine spells one class two ways, cUI_Blacksmith in its RTTI against cUI_BlackSmith in its own string, so the comparison ignores case. Swapping class and method in the tool turns both agreements into failures.

The port had no global.res reader at all -- every one of the 1521 NPC display-name references startcode.gd decodes sat unresolved as a raw `res:N` string. engine/formats/resources.gd now implements both namespaces (slot for the bytecode's res:N, and the engine's own name hash for numeric resource ids), with engine/checks/resources_check.gd as its gate; 25 of 25 port gates pass. Implementing it corrected the format doc. The entry count is first_offset/16, NOT (first_offset-4)/16 as global-res.md said: entry 0's offset is four bytes SHORT of the index end and (first-4) leaves a remainder of 12, so the index runs to first+4 and the count is 369968/16 = 23123 exactly. The last entry is real -- hash 2147266699, size 26, 'Gero Wachholz' -- and its size field lands on the four bytes in front of entry 0's text, which is the same 'u32 at offset that is not the size' every payload carries. globalres.py's range(4, first, 16) got 23123 by overshooting rather than by the rule, and the port's first draft used i+16 <= first and silently lost the entry; both now state first+4 explicitly. Two decoders agreeing for different reasons is the failure this catches. Also found: NOT EVERY res: OPERAND IS NUMERIC. 144 of the 1521 references are res:D1Dorf_01 through res:D1Dorf_18, 18 word names repeated across all eight character classes, and they resolve under NEITHER namespace -- not by slot because the tail is not an integer, and not by hash because the substring 'Dorf' appears in none of global.res's 23123 entries. Retail cannot resolve them either: its tag handler strtols the tail, which gives 0, and resource 0 does not exist. They are dangling references in the shipped data, and they do not contradict row 877 -- global.res still contains only numeric NAMES, it is the REFERENCES that are not all numeric.

engine/formats/startcode.gd has said since it was written that its tag 0x01 is 'the NPC's display name'. Now that global.res is readable the claim could finally be tested, and it does not survive. The reasoning was that a display name is short where global.res is mostly quest prose, so the documented slot should read much shorter than a neighbouring one. Reading the same 1377 references at slot offsets -2, -1, 0, +1, +2 gives a short-text fraction of .432, .468, .444, .497, .513 -- offset 0 is not the best and sits inside the spread, so the instrument cannot distinguish the documented reading from one two slots away and is evidence of nothing. What the resolved text actually holds is a MIX: 'Wolff von Lindenau' and 'Cerebropod' beside dialogue lines ('Hello, stranger... You're not from these parts, are you?') and item names ('Mundane Armor of Battle'), and the 1377 references share only 161 distinct texts. The failed control is kept IN the gate with its numbers, and startcode.gd's docstring now says the claim is unverified, so the next person does not repeat the attempt or inherit the assertion as fact. The gate asserts what it can: the reader itself (slot 0/1/18101, by_id 9400/1100/1078/1081, the negative-id round trip, that the two namespaces DISAGREE at 9400, the 33-skill block with descriptions at id+50, 23123 entries) and the reference partition 1377 numeric / 144 dangling.

Asked whether the data now exists to render an NPC properly, the answer is that five of the six legs are already standing and the sixth is TEXTURES, whose data is present but whose binding is unread. Standing: mesh geometry decodes with real UVs (the models.gd docstring saying 'uvs is currently always empty' is STALE and predates the RenderPass work -- measured one UV per vertex on GLADIATOR 1195, WOLF 571, BEAR 573, WALDELFE_DARK 1656, NOBLE_FEM 1449, SOLDIER 1656, and the comment is now corrected); skeleton and skinning are real and row 799 hand-verified the skinning product exact at ratio 1.00 on every axis; clips retarget and PLAY IN THE LIVE STREAMED WORLD via main.gd _build_npcs; positioning is retail-exact, with startcode_check asserting 18586 of 18586 NPC placements resolved; and bin/rust.bin gives equipment-to-mesh at 506 of 506 pairs. MISSING: no creature mesh has a texture. model_view.gd assigns a flat albedo_color of (0.78,0.74,0.68) and no albedo_texture is set anywhere in the project. But the DATA is there. A creature .GRN names its own textures in its string table as original authoring paths, and they resolve in texture.pak once matched by STEM rather than by filename -- the authoring names say .bmp where the shipped pak says .tga (WOLF.BMP against WOLF.TGA, SORCERESS_BODY.BMP against SORCERESS_BODY.TGA). Corpus-wide, 2501 of 3749 texture names in models.pak resolve by stem, and every one of the 1035 model entries that names a texture has at least one that resolves, with all names resolving in 816 of them. GLADIATOR resolves 7 of 7, WALDELFE_DARK 14 of 14, BEAR 2 of 2, NOBLE_FEM 2 of 2. So the gap is three joins rather than a missing format: models.gd has no walker branch for MaterialSection or TextureSection, so WHICH texture a submesh wants is unread; mesh_arrays concatenates all submeshes into ONE Godot surface, and one surface cannot carry the three materials GLADIATOR needs; and no loader pulls a model .tga out of texture.pak, formats/texture.gd being terrain-atlas-only and answering a different question. The string table alone is not enough to skip step one -- SOLDIER.GRN lists nine names and all nine are SORCERESS_*, so the table holds more names than the mesh uses. Still genuinely unknown, and none of it blocks a textured NPC: facing is hardcoded 0.0 because no field has been shown to carry it; absolute scale is relative-only, with the port's wolf/elf height ratio at 0.56 against retail's measured 0.66, unexplained; weapons are not drawn because nothing has measured which bone they hang from, though the skeletons do carry Bone_weapon_01 and _02; and root motion is dropped, BIND_POSITION_TRACKS being false.

Creatures are no longer flat clay. Three joins implemented and gated by engine/checks/skin_check.gd, which passes with the other 25. JOIN 1, WHICH texture: Models.texture_names() walks the .GRN's own TextureSection 0xCA5E0304 and each Texture node's DataExtensionReference -- the same two-hop chain bone_names() already used, asking the extension for __FileName instead of __ObjectName. The TextureSection's children run in fours (an 0xCA5E0301 wrapper, an 0xCA5E0305, the Texture, then the reference at rel+12) with a 16-byte stride, measured on GLADIATOR.GRN at 24 children for 6 textures. object_names() is now a one-line call on a shared _extension_values(entry, key) so there is no second copy of the three-level nesting. JOIN 2, WHERE it lives: the names are the artist's authoring paths and the EXTENSION DOES NOT SURVIVE THE BUILD -- ...\animals\wolf\maps\wolf.bmp is WOLF.TGA in texture.pak, SORCERESS_BODY.BMP is SORCERESS_BODY.TGA. Sacred.TextureFormat.find_model_texture() joins on the STEM, with a lazily built stem index keyed on the pak's file size so a different install rebuilds rather than reusing another corpus's map. JOIN 3 is not a new decode: a model skin sits in the same container decode_texture() already read for terrain, u16 w, u16 h, kind 4, zlib from +80, RGBA4444; terrain's 18-diamond atlas geometry does not apply and is not used. SCOPE, deliberately limited: mesh_arrays() concatenates every submesh into ONE Godot surface, so a rig carries one material, and the binding is gated on the file naming EXACTLY ONE texture rather than taking the first name. That covers 1393 of the 1558 mesh entries; GLADIATOR names six over three submeshes and WALDELFE_DARK seven, and those stay clay until MaterialSection/Material 0xCA5E0D01/0xCA5E0D00 get a walker. A confidently wrong skin is worse than no skin. Corpus rate: 1364 of 2082 named textures resolve, 65.5 percent. Wired through PlayerView into both world spawners, so --npcs and --creatures now draw skinned rigs.

Row 882 said the .GRN string table holds more texture names than a mesh uses, citing SOLDIER.GRN as listing nine, all of them SORCERESS_*. That is wrong and the new gate caught it while I was asserting it. Models.strings(), which walks the bounded StringTable node 0xCA5E0200, returns exactly ONE texture-shaped name for SOLDIER.GRN, matching its one Texture node. My nine came from a Python regex over the raw entry bytes, which reads past the StringTable into the rest of the entry. Measured properly, the string table and the Texture nodes agree on the DISTINCT set every time -- SOLDIER 1/1, WOLF 1/1, BEAR 1/1, NOBLE_FEM 1/1, WALDELFE_DARK 7/7, GLADIATOR 3 distinct against 6 nodes. So the node walk does not find names the table lacks; what it adds is ORDER AND MULTIPLICITY, which is the per-material assignment and the reason it is needed at all. skin_check.gd now asserts the set agreement as a cross-check between two readings that share no code path, and separately asserts that GLADIATOR's node count EXCEEDS its distinct count, so the multiplicity the walk exists for cannot silently vanish. The premise was overstated, the conclusion that the node walk is required still holds, and it holds for a different reason than the one I gave.

The material chain is read and multi-skin creatures are textured: GLADIATOR builds 6 surfaces with 6 images, WALDELFE_DARK 7 with 7, and the single-texture creatures 1 with 1. Models.material_groups() reads the ModelSection's draw batches -- 0xCA5E0E02 carries {u32 mesh, u32 material_index ONE-BASED, f32, f32} and the group's own 0xCA5E0E04 carries its triangle count. The check that the fields are what they look like is arithmetic: the group counts sum to the entry's triangle total exactly, 212+230+260+258+350+385 = 1695 for GLADIATOR and 1792 over seven groups for WALDELFE_DARK. A TRAP THE GATE CAUGHT BEFORE IT SHIPPED. The group's mesh number is NOT mesh_arrays()' submesh number. GLADIATOR's groups total {0:442, 1:868, 2:385} per mesh while the reader lays its submeshes out as {0:868, 1:385, 2:442}, and WALDELFE_DARK permutes differently again. Slicing the concatenated index array in group order -- the obvious implementation, and the one I wrote first -- would have skinned the wrong triangles confidently and invisibly to any check comparing only totals. It was caught because skin_check asserts the PER-MESH partition and not just the sum. The two orderings are reconciled by TRIANGLE COUNT, and only when unambiguous: if two submeshes share a face count the mapping is undetermined and the split is refused, falling back to one surface. skin_check now asserts the MULTISETS of counts match (index-to-index comparison is wrong and fails here) and that the counts are distinct, so the reconciliation cannot become a guess. Residual assumption, stated in both the code and the gate: groups of the SAME submesh are taken in file order, unmeasured, so the worst remaining error swaps two batches within one submesh and never across submeshes. 26 of 26 port gates pass. Not every model is skinned even now -- SOLDIER.GRN builds 1 surface with 0 images because soldier_black_cloth1.tga is genuinely absent from texture.pak, one of the 35 percent of names that do not resolve.

Equipment attachment is read, and it is a named socket pair rather than a shared skeleton. Census over all 1571 rigged models.pak entries: Bone_weapon_01 appears as a child of Bip01 R Hand on 235 entries and Bone_weapon_02 as a child of Bip01 L Hand on 192, while on another 206/176 entries the same two names are children of __Root. Zero entries cross -- _01 never hangs off a left hand and _02 never off a right one -- so the two populations are disjoint by parent and one pair of names carries two meanings: 'where I hold it' on a wearer and 'where it is held' on a weapon. Docking is aligning the second to the first, and the port now does exactly that through a BoneAttachment3D with the piece transform set to the grip's inverse. The first attempt composed the piece's own coordinate basis into that transform and applied it twice, landing the sword 18.8 units off the hand while still satisfying its own grip-on-socket identity; the basis is applied once by the body's ModelView above the skeleton, so everything under it is raw model space.

A weapon does NOT share the wearer's skeleton, and the instrument that says otherwise is degenerate. equip_check's local-rest agreement confirmed R1.4 for armour, so it was pointed at the hand meshes startcode gives every armed NPC; it returned median own-agreement 1.0000 and median cross-control 1.0000, the control scoring exactly as well as the subject. Printing the bone NAMES instead of their positions shows why: a weapon carries 3 to 16 bones of its own and shares only __Root and the two socket names with a body, so the handful of matched names were the sockets agreeing with themselves. 199 of the 221 entries carrying a weapon-side grip declare no vertex weights at all -- SWORD.GRN has a MeshWeights node whose span is exactly the 12-byte header -- so a weapon is an unskinned rigid prop on a moving socket. ModelView now builds those as props rather than calling them decode failures, with Models.has_mesh_weights separating 'declares no weights' from 'weights did not decode' so the second stays loud.

Which socket is which hand is measured, not inferred from the number. startcode's tag-0x02 occurrences 1 and 2 are the two hand slots; over the 1111 armed slots the eight classes declare, shields are 58.8 percent of slot 2 against 10.5 percent of slot 1, a 5.6x separation. The structural half is stronger than that rate and is what the gate asserts: all 272 slot-2 meshes carry Bone_weapon_02, while 97 of the 839 slot-1 meshes do not -- the polearms PIKE, SPEAR, HELLEBARDE and STAFF_FIGHT, which have only a main-hand grip. Zero items sit in the off hand without an off-hand grip, which the opposite slot assignment could not produce. Only 192 of 1571 entries carry the off-hand socket at all, so a body lacking it falls back to Bip01 L Hand -- measured coincident with the socket on the two NPC bodies carrying both, but 3.86 units away on the DAEMONIA set, so the fallback is counted and reported rather than treated as equivalent.

Two gated commits shipped with the live world crashing. The material chain replaced ModelView's single mi.material_override with one override material per draw batch; PlayerView still read _mesh.material_override and mutated it, so every rig it builds -- every NPC, every creature, the player -- died on a null instance from commit 315120f onward. All 26 gates passed throughout because nothing in checks/ ever built a PlayerView: the checks covered the reader and the ModelView layer, and the class that composes them had no gate at all. Found by writing the first check that does build one. The lesson is not about materials but about coverage shape -- a per-layer gate suite can be complete at every layer and still miss the seam between two of them, and the seam is where a refactor lands.

Row 886's dock is correct but its FALLBACK was not, and the fallback is withdrawn. Where a wearer names no Bone_weapon_0N, the port substituted the parent hand (Bip01 R/L Hand) on the strength of a position measurement: on the two NPC bodies carrying both, socket and hand sit ~1e-6 apart. A dock uses the whole transform, and the ROTATION does not follow. Over the 441 wearer-side sockets the rest rotation relative to the parent hand is under 15 degrees on 299, 30-60 on 13, and 90-180 on 107 -- right about two thirds of the time and a quarter-turn or worse for a quarter of the corpus, with no way to tell which group a socket-less body belongs to. On SOLDIER it laid a kite shield flat across the character's chest and hid the body behind it, which is how it was noticed: from a screenshot, not from a gate. A wearer with no socket is now refused and counted. The cost is that almost the whole scripted cast goes unarmed -- only 2 of the 49 NPC body meshes name a socket at all -- and the open lead is that the socket turns up on ARMOUR instead (DAEMONIA_ARMOR01_GLOVES carries one), so retail may supply it with the equipped piece rather than the body.

Every character rendered near-invisible for one wrong flag, and the flag had been wrong since the texture join landed the same day. decode_texture(render=true) hands the ARGB4444 payload to Godot as FORMAT_RGBA4444, which rotates every channel by one: measured on Gladiator_body.tga, the render path gives rgb=(1.00,0.41,0.32) a=0.28 where the ARGB path gives rgb=(0.41,0.32,0.28) a=1.00 -- the real alpha arriving as red and the real blue as alpha. Terrain survives it because it samples through its own shader; a StandardMaterial3D does not, and combined with the TRANSPARENCY_ALPHA player_view.gd sets for depth sorting, an average alpha of 0.28 with no fully-opaque pixel made bodies vanish while untextured weapons stayed solid. Correctly decoded the alpha is real: Gladiator and Wolf are fully opaque and Horse carries genuine cutouts. skin_check.gd now asserts the two paths differ by exactly that one-channel rotation, so changing both to the wrong one still fails, and that the ARGB decode is over 95 percent opaque.

The reason characters read as absent in the streamed world is an animation defect that predates the equipment work and is not caused by it. WOLF.GRN under the clip Sacred.Rigs picks for it, WOLF_ATTACK_BH_A, renders as a flattened ribbon with a detached oversized head in --grn= ISOLATION -- no placement, no equipment, no world, no PlayerView -- so the fault is in the clip-to-skeleton binding and nothing downstream. SOLDIER.GRN under SOLD_WALK_BH renders correctly under the same route, so it is per-clip rather than universal, and anim_check passes throughout because it measures a retargeting ratio rather than whether the posed mesh is a body shape. This is rows 609 and 739 unresolved (the clip and the mesh do not share the bone chain above Bip01). A splayed rig is indistinguishable from a missing one at world zoom, which is exactly how it was reported; --npcs-noanim now exists alongside --creatures-noanim so the two can be told apart without a screenshot.
